2000: South-east Asia is a hotspot for sharks and ray diversity while at the same time, threats facing this group of animals. Singapore is recognized as the second largest global trade hub for illegal wildlife trade, which positions Singapore Oceanarium geographically to contribute work that directly impacts sharks and rays’ conservation and research. Taking inspiration from the IUCN SSC Conservation Planning Specialist Group’s ICAP model alongside the WAZA Population Management Goal (27PMG) and applying it at an institutional level, each species is carefully evaluated, assigned defined roles with clear action plans that combine strategic priorities with reactive flexibility. This ensures transparent, science-based planning for long-term success. Singapore Oceanarium’s Institutional Collection Plan (ICP), animal breeding programs, longterm management plans and acquisition and disposition policy for sharks and rays lays the foundation for positive collaborative potential with international organizations, working groups and in-situ conservation programs and projects. The goal is to provide insights and a working model for other aquariums interested in focusing their efforts on sharks and rays, firstly through ex-situ population management and planning followed by direct species conservation in the wild. At a time when over one-third of shark and ray species face extinction, aquariums are uniquely positioned to amplify conservation impact beyond their walls.

2003: India, despite being one of the world’s top three shark-fishing nations and home to 160+ elasmobranch species, has no systematic monitoring of shark landings. The 1OCEAN Citizen Science Project addresses this gap by advancing citizen science-driven shark conservation. A dedicated 1OCEAN citizen science website, first of its kind, was developed to record marine fish landings from fishing harbors, on-board vessels, underwater, fish markets, and beaches. Eight colleges near key shark & bycatch landing centers across three states, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka that make up around one-fourth of Indian coastline were engaged. 300+ undergraduate, graduate, and PhD students from fisheries, marine science, and zoology departments were trained in shark identification, scientific documentation, field data collection methods, and to conduct ethical community surveys with fishers & traders. Trained students conducted surveys at fishing harbors, contributing over 1,500 observations to the 1OCEAN Cit-Sci Portal, establishing one of the largest student-led datasets on shark and bycatch landings in the region. The Cit-Sci initiative led to two publications with five more underway, documenting the scale of shark and bycatch fisheries in regional fishing harbors. This progress demonstrates the potential of citizen science as an effective long-term tool to monitor shark populations & bycatch trends, map trade dynamics, discover new/unrecorded species, and understand the drivers of shark exploitation. Going forward, this initiative will expand across the entire Indian coastline by establishing credit-based collaborations with coastal universities/colleges while further growing the 1OCEAN Youth Network, empowering students to take long-term stewardship of marine conservation.

2008: Large, long-lived marine animals (‘marine megafauna’) - such as sharks, rays and turtles - are amongst the world's most threatened taxa, primarily due to overfishing. Reducing fisheries' impacts on marine megafauna is particularly challenging in small-scale fisheries, where threatened species have consumptive use value for food and income. Incentive-based interventions, such as direct cash transfers or alternative livelihoods, have been proposed as a potential solution, which can motivate pro-conservation behavior while maintaining fishers’ economic security and wellbeing. However, there is limited empirical evidence on how such incentives might be designed for success in practice. We used scenario interviews with contingent valuation to design locally-appropriate conservation incentives – to reduce threats to Critically Endangered elasmobranchs while maintaining or improving fisher wellbeing – in three case study. in Indonesia (located in East Lombok, Sumbawa and Aceh Jaya Regencies). These studies provide empirical evidence that incentive-based approaches can be costeffective and socially-just. Moreover, the methods facilitate fisher participation and co-design of conservation solutions, thus promoting legitimacy and compliance. The findings can be used to inform programs and policies that balance biodiversity goals with local livelihoods, as well as contribute to the broader discourse on incentive-based approaches to conservation.

2009: Batoid rays represent a critical yet vulnerable component of coastal elasmobranch assemblages in India. The sandwich-tail whipray Brevitrygon manjajiae (Dasyatidae) is a recently validated dasyatid species described from the northern Arabian Sea, previously misidentified as B. walga or B. imbricata. This taxonomic clarification has prompted the need to re-examine its distribution, fishery occurrence, and biological characteristics in Indian waters. The present study documents the occurrence and biological aspects of B. manjajiae from trawl bycatch along the Maharashtra coast, eastern Arabian Sea. The species, though forming a minor component of elasmobranch landings, appears consistently in demersal trawl catches and is retained for local consumption, highlighting its economic relevance to small-scale fisheries. Morphometric examination confirms diagnostic characters that differentiate B. manjajiae from its congeners, contributing to improved species identification in fishery-dependent datasets. Preliminary biological observations indicate characteristics typical of dasyatids—low fecundity, extended gestation, and delayed maturity—suggesting high susceptibility to fishing mortality. Species-specific data on size composition, sex ratio, and maturity stages are being used to establish a baseline for assessing its population structure and reproductive potential. Given the increasing conservation concern for batoid rays, such information is vital for accurate catch reporting, resource assessment, and the formulation of region-specific management and conservation strategies. This study contributes to refining the understanding of Brevitrygon diversity in the Arabian Sea and underlines the importance of taxonomic resolution in the sustainable management of elasmobranch fisheries.

2011: Anthropogenic activities continue to alter marine ecosystems with ramifications for how species utilise habitats. For threatened species that rely on few specific habitats for critical ecological functions, understanding how abiotic factors drive site selection forms the basis for conservation management in an uncertain future. The critically endangered sand tiger shark (Carcharias taurus) has only one known gestation aggregation site in Australia: Wolf Rock, Queensland. It is not known why pregnant females spend the majority of their gestation at this site-which is located towards the northern extent of their east Australian distribution-or how physical environment factors, like temperature, drive site use. With the east coast of Australia experiencing one of the highest rates of ocean warming globally, identifying the determinants of site selection is essential for predicting future site viability. Here, we characterised the environmental conditions driving site selection for gestating sand tiger sharks in east Australia. We employed acoustic and satellite telemetry alongside satellite-derived remote sensing to investigate how temperature, and current direction and strength, influences fine-scale horizontal and vertical movements of female sand tiger sharks within the Wolf Rock Marine Protected Area. We supplemented a historical dataset of female sand tiger sharks with additional females tagged at Wolf Rock in 2024. We identified signals of site fidelity during the gestational season and explored seasonal differences in the thermal environment for gestating sharks. Our findings have important implications for the management of this threatened population in the face of global ocean warming.

2012: The Amazonian Coast is a potential stronghold for sawfish (Pristidae). The status of these critically endangered batoids in northeastern South America has become uncertain due to population declines driven by fishing and habitat loss. Along with the presence of unique marine, estuarine, and riverine habitats ideal for sawfish, the lack of information makes this a critical region for research, but it is chronically understudied, largely due to the logistics difficulties in conducting research. For instance, many places can only be accessed by boat or lengthy road travel, so fieldwork is costly and time consuming. The occurrence of multiple countries that speak different languages and dialects contributes to the use of various common names and hinders the sharing of information. Also, these countries often have limited resources available for research, conservation, and the regulation of significant illegal or underregulated commercial fishing. Sawfish captures are known to still occur, whether through recorded sightings, word-of-mouth, or trade, but these are increasingly rare, with fishers across the region reporting limited sightings reliant mostly on trust shown to interviewers. All this renders any work requiring live sawfish or fishery landings extremely challenging. Sawfish parts, mainly rostral teeth, are still valued culturally and in trade, providing an incentive for sawfish bycatch to be kept and sold. Trade is difficult to regulate due to the small size of the teeth and the unfamiliarity of enforcement agents with sawfish parts. Continued research, conservation efforts, and collaboration with local communities to preserve these populations are crucial for sawfish conservation.

2014: Singapore Oceanarium formerly known as the S.E.A. Aquarium has successfully maintained over shark, ray and chimaera species, with success in breeding, research and advancing husbandry practices for the past thirteen years. While our work focuses on education, research, and ex-situ care, the alarming decline of wild populations driven by overfishing, habitat loss, and inadequate enforcement underscores, we have witnessed firsthand the growing urgency of global chondrichthyan conservation within the region. Our experience demonstrates that aquariums can serve as living laboratories, providing critical insights into species biology and life history, husbandry, and welfare that inform conservation strategies. Long-term care has allowed us to gather data on growth rates, reproductive cycles, behavior management and stress responses – information that can complement field research and strengthen NonDetriment Findings (NDFs), bycatch mitigation, and trade regulation frameworks. There is an opportunity to explore how aquariums can bridge gaps between research and policy by sharing practical lessons on species resilience, public engagement, and capacity building. We will highlight how collaborative programs linking aquariums, scientists, and enforcement agencies can translate knowledge into actionable protections, particularly in regions with limited resources. The goal is to share our insights on the species we have, have bred, population dynamics and life history info for sharks and rays within aquariums.
2016: Sharks and rays are experiencing unprecedented global declines, primarily due to overfishing. This is particularly true in data-poor regions as Angola, where small-scale fisheries (SSF) are extensive, weakly documented, and minimally regulated. As protein sources decline and elasmobranch products gain value, SSF increasingly retain sharks and rays, intensifying pressure while widening knowledge gaps. We present the first assessment of shark and ray diversity in southern Angola (2021-2025) using standardized landing surveys and fishers’ interviews. Across seven surveys, ~50,000 individuals were recorded, biological data were collected for ~10,000 animals, including adults, gravid females, and juveniles. Landings from October to December were dominated by Smoothback Angelshark (Squatina oculata), Smoothhound (Mustelus mustelus), Smooth Hammerhead (Sphyrna zygaena), and stingrays (Dasyatis spp.), coinciding with presumed reproductive and feeding aggregations. From March to May, landings shifted toward juveniles, consistent with seasonal recruitment. Fisher interviews (n = 83) attributed observed declines primarily to overlap with industrial fleets and to expanding regional/international trade that increases demand and effort (69% of respondents). Fishers’ observations, combined with landing data, enabled temporal comparisons and strengthened data reliability. These findings deliver the first validated baseline for Angola, identify key species and seasonal patterns, and document rising fishing pressures. Integrating fishers’ knowledge with fishery-dependent monitoring provides actionable evidence to inform national management (e.g., seasonal closures, bycatch mitigation, retention controls), designate critical habitats for protection, and strengthen trade oversight. This baseline establishes a foundation for long-term monitoring and policy and contributes urgently needed information from a historically understudied region. We outline participatory approaches to co-develop measures with communities and agencies, enhancing effective compliance and monitoring.

2017: Illegal trade in shark commodities remains a major challenge for global conservation, driven largely by the international fin trade despite CITES protections. Effective enforcement depends on rapid, species-level identification, yet current forensic methods—primarily DNA barcoding— are slow, costly, and largely inaccessible to officers working in field or customs settings. Here, we investigate dermal-denticle microstructure as a reliable morphological fingerprint for differentiating shark species commonly encountered in international trade. We are developing a standardized reference library of denticle images from verified museum and research specimens, incorporating skin from multiple body regions to assess intra-body variation and ensure broad applicability. Machine-learning models trained on these curated datasets will be evaluated for accuracy, robustness across skin regions, and suitability for real-world enforcement contexts, with the goal of integrating these classifiers into a portable microscope-based identification system. This work aims to deliver an accessible, scalable identification tool to support customs agencies, fisheries authorities, and conservation practitioners in improving traceability and strengthening compliance with CITES regulations. It will contribute to more effective protection of CITES-listed shark species while providing a foundation for future applications to rays.

2018: Accurate species delineation is fundamental to conservation, as biodiversity cannot be protected if it is not correctly recognised. Over the past three decades, molecular studies on elasmobranchs have uncovered hundreds of cryptic lineages. During this same period, global chondrichthyan populations have declined sharply, raising the risk that species may be pushed to extinction before they are discovered. This is notably the case in Eastern Africa, where elasmobranchs are harvested but molecular reference data remain sparse. In this framework, we undertook a molecular survey of batoids from Tanzanian landing sites, performing de novo species delimitation to establish regional molecular references. Using the Oxford Nanopore platform, we generated multi-locus data by sequencing a mitochondrial amplicon spanning the ND2 and COI genes, together with the nuclear gene RAG1. These sequences were analysed using multiple delimitation approaches to infer species boundaries. Mitochondrial amplicons were further used to retrieve putatively conspecific sequences from global databases through a newly developed, empirically calibrated pipeline. All mitochondrial data were then integrated into an ND2/COI supermatrix, enabling a secondary, tree-based delimitation across the expanded dataset. Across all analyses, species were identified. The resulting delimitations resolved several long-standing taxonomic ambiguities in Western Indian Ocean batoids. Molecular evidence clarified cases where morphological variation had obscured species boundaries, exposed historical misidentifications, and revealed a previously unrecognised cryptic species. Together, these findings establish the first integrated molecular baseline for batoid diversity in Tanzania and demonstrate the value of combining long-read sequencing, database mining, and multi-locus species delimitation to uncover overlooked diversity.

2019: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) hosts a high diversity of chondrichthyans, yet many species and their critical habitats have historically been poorly documented. To address these knowledge gaps, early multi-sector collaborative efforts surveyed areas locally recognized as important for elasmobranchs and supported the identification of Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs) in the UAE. Pressing challenges in these areas now require a transition from ISRA identification to the implementation of evidence-based management actions and actionable marine policy. To support this shift, we expanded our field surveys using environmental DNA, baited remote underwater videos, and targeted dive surveys across ISRAs. Results revealed higher elasmobranch diversity than previously reported (15 species), direct evidence of reproduction (including pregnant individuals and egg cases), and species aggregations, strengthening the ecological significance of ISRAs and their value for informing spatial planning. In the UAE, ISRAs are already guiding management decisions. For example, the overlap between an ISRA and a marine protected area adjacent to an urbanised coastline, has prompted discussions on mitigating impacts and refining management priorities. In another case, ISRA-aligned evidence directly informed the closure of one-third of a coastal lagoon to fishing to protect critical habitats for elasmobranch and other megafauna. These early successes illustrate how ISRAs can strengthen the effectiveness of existing MPAs and guide practical conservation actions in rapidly changing seascapes. More broadly, ISRAs provide a robust framework for integrating biodiversity priorities into national planning and ensuring that elasmobranch conservation remains central to sustainable coastal development in the UAE.

2020: Understanding threatened elasmobranch distribution is critical for developing effective area based management. However, our knowledge of fine scale elasmobranch habitat association and distribution in temperate nearshore systems is limited. Here, we examined the presence, relative abundance and habitat association of sharks, skates and rays using benthic baited remote underwater stereo-video systems (SBRUVs). From deployments (682 total hours, minutes average soak time) across three years (2021-2023) and two Scottish sea lochs and adjacent bays with varying levels of marine conservation protection, elasmobranchs were detected on 31.2% of deployments (n = 241). Our surveys detected six species of elasmobranchs, flapper skate (Dipturus intermedius), thornback ray (Raja clavata), spotted ray (Raja montagui), lesser spotted dogfish (Scyliorhinus canicula), spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) and porbeagle (Lamna nasus) representing 17.6% of the resident elasmobranch diversity reported to date in UK nearshore waters < m depth. The species detected include two species listed as globally Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, spiny dogfish and porbeagle and one Critically Endangered species, flapper skate. Critically Endangered flapper skate were detected in 5.2% deployments (n = 40) and were the only species recorded which did not show a relationship between the probability of presence and substratum type. Our findings provide critical data on the fine scale spatial distribution, habitat association of elasmobranchs, which could be used to inform evidence-based area conservation measures and support more consistent and targeted policy action for these species in Scotland.
2022: The whale shark (Rhincodon typus), the largest extant fish species, remains poorly understood in key aspects of its biology and life history, particularly regarding reproduction and early developmental stages. Neonate whale sharks, defined as individuals under 1.5 metres in length, are exceptionally rare and infrequently recorded. Between 2014 and 2025, the Maldives Whale Shark Research Programme (MWSRP) compiled verified records of neonate encounters within Maldivian waters, reported primarily by local fishers and citizen scientists. These observations underscore the scientific value of fisher knowledge and the need for a standardised framework to ensure proper documentation and safe handling of neonates. In response, MWSRP developed a bilingual (Dhivehi and English) illustrated policy booklet outlining a protocol for the documentation and release of neonate whale sharks when extraction is unavoidable. Funded through an Artist Partnership scholarship from Creature Conserve, the project integrates scientific research with visual science communication to enhance understanding and accessibility. Detailed illustrations and visual sequences convey procedural guidance suitable for audiences across varying literacy levels, while culturally relevant imagery reflects Maldivian fishing traditions and local ecological knowledge. This initiative exemplifies how interdisciplinary collaboration can improve data collection methodologies, strengthen participatory conservation, and advance the application of visual communication in marine science. The resulting protocol provides a replicable model for integrating community engagement and evidence-based management in the conservation of endangered marine megafauna.
2023: Ecuador’s groundbreaking debt-for-nature-conversion in 2023 funds the protection of the marine natural capital of the Galapagos Islands and supports community sustainable initiatives. This financial deal is the world’s largest debt conversion for marine conservation to date: it issued a marine-conservation blue bond to restructure $1.6 billion of commercial debt with savings of over $1 billion in lifetime debt service for the country. Further, it is projected to generate about US$ million for marine protection and sustainable ocean management over the next years — including a growing endowment, through the Galápagos Life Fund. A strong political will together with key public and private partners, national and international, made the transaction a reality. The motivation behind exploring a sustainable financial mechanism started with the establishment of a new marine protected area — the Hermandad Marine Reserve (60,000 km²) — explicitly to protect endangered sharks and sea turtles by covering crucial migratory corridors between Galápagos and Cocos Island, Costa Rica. For this reason, the deal structure involves not only financing but also legal, governance and conservation commitments: monitoring, enforcement, fisheries regulation, vessel-monitoring systems, restrictions on certain fishing gear (e.g. limits on fish-aggregating devices and observer requirements) — all relevant to reducing shark bycatch and protecting shark habitat. The Galapagos deal is widely recognized as a blended-finance innovative model, coupling sovereign debt relief and marine conservation funding, and has high potential replicability for other countries with critical marine ecosystems, threatened marine species and goals for a sustainable blue economy.

2024: Whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) are globally Endangered, yet their ecology in the Gulf of Oman remains poorly known despite growing human pressures. After identifying the Seeb Coast as a potential seasonal aggregation site, we conducted the first focused field programme in June 2025 to establish baseline information on population structure, habitat use, movements, and threats. Over days of boat-based surveys, we photo-identified individual sharks, contributing to a national catalogue of sharks recorded since 2007, which was collated by Shakwatch Arabia. Most individuals encountered (81.5 %) during the 2025 fieldwork were immature males (4-7 m), consistent with global aggregation patterns. Feeding events were often associated with dense slicks of floating fish eggs. Photo-identification data were crossreferenced with Sharkbook.ai, revealing movements between the study area, the Musandam region (Oman) and Qatar’s Al Shaheen field. Nine MiniPAT satellite tags were deployed to examine horizontal and vertical movements. Early-released tags documented offshore travel, deep dives exceeding 1600 m, and distinct coastal and offshore depth-use patterns. Threat assessments showed a high incidence of vessel-strike injuries (50%) and additional evidence of fishing-gear interactions, underscoring significant conservation concern. Extensive engagement with government agencies, universities, tourism operators, and the public fostered strong national support for whale shark protection. Collectively, these initial results confirm the Seeb Coast as a regionally important area for whale sharks and provide essential baseline data to guide threat mitigation, sustainable tourism management, and long-term conservation planning in Oman.

2027: Northwestern Australia is thought to have some of the world’s last remaining viable sawfish populations, although little quantitative data exists on their status or trends. This study examined years of logbook bycatch records (n = 815) for green sawfish Pristis zijsron and narrow sawfish Anoxypristis cuspidata from a trawl fishery operating on the Australian North West Shelf. Incidental sawfish captures by the fishery are rare, occurring approximately once every trawls (~199 trawl hours). To standardize catch rates and account for excess zeros in the data, we employed generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSSs) using a zero-inflated Poisson distribution. For green sawfish, catch rates approximately doubled over the study period, while an oscillating trend was observed for narrow sawfish catch rates. Reported captures occurred throughout the management boundaries of the fishery, which operates in mid-shelf waters from to m. A weak seasonal signal in catch rates was detected for both species, with the highest capture numbers occurring during autumn–winter, consistent with an expected inshore migration for parturition during spring–summer. Logbook trends were partly corroborated by independently verified data collected in a subset of years, which also showed an increasing proportion of green sawfish in the catch. Our findings emphasize the importance of sawfish populations in northwestern Australia within the context of global conservation efforts for this taxon.

2028: The global fin trade poses a significant threat to shark populations; many species of shark are at risk of extinction due to overfishing and unsustainable practices. This study examines the fin trade in Singapore, a globally significant fin trading hub, market and transit point. Using DNA barcoding techniques, we attempted to determine the species of origin for processed fins that could not be identified by visual techniques. Fins were collected from a variety of outlets across Singapore. We identified species, eight of which were identified as threatened on the IUCN Red List of threatened species (critically threatened n = 2, endangered n = & vulnerable n = 2). Of all the samples we identified to the species or genus level, (12 species and entire genus) are listed on CITES Appendix II. This listing means that international trade has to be controlled to prevent further population declines and utilisation incompatible with their survival. Ninety-eight percent of all the identifications made in this work belonged to species that are listed on CITES Appendix II. Demonstrating the importance of regular and repeated monitoring, we identified the blackchin guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus); this is the first occurrence of fins from this species within Singapore and the wider Southeast Asian region. This is a CITES Appendix II listed species and one that has been designated as critically endangered by the IUCN. Without repeated monitoring, the presence of this species in Singapore would likely have gone undetected.

2029: The Brownbanded bamboo shark (Chiloscyllium punctatum) is one of the most frequently landed elasmobranch species in Malaysia, yet its biological characteristics remain poorly documented. This study examined the age structure and growth parameters of C. punctatum from the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia between June 2022 and June 2023. A total of individuals were sampled from local landing sites. The vertebral centra were burned and examined to estimate age based on the count of opaque growth zones. Eight distinct age classes were identified, indicating a broad representation of sub-adult to mature individuals in the fishery. Growth was described using the von Bertalanffy growth function LT = 82.67 [1 – exp (–0.36 (t – 0.94))], suggesting that C. punctatum is a moderately growing species of small coastal sharks. The growth parameters reported here are consistent with patterns observed in other Indo-Pacific populations and provide important baseline information for stock assessments. This study represents the first detailed age and growth analysis of C. punctatum in Malaysia. The findings contribute essential biological data needed to inform conservation planning, sustainable harvest guidelines, and long-term management strategies for this increasingly exploited species.

2031: Human wildlife conflict has been well-characterized on land, with decades-long examinations on the effectiveness of coexistence solutions on communities and vulnerable species. In the marine space, however, this research is sparse and primarily centered on mitigating humanshark interactions to avoid shark bites. Limited research has examined human wildlife conflict in fisheries, or the negative impacts on both humans and sharks from their interactions. Our research in Pacific Islands countries shows that small-scale coastal communities, who have limited adaptive capacity and rely on fisheries for food security and livelihoods, face reduced catches, income loss, and social conflict from shark depredation. Frustrated by the loss of gear and food, fishers often retaliate by killing sharks, including species threatened with extinction like the Oceanic Whitetip Sharks and Silky Sharks that are banned from retention in industrial tuna fisheries. Fisheries issues are exacerbated by climate change, which is altering ocean temperatures and currents, shifting shark and fish distributions, and increasing the frequency of negative shark–fisher interactions. Lacking the necessary ecological, socioeconomic, and cultural considerations, solutions proposed to coastal communities to tackle food security and climate-induced impacts, like advocating for additional fish aggregating devices or more MPAs, are compounding problems for fishers and sharks. This talk gives an overview of and introduction to human wildlife conflict between sharks and artisanal fishers in Pacific Islands communities. We will highlight the multifaceted research that is both necessary and underway to co-develop mitigation solutions with communities in the Pacific to promote coexistence of both sharks and artisanal fisheries.

2033: There is growing interest in establishing shark and ray awareness initiatives in Seychelles, driven by diverse local stakeholders. While education remains a critical tool for raising awareness, it faces limitations, particularly in achieving long-term engagement and securing sustained funding. The Save Our Seas Foundation - Island School Seychelles (SOSF - ISS) seeks to address these challenges by fostering dialogue and promoting new narratives that move beyond the often-intimidating image of sharks and rays, reaching across age groups and communities. The flagship program of SOSF - ISS, The D’Arros Experience, will mark its fifth year of operation in 2026. Designed to immerse young Seychellois in the ecosystems that form part of our national heritage, it offers hands-on field learning in the ecological hotspot and open-air classroom of D’Arros Island and St Joseph Atoll. Over five years, the program has tracked key indicators to evaluate its effectiveness and guide future development. These include school participation trends and the factors influencing them; gender representation; follow-ups with alumni to assess how many pursue related studies or careers; applicant retention and reapplication patterns; levels of continued involvement through alumni activities; barriers to participation; and the cumulative outreach hours delivered. This presentation will reflect on successes, adaptive improvements, and areas needing further growth. By synthesising five years of data and experience, we aim to inform the future direction of The D’Arros Experience and broader conservation education efforts in Seychelles, while contributing to a global exchange of ideas among environmental educators.

Vertical movements varied between males and females and TL had opposing effects on surface use between the sexes, which decreased with TL in females and increased with TL in males. Vertical movements varied offshore with higher incidence of reverse diel vertical migration and increased deep diving in both sexes and greater surface use in females. 2038: Effective elasmobranch monitoring in Northeast Atlantic waters has been constrained by limited historical data and the lack of dedicated monitoring programs. This project evaluates environmental DNA (eDNA) as a cost effective, scalable approach for monitoring elasmobranchs in coastal, inshore environments. We conducted fine scale eDNA surveys around Galway Bay, an Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA) in the West of Ireland, sampling weekly for three weeks in May/June of 2024 and 2025. At each site, we deployed three passive “metaprobe” eDNA samplers for hours. These inexpensive 3D printed devices are filled with absorbent material, which captures DNA. Concurrently we filtered 6L of water using 0.45µm pore Sterivex filters to compare active and passive sampling performance. All samples were sequenced using the elasmobranch targeting Elas02 primer set. To improve taxonomic resolution and accurate species assignment, we developed a curated mitogenome reference database by sequencing and assembling regional species. We further validated our workflow in an aquarium system, where both sampling approaches detected all six species present, and accurately ranked species biomass (Spearman's ρ ≈ 0.86–0.90). Preliminary results from our 2024 dataset detected elasmobranch species at one site, with weekly shifts in community composition. Metaprobe replicates alone detected of these species. Processing of the remaining sites is underway and will be integrated into the discussion. This work aims towards developing a transferable, cost-efficient workflow for coastal elasmobranch eDNA monitoring using emerging sampling tools.

2039: There is a long culinary tradition of eating sharks across many countries with varying degrees of labeling reliability. Throughout Commonwealth countries and mainland Europe, smaller bodied coastal sharks are often used for fish and chips and marketed with generic names (e.g. ‘flake’, ‘rock salmon’, ‘bull huss’). These generic names highlight the degree to which species are substitutable in many supply chains and end markets, making it difficult to estimate the footprint of particular dishes. Here we examine the global footprint of fisheries and trade for species used for fish and chips (Galeorhinus galeus, Squalus spp., Mustelus spp., and Scyliorhinus spp.) To estimate the effects of fisheries and supply chains we used species specific estimates of landings and trade from the Global Shark Meat project and the ARTIS seafood trade database combined with a literature search of culinary traditions. Estimates of landings and trade were then compared with the range weighted IUCN Red List Indices for fishing countries. We find that many European countries exhibit a higher consumer red list score than producer red list score for fish and chips species, suggesting that they are sourcing their products from countries with lower capacity for fisheries management and trade enforcement. These findings will help refine efforts for CITES implementation and compliance in light of recent listing of species in the fish n chips trade.

2041: The Baited Remote Underwater Video (BRUV) system has proven itself worldwide as an attractive tool that provides valuable scientific repeatability and is easy to implement from a technical standpoint. However, constraints mainly related to the autonomy of video systems and the storage of large images effectively limit usage time and collection efforts. These limitations can be very detrimental in a context where the targets of olfactory attraction are found in very limited densities, which is the case for elasmobranchs in the Mediterranean Sea. In this context, Shark Med association has developed a first type of low-cost BRUVs, adapted to sampling efforts in pelagic environments (surface and water column) without human input: the BRUV-24h. This device has made it possible to contribute complementary information from fishery-independent techniques on the blue shark Prionace glauca populations around the Balearic Islands. Deep Mediterranean habitats are also an important conservation issue and have led the NGO to develop a DEEP-BRUV-48h capable of filming continuosly for two days at depths of over m. This low-cost technology has made it possible to collect unprecedented information on the bluntnose sixgill shark Hexanchus griseus, a deep-sea species that scarcely swims in shallow waters.

2042: The crocodile shark Pseudocarcharias kamoharai is one of the least studied lamniform sharks, with major gaps in knowledge on its life history, reproduction, and distribution. Most global records arise from isolated by catch events or single landings, gives limited information to understand population structure and ecological patterns. In India, the records are majorly from East Coast and only one report from West Coast landed by the different fishing gears with a very small sample sizes, restricting robust assessments of this species in the Indian Ocean. In this context, the present study provides the largest regional dataset of more than individuals landed between 2022-2025 in Kakinada Fish Landing Center, Andhra Pradesh on the eastern coast of India. This represents the most comprehensive and continuous record of P.kamoharai from the region. Notably, the dataset includes approximately gravid females, marking the highest concentration of reproductive individuals ever documented from Indian waters and suggesting the potential importance of the Bay of Bengal as a reproductive habitat or migratory pathway. The size distribution spans early juveniles to mature adults, indicating multi stage utilization of the region. The recurrent presence of gravid individuals, coupled with consistent bycatch in gillnets and trawls net fisheries, provides new evidence that the eastern Indian Ocean may support critical life history functions previously undocumented. Given, the species IUCN status as Least Concern but with significant knowledge gaps, our findings emphasize the necessity for coordinated regional monitoring, dedicated life history research and integration of ecological and genetic approaches.

2043: The promotion of crude shark cartilage as a cancer cure has produced two major adverse consequences: accelerated declines in global shark populations and the diversion of patients from evidence-based treatments. A central claim driving such use—the alleged absence of cancer in sharks—remains scientifically unfounded. Benign and cancerous neoplasms in sharks and their chondrichthyan relatives were documented in the 19th century and continue to be reported. We previously summarized, and added new cases to, a dataset comprising chondrichthyan species exhibiting 40+ distinct tumor types. As of 2025, the number of verified cases exceeds 50, underscoring that chondrichthyans are not immune to cancer. Additional rationales for shark cartilage consumption arise from misinterpretations of studies identifying antiangiogenic compounds in cartilage. Current evidence does not support the therapeutic efficacy of crude cartilage extracts, nor does it demonstrate bioactive molecules that can be delivered in vivo at concentrations capable of eradicating cancer cells. The persistence of the belief that shark cartilage can cure cancer exemplifies the broader societal risks posed by pseudoscience, particularly when paired with commercially motivated misinformation. Framing recent reports of shark cancers within a triad of interacting factors—(1) efficient modern harvesting technologies, (2) the reach/influence of mass media, and (3) public susceptibility to pseudoscientific claims—will illustrate how these forces magnify the ecological consequences of shark cartilage promotion. Addressing these intertwined issues through evidence-based dialogue will equip chondrichthyan researchers and conservation advocates with a shared framework to counter misinformation and to advance sustainable strategies that support both human health and marine biodiversity.

2047: Local ecological knowledge (LEK) is a powerful tool for understanding long-term ecological change, particularly for data-limited species. To harness this knowledge for conservation planning around the Isle of Man, we conducted in-person semi-structured interviews with recreational boat, shore, pier, and charter anglers across the island. Using purposive snowball sampling, participants were recommended by fellow anglers as highly knowledgeable, ensuring we captured insights from the most experienced individuals. Interviews explored: (1) demographics, (2) species composition, (3) spatial and temporal patterns, (4) motivations and drivers, (5) conservation perceptions. Evidence of breeding, perceived population trends, changes in fish communities and perceived threats to local populations were also explored. Anglers reported substantial ecological change over their fishing lifetimes, including marked declines in shark abundance, body size, prey communities, and a pronounced reduction in fish availability. Participants consistently attributed these changes to commercial fishing pressures and offered crucial historical context for understanding local population trajectories. Anglers also offered crucial insights into evidence of breeding for Critically Endangered tope shark. Across interviews, anglers expressed strong support for conservation, enthusiasm for sharks, and a clear willingness to contribute to research. This study highlights the significant value of LEK in addressing critical knowledge gaps for Isle of Man elasmobranchs, identifying key areas and species of interest. The insights gained here will directly inform the design of conservation research - including BRUV surveys and acoustic telemetry planning - ensuring that future monitoring and management strategies are driven by both community expertise and the conservation priorities identified.

2049: Understanding the population genetic structure of blue sharks (Prionace glauca) is critical for effective management and conservation, yet existing studies often rely on invasive techniques, including tissue biopsies from captured sharks. Non-invasive sampling approaches offer a promising alternative to traditional methods, enabling broader participation, including collaboration with fishers and the tourism industry, who regularly encounter blue sharks, to facilitate large-scale population studies. In this study, we evaluated the efficacy of a novel noninvasive method to collect genetic material from free-swimming blue sharks in the Celtic Sea, United Kingdom. Epidermal swabs and fin clippings were collected from sharks, and total genomic DNA was extracted. Regions of both mitochondrial and nuclear DNA were successfully amplified, and additional sequences from other genomic regions were incorporated to assess genetic diversity. Results across all markers confirmed low genetic differentiation between regions, supporting previous evidence of global panmixia in blue sharks. Correct identification of sequences from the same individuals demonstrates the potential of this method for genetic mark-recapture studies. To further enhance field applicability, we incorporated in situ nanopore sequencing to demonstrate remote sequencing capabilities, reducing the need to transport samples away from collection sites. This approach highlights the feasibility of integrating noninvasive sampling with on-site genomic analysis, providing a resource-efficient strategy for large-scale genetic studies.

2053: Global commitments such as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM GBF) call for gender responsive conservation, yet marine governance continues to overlook women's roles, particularly in shark and ray capture and processing. Although women rarely participate in shark and ray capture, they play essential roles in pre-harvest preparation, post-harvest processing, and local trade in small-scale fisheries, while their involvement in commercial fisheries is concentrated in post-harvest work. Despite this, their potential contributions to shark and ray conservation remain poorly integrated into policy. This study draws on bycatch landing data in commercial bottom trawl fisheries (2019-2024), a socioeconomic survey (20222024), and qualitative interviews with key stakeholders to examine gendered labor dynamics in the wedgefish and guitarfish bycatch of Rembang District, Indonesia. Over 12,000 critically endangered individuals were recorded over five years, with more than 80% below maturity size, indicating severe conservation challenges. Men dominate vessel operations and make bycatchrelease decisions, but motivations differ: captains tend to release due to regulatory awareness, while crew members release very small individuals because their market value is negligible. In contrast, women processors often prefer smaller sharks and rays as they are easier to handle, smoke, and prepare for the local market, creating a gendered divergence in valuation and use of bycatch. Women sustain household economies through these microenterprises, yet their labor remains undervalued and excluded from governance. These findings underscore the need for gender-responsive management that recognizes women's contributions, addresses differing incentives across the value chain, and links livelihood security with effective elasmobranch conservation.

2057: Across the Western Indian Ocean (WIO), a broad body of scientific evidence, from BRUVS to fishers dialogues, catch-landing monitoring and two decades of underwater visual census data, demonstrates a sharp and ongoing decline in elasmobranch populations. Consequently, scientific knowledge is advancing faster than policy mechanisms can absorb it. A coordinated regional approach is therefore essential. 2060: Three decades of shark conservation in the Philippines reveal a dynamic interplay of science, policy, civil society, and sheer persistence. 2061: Global climate change is expected to intensify environmental variability in the world’s oceans, altering the predictability of habitats and the distribution of prey resources. These changes are particularly consequential for migratory marine predators whose movements and foraging success are tightly coupled to climate driven prey availability. In dynamic environments, like the open ocean, individuals may employ different behavioral strategies to optimize foraging success. Site fidelity, the tendency to return to a previously visited area, is one such strategy that may confer advantages by allowing individuals to exploit familiar habitats and resources. Salmon sharks (Lamna ditropis) exhibit broad-scale seasonal fidelity across the northeastern Pacific yet show high intraspecific variation in individual movement patterns. This combination of demonstrated capacity for fidelity and substantial individual variability makes them an ideal species for investigating how behavioral strategies are shaped by environmental stability. 2067: Shark conservation in the Eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP) varies widely among countries, despite the region’s shared ecological importance and international commitments. This study evaluates the strength of national shark regulations across ten ETP countries by compiling all sharkrelated norms in force and assigning each country a protection score based on whether their legislation is conservation-oriented, mixed, or primarily fisheries-based. A positive correlation was found between participation in international agreements and stronger domestic frameworks. When incorporating exportation data, countries with lower protection scores tended to export more shark products or maintain less restrictive trade pathways, suggesting a gap between formal commitments and actual management outcomes. As a recommendation, future regional efforts could benefit from more consistent definitions of fisheries terms to reduce ambiguity, but the main finding remains the clear link between weak protection frameworks and higher export activity.

2069: Automation is key to scaling research beyond anecdotal data. Yet this remains challenging-especially for video-based surveys that produce large volumes of data. Once recorded, the central task is to extract relevant information before analysis can begin--typically through detection, classification when needed, tracking, and trajectory correction to maintain individual identities. This facilitates novel approaches to monitoring, conflict mitigation, and policy making. With TRex, we designed a software that supports each of these steps, enabling generalized, video-based, markerless multi-animal tracking--from small behavioral assays to thousands of individuals in large laboratory arenas, and drone surveys in the wild. The solution has been demonstrated to be effective with sharks, rays, and other similar systems. In this talk, I will highlight the potential of combining drones with automated analysis and introduce our open-source tool by demonstrating its capabilities and examples of successful applications in ongoing and completed studies. The talk is structured to convey practical insights beyond a single software solution, offering guidance for everyday research workflows from recording to analysis. Sensor proliferation shifts the bottleneck from collection to interpretation; our approach shows one adaptable way to meet this challenge in any data-rich field. As the world keeps moving towards quantitative studies across fields, let us not get left behind.

2072: In Kakinada, understanding sharks, rays, and rhino rays has meant sitting on boats, walking landing sites, and listening closely to fishers, traders, and other stakeholders who know these waters and the trade best. 2073: The California Current Large Marine Ecosystem (CCLME) is a highly productive upwelling zone of ecological and economic importance along the west coast of North America and is home to the broadnose sevengill shark (Notorynchus cepedianus; BSS), a large, high-order marine predator found in temperate coastal waters worldwide. 2074: Large marine predators play essential roles in pelagic ecosystems, shaping food webs through both direct predation and non-consumptive effects. However, the size-structured nature of these interactions remains poorly understood, particularly for pelagic sharks whose early life stages are rarely observed. Unlike many coastal species that use well-defined nurseries, juvenile pelagic sharks occupy vast, dynamic environments where prey availability and predation risk are difficult to quantify. By classifying wildlife into juvenile-prey, adult-prey, and non-prey size categories, we construct “pelagic preyscapes” that reveal insights into how prey availability and predation risk may shift throughout life stages. Our findings offer rare empirical insights into early life stage ecology in pelagic sharks and demonstrate the central role of body size in shaping ecological interactions, highlight the importance of integrating size structure and ontogeny into conservation planning and developing size-explicit benchmarks for monitoring.

2084: Elasmobranchs are among the most threatened vertebrate groups worldwide, yet conservation and management remain limited by fragmented and geographically uneven data. Addressing these gaps requires a structured approach to identify and prioritise research needs; this is essential where financial and logistical resources are limited. The SharkScape project responds to this challenge by developing a generalisable research-priority framework for nine focal species, presented here using the central and northern North Sea, Orkney, and Shetland as a case study. We undertook a systematic literature review to identify knowledge gaps across lifehistory, ecological, genetic, and management domains. Spatial datasets from fisheries surveys, tagging programmes, industry sources, and citizen science initiatives were standardised, validated, and mapped to establish confirmed presence across regional and local scales. In parallel, a structured gap analysis organised the literature by species, topic, and geographic coverage to determine where biological and ecological information was lacking. To prioritise these gaps, we developed a Biological Vulnerability Index integrating life-history, ecological, and genetic traits, alongside a four-tier framework ranking research parameters by their management value. Feasibility was incorporated through a presence-weighting factor, ensuring that priority gaps were only elevated where species occur often enough to support viable research. Finally, we aligned biological priorities with conservation status and listing frameworks to integrate intrinsic vulnerability with existing or emerging policy obligations. Together, this framework provides a transparent and transferable approach for identifying high-impact evidence needs and demonstrates how priority gaps can vary across spatial scales, offering a robust foundation for targeted research and conservation planning.

2090: Maintaining buoyancy is essential for many aquatic species to regulate their vertical position in the water column. While most pelagic fishes have a swim bladder that can be adjusted to regulate buoyancy, sharks lack such a gas-filled organ. Most species are negatively buoyant and only rely on their large lipid-rich liver and active locomotion to generate lift. Carcharias taurus, a large shark distributed in coastal waters worldwide, is the only shark species known to gulp atmospheric air to hold in their stomachs. Although this behavior has been speculated to provide buoyancy control, the underlying drivers and implications of this behavior have not been investigated. Our study assessed the prevalence of air gulping in Carcharias taurus and the energetic and behavioral consequences of this behavior, especially regarding buoyancy control. To this end, eight C. taurus individuals were fitted with high-resolution acceleration data loggers in Delaware, USA, for periods of 1-4 days. Body posture and relative energetic expenditure were estimated from the acceleration data and used to assess buoyancy dynamics following the gulping events recorded. Movement metrics such as tailbeat period and path tortuosity were derived and used to classify discrete behavioral phases to investigate the behavioral implications of gulping. Preliminary data revealed a steep increase in buoyancy following gulping events, and that C. taurus can retain gulped air in their stomach for at least hours. These results support our hypothesis that air gulping by C. taurus is a unique strategy to perform buoyancy control among sharks.

2091: Insufficient data is a major challenge in conservation, particularly in the Eastern Mediterranean where research and historical records are scarce. Citizen science offers an efficient, costeffective, and non-intrusive tool for gathering information on species abundance, trends, and distributions. This study compiled photographed encounters of elasmobranchs along the shallow Israeli coast (0–40 m), reported between 2014–2023 by divers, fishermen, and other sea enthusiasts. Each verified observation was added to a database with date, location, species, sex, reproduction status, and environmental details. Around contributors reported 5,400 observations of five shark and seventeen ray species. We identified a gradual shift in community composition from south to north, likely driven by habitat differences. Distinct seasonal patterns emerged, with some species aggregating mainly in spring (e.g., Dasyatis pastinaca), others more common in autumn (e.g., Aetomylaeus bovinus, Rhinoptera marginata), and some present year-round (e.g., Taeniurops grabatus, Himantura spp.). Temporal trends over the past decade suggest possible recovery in several species, while others showed no clear increase. This study provides the first regional-scale description of species composition, seasonal distribution, and temporal dynamics along the Israeli coast, revealing a community structure distinct from the Western Mediterranean and supporting the identification of key sites for protection, such as reproduction and aggregation areas.

2101: Reef-associated shark populations have strongly declined globally, mainly due to fisheries and habitat degradation. In large parts of the Caribbean, status and movement ecology of shark species that use coral reefs during at least one life stage remain largely unknown. This longterm study focuses on tracking individual behaviour of reef-associated sharks with acoustic telemetry to determine their movement ecology at different scales. A network of acoustic receivers was deployed on the reefs around Saba, St Eustatius, St Maarten and the Saba Bank in the northeast Caribbean. Small marine parks are present around Saba, St Eustatius and St Maarten. The large “Yarari” marine mammal and shark sanctuary encompasses the Saba Bank, Saba, St Eustatius reefs and the pelagic waters in between these reefs. Since 2014, sharks were implanted with acoustic transmitters (V16/V16p, InnovaSea): Caribbean Reef Shark Carcharhinus perezi, Nurse Shark Ginglymostoma cirratum, Tiger Shark Galeocerdo cuvier and Silky Shark Carcharhinus falciformis. Juvenile and adult Caribbean reef sharks, and juvenile nurse sharks showed strong residency within relatively small home ranges. Juvenile silky sharks mainly occupied one site on the Saba Bank. adult nurse sharks and juvenile tiger sharks showed higher mobility and shorter lasting residency. Larger scale movements between reefs separated by deep waters (>500m) were observed for adult Caribbean Reef sharks, often short and directed back-and-forth trips, juvenile silky sharks, adult nurse sharks and juvenile tiger sharks. The results of this study have implications for assessing the effectiveness of marine protected areas.

2103: Sharks are apex predators that play a vital role in structuring marine ecosystems, yet their populations are increasingly threatened by anthropogenic stressors such as fishing, pollutants, and habitat degradation. Traditional measures of stress in sharks have relied on corticosteroids, but these are difficult to quantify in elasmobranchs, emphasizing the need for alternative biomarkers. We investigated stress physiology in four species that inhabit a highly urbanized estuarine system, Tampa Bay: Bonnethead Shark (Sphyrna tiburo), Blacknose Shark (Carcharhinus acronotus), Blacktip Shark (Carcharhinus limbatus), and Atlantic Sharpnose Shark (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae). Plasma samples were analyzed for metabolic (ketones) and oxidative (malondialdehyde) stress markers, and compared to proteome profiles generated by LC-MS/MS (Mass spectrometry). We identified over proteins, including acute phase proteins, enzymes involved in glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, and proteins linked to lipid and biotin metabolism. Principal component analysis revealed species-, size-, and sex-specific proteomic variation, with several proteins significantly correlated with ketone and oxidized lipid levels. These findings provide the first plasma proteome profiles for these four shark species, identify candidate protein biomarkers of metabolic and oxidative stress, and suggest physiological mechanisms that may underlie differences in life history and ecological resilience. Our results establish a foundation for developing non-lethal, protein-based metrics of shark health in disturbed coastal ecosystems.
2104: Sharks, rays, and skates (elasmobranchs) are experiencing global population declines, leading to increasing concern over the impacts of target fishing and bycatch on their populations. Globally, elasmobranchs are often sold under general or misleading seafood labels, leading to confusion about species identity and often inhibits proper enforcement and traceability for these species along the seafood supply chain. Therefore, it is important to increase transparency about the identity of species sold to address the potential impact of mislabeled or illegally harvested threatened elasmobranchs.We performed DNA barcode sequencing to identify the composition of rays sold in markets in La Paz, Baja California Sur, Mexico. We identified samples collected between 2020-2022 representing species belonging to eight families. None of the samples were accurately labeled to the species level, and were instead sold under four categories: mantarraya, pescado seco, machaca, and cubana seca. The most common species identified by genetic analyses were diamond stingray (Hypanus dipterurus), longtail stingray (H. longus), and California butterfly ray (Gymnura marmorata). Greater than 78% of the samples surveyed are considered threatened by the IUCN Red List. Among these were two species of devil ray (Mobula munkiana and M. thurstoni), both of which are federally protected in Mexico. We recommend expanding point of purchase identification for fresh products weighed and packaged in markets with Mexican authorities to better understand the extent of elasmobranch fishing.

2110: Sharks and rays are ecologically important species in the wider North Sea ecosystem, and although several species historically occurred throughout the Dutch Continental Shelf (DCS), major knowledge gaps remain regarding their movement ecology, habitat use and ecological roles. Addressing these knowledge gaps, as required under the North Sea Agreement, provides a basis for more effective management of the wider North Sea ecosystem. The MONS Shark and Ray Research program (2025-2028) addresses two major knowledge gaps: the movement ecology and habitat use of sharks and rays, and the trophic ecology and ecological role of sharks and rays. To study the movement ecology and habitat use of sharks and rays we combine telemetry (acoustic, data-storage, and pop-up archival tags) and fisheries-independent surveys to: determine long-distance movements between the DCS and adjacent waters, fine-scale movements in coastal areas, estuaries and offshore wind farms, and determine the function of specific areas as (seasonal) nursery or feeding areas for different life stages. To address knowledge gaps in the trophic ecology of sharks and rays, we use a combination of techniques (stable isotope analysis, diet metabarcoding and stomach content analysis) to determine how trophic niches, food web positions, and diet change across species and life stages. We integrate this information with the movement ecology and the ecomorphological traits of these species to determine to what extent diet drives movement and habitat use. By resolving these interconnected knowledge gaps, this research program provides the ecological insights needed for evidence-based management of a rapidly changing North Sea

2114: The broadnose sevengill shark, Notorynchus cepedianus, is a coastal apex predator considered Critically Endangered in Brazil, with limited recent data on its occurrence. In October 2025, new records were documented at Cassino Beach, Rio Grande, Rio Grande do Sul State, through verified reports from recreational fishers and local observers engaged in beach monitoring activities. Five confirmed events were registered, including three individuals captured by rod and line and released alive, and two stranded specimens found dead on the beach. Photographic and video evidence enabled accurate species identification, and the largest individual measured approximately cm in total length, indicating that juveniles and subadults use these shallow nearshore waters. These reports were voluntarily submitted through the social media network of Projeto Tubarão, demonstrating how digital platforms can facilitate rapid communication, strengthen trust between scientists and fishing communities, and overcome longstanding barriers that have historically limited collaborative research. Although the broader trajectory of Projeto Tubarão is beyond the scope of this study, its established network across multiple Brazilian states, played a pivotal role in enabling fishers to proactively share reliable information, reinforcing collaborative monitoring efforts. Our findings confirm the persistence of N. cepedianus in the cold, high-productivity coastal waters of southern Brazil and extend the temporal window of confirmed occurrence for the species in the southwestern Atlantic. This collaborative approach between scientists and local fishers highlights the growing importance of participatory monitoring as a complementary tool for enhancing species assessments, guiding conservation priorities, and improving data availability in data-poor regions.

2116: Implementation of CITES listings for shark and ray species has expanded rapidly over the past decade, with increased listings, creating an urgent need for efficient, standardised, and scientifically robust Non-Detriment Findings (NDFs) to inform authorities of the potential for trade. To support Parties in meeting these obligations, the electronic Non-Detriment Finding (e-NDF) software tool has been developed. The e-NDF streamlines the NDF process by combining standardised guidance, species-specific biological and trade information, and a decision-support logic that evaluates key indicators, including population productivity and conservation concern, trade and fishing pressures, and the effectiveness of current management regimes. For shark and ray taxa, which often suffer from data gaps and complex supply chains, the e-NDF provides a clear pathway to document expert reasoning while also highlighting critical uncertainties and further monitoring or management needs. Since its public release in 2022, the e-NDF platform has been used by multiple CITES Parties worldwide to develop their shark and ray e-NDFs. It has since expanded to cover sea-cucumber species and additional languages, further increasing its use and accessibility. With the recent Review of Significant Trade (RST) process focusing on sharks and rays, it is clear that robust NDFs have become a cornerstone for Parties in meeting their CITES obligations. This presentation introduces the structure and functionality of the CITES e-NDF. It explains how it links scientific data with the practical implementation of Appendix-II listings to ensure that any trade in elasmobranchs or their derivatives is sustainable.

2117: Scalloped hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna lewini) are globally threatened or endangered, with the exception of the central Pacific distinct population segment (DPS). Current conservation assessments for this DPS rely largely on genetic data from juveniles sampled at a single nursery site, leaving population specific adult ecology, particularly for females, poorly understood. Given known sex-specific habitat use in this species, this data gap limits effective management. We examined vertical movement patterns of adult female scalloped hammerhead sharks tagged with pop-off archival satellite tags and temperature-pressure sensing acoustic tags off the leeward coast of Hawaiʻi Island over a three-year period (tag retention ~11–240 days). In this study, we focused attention on examining diel dive behaviors, with a particular focus on the relationships between dive profile dynamics, the ascent transition point phenomenon, and a suite of possible biotic and abiotic variables that may influence the point at which the transition point occurs within the ascent profile. Ascent transition point depth was strongly related to excursion duration, descent rate, maximum dive depth, temperature, and dissolved oxygen, indicating sensitivity to fine-scale environmental gradients. Seasonal shifts toward deeper or offshore habitats suggest environmentally constrained and dynamic habitat use. These findings provide critical insight into the spatial ecology of adult females—the reproductive core of the central Pacific DPS—and highlight sustained connectivity between insular shelves and offshore deep-water habitats. This three-dimensional habitat use has important implications for spatial management and underscores potential vulnerability to climate-driven changes in ocean temperature, oxygen structure, and deep-water prey availability.

2119: Tropical tuna fisheries are among the largest fisheries in the world and interact with a range of bycatch species. Understanding the impacts of these fisheries on bycatch species is important for fisheries management, however the sustainability of many of these species remains largely unknown. Here, a new length-based ecological risk assessment method, Ecological Assessment of the Sustainable Impacts of Fisheries (EASI-Fish), was applied to elasmobranch species caught in western and central Pacific Ocean (WCPO) tropical tuna fisheries. In summary, of species assessed were considered ‘least vulnerable’, with considered ‘most vulnerable’ and a further eight ‘data deficient’. Species considered ‘most vulnerable’ included several Carcharhinids given their low productivity, as well as several Sphyrna species that are particularly susceptible to mortality when interacting with fishing gears. Deep-set longline fishing gear was responsible for most fishing mortality given its cosmopolitan effort distribution throughout the WCPO. A compilation of key life history and fisheries information for bycatch species was also undertaken during this process, with eight species considered data deficient, identifying future research priorities. Further developments of EASI-Fish were also explored which should improve the method’s robustness and its future use. This assessment can assist the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission revise its management and research priorities for shark bycatch.

2120: Conserving sharks in Bangladesh’s Bay of Bengal faces challenges due to limited scientific data and inadequate fisheries management infrastructure. To address this, we’ve implemented a comprehensive approach integrating local ecological knowledge (LEK), community capacity building, and adaptive co-management. A key component is the ‘SAROB’ mobile app, empowering artisanal fishers as citizen scientists in a standardized, incentive-driven data collection model. The app enables real-time documentation of shark landings, providing crucial data on species composition, catch locations, and seasonal trends. This information aids conservation efforts by identifying critical hotspots for intervention and engaging fishers in sustainable fisheries management. SAROB's cost-effective model equips fishers with mobile devices for tracking shark landings, combining modern technology with traditional knowledge to foster a participatory conservation approach. Success hinges on building trust with local communities, as many top-down conservation efforts fail due to limited engagement. SAROB ensures fishers are involved in shaping the initiative through sustained dialogue, capacitybuilding workshops, and recognition of their expertise. Beyond monetary incentives, SAROB offers social rewards such as improved fisheries management, increased safety, and community development. By aligning conservation goals with practical benefits, the project ensures conservation is a shared priority. Additionally, SAROB upholds strict data privacy policies, ensuring that data is used solely for conservation purposes, protecting fishers' confidentiality. This approach, grounded in ethical data practices, promotes long-term trust and sustainable community stewardship.

2122: Chondrichthyans and their parasites represent one of the most ancient host-parasite systems on the planet with a co-evolution that exists for more than million years. However, this hostparasite system now faces unprecedented anthropogenic threats. Chondrichthyans are among the most threatened marine vertebrates, with numerous species at risk of extinction. Their parasite assemblages, most notably cestodes, monogeneans and copepods, are even more threatened due to their high host specificity, complex life cycles and/or limited dispersal capabilities. As host populations decline, many parasite species face an increased risk of coextinction and may disappear well before their threatened host species. Conserving parasites is of critical importance to marine systems. These organisms structure food webs, regulate host populations and preserve evolutionary relationships. However, parasites remain neglected and largely absent from current conservation frameworks. This is mostly attributed to vast knowledge gaps in their diversity and taxonomic bias to more charismatic organismal groups. Full parasitological surveys of chondrichthyan hosts are rare and many species have never been assessed for parasites, leaving a large proportion of their diversity unknown and undocumented. This not only obscures patterns of host specificity but also severely undermines our ability to assess their threat levels and identify parasite losses. Failure to integrate parasites into conservation strategies will lead to irreversible losses of symbiotic relationships and the evolutionary processes they maintain. Parasite conservation is therefore essential, given that global biodiversity management can no longer afford to exclude these hidden yet crucial components of marine ecosystems.

2123: Straddling and highly migratory marine species face mounting threats from overfishing, climate change, and systemic governance failures, particularly in the high seas and across jurisdictional boundaries. Regional Fisheries Management Organizations (RFMOs), designed to manage shared fish stocks, have struggled to adapt to these challenges due to limited taxonomic mandates, inequitable quota allocation frameworks, and weak operational oversight. This paper will present a transformative blueprint for international fisheries governance centered on two pillars: structural reforms—such as the expansion of taxonomic mandates, climate-responsive quota redistribution, and the closure of the high seas to commercial fishing—and operational innovations, including the widespread adoption of Management Strategy Evaluation (MSE), electronic monitoring, and ecosystem-based spatial planning through ecoregions. Drawing on a comprehensive review of legal, ecological, economic, and human rights literature, we propose an integrated governance model that aligns access rights with ecological reality, incentivizes stewardship by coastal and island States, and embeds sustainability and equity at the core of fisheries management. These reforms offer a pathway to resilient and just ocean governance in an era of rapid environmental change.

2124: The Eastern Pacific Ocean (EPO) and its highly migratory species are among the most vulnerable marine systems worldwide, facing combined pressures from intense fishing and strong climate variability. Despite the exceptional monitoring conducted by the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC), current management strategies remain largely static. Previous research has demonstrated the benefits of dynamic ocean management for reducing bycatch and balancing ecological and socio-economic objectives; however, no study has explicitly evaluated how conservation priorities are reorganized under contrasting oceanographic conditions. In this study, we assessed how spatial conservation priorities shift under three environmental scenarios using Zonation to identify priority areas for fourteen species: four target tunas, five billfishes, and five sharks. Overall, high-priority areas corresponded to regions with lower degradation and more suitable habitat conditions. These included the western coast of the Baja California Peninsula, the Gulf of California, offshore waters of Central America, the coast from Colombia to Peru, and equatorial regions encompassing oceanic islands such as Cocos, Malpelo, and the Galápagos. Our results show that conservation priorities for these pelagic species shift substantially across environmental conditions—particularly under warm scenarios. The most vulnerable and dynamic areas were the western Baja California Peninsula, Central American coastal waters, and coastal and equatorial upwelling zones. These findings highlight the urgent need for dynamic, climateinformed management strategies that extend beyond existing protected areas in the EPO, ensuring more effective conservation of highly migratory species under changing ocean conditions.
