While the decline of Eastern Diamondback Rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus; EDB) populations has been widely attributed to anthropogenic activity, further research is needed to address how environmental pressures drive behavior, which can inform predictions regarding species-level resilience. Disease susceptibility and environmental influences (i.e., temperature, precipitation) on reproductive phenology make gravid females a particularly vulnerable demographic due to the physiological demands of reproductive cycles. Using datasets from two isolated coastal populations, we examined the effects of biotic and abiotic predictors on daily and seasonal activity patterns of EDBs. Using logistic regression, our goal was to examine the effects of environmental conditions, reproductive condition, and disease on phenology, surface activity, and ecdysis cycles. We hypothesized that winter surface activity and shortened brumation periods would be associated with increasing temperatures. Additionally, we hypothesized that individuals with skin lesions suggestive of ophidiomycosis (also known as snake fungal disease) concurrent with the detection of Ophidiomyces ophidiicola would express increased ecdysis frequency and winter surface activity. Lastly, we expected that geographically distinct populations would differ in phenology and surface activity. Our investigation will improve our understanding of population-level vulnerability and processes that drive population decline.
2185: The Guana and Tolomato rivers provide essential habitat to several ecologically and economically important species, including serving as nursery habitat to a variety of shark species, most notably the scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini). Spanning the Northeastern Florida coast, they are home to over 50 endangered or threatened species and hosts several habitat restoration projects due to the rivers’s ecological significance. Due to their proximity to developed areas along the coast, they can be threatened by human influences, such as pollution. While the negative effects of human interaction with the environment are of growing public interest, the effect of pollution in the Guana and Tolomato rivers has not been well studied. Therefore, the overall purpose of this project is to examine pollutant exposure in species residing within the Guana and Tolomato rivers, specifically that of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). PFAS have been shown no clear pattern of accumulation or biomagnification in marine ecosystems and pose significant health risks to marine organisms and the humans that consume them. This presentation will discuss preliminary PFAS data in a variety of shark species and their prey, including sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus), bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas), and scalloped hammerheads. These results will be analyzed in conjunction with stable isotope data and be compared to Maximum Contaminant Levels in drinking water as identified by the EPA.
2186: Invasive species are an ongoing concern to our natural world and pose a unique threat to aquatic ecosystems. Amphibians are especially vulnerable to stressors imposed by invasive species. For this study we will investigate direct and indirect impacts the invasive plant species amur honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii) and tree of heaven (Alianthus altissima) may be having within aquatic ecosystems using small-mouthed salamanders (Ambystoma texanum) and American bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana) as model organisms. In addition, we will use American bullfrogs as a model organism for amphibian invasion and investigate their impact on small-mouthed salamanders. 36 cattle tank mesocosms have been setup to mimic ponds found in the midwestern United States. Treatments have been assigned to 28 of the 36 tanks, allowing for 8 control tanks. Small-mouthed salamander tanks received one of five treatments: addition of amur honeysuckle, addition of tree of heaven, addition of bullfrogs, addition of amur honeysuckle and bullfrogs, or addition of tree of heaven and bullfrogs. Bullfrog tanks received one of two treatments: addition of amur honeysuckle or addition of tree of heaven. The results for this experiment are pending, but we predict that both species of amphibians will experience increased mortality and decreased body mass at metamorphosis when exposed to the invasive leaf litter. We also predict small-mouthed salamanders in the presence of bullfrogs will have decreased body mass at metamorphosis
2187: Stable isotope analysis has long provided insight to feeding ecology, habitat use, and physiological status in chondrichthyan fishes. Recent work quantifying the isotopic composition of organic material bound within the mineralized portions of shark teeth has suggested that teeth of different ages (i.e., sampled from different rows) may preserve ecological chronologies given that they represent different temporal windows. As such, teeth from individuals associated with more isotopically homogenous environments, such as pelagic species, should exhibit more constrained isotopic variability than coastal species. This prediction has not been robustly tested across a diversity of species and is required to refine estimates of functional plasticity. We quantified δ13C and δ15N variation in organic material extracted from teeth by measuring those of different ages and positions across jaws from individuals associated with different habitats. Specifically, we explored whether isotopic variation observed across shark teeth of adult bull (Carcharhinus leucas, coastal Indian Ocean), adult dusky (Carcharhinus obscurus, pelagic Indian Ocean), and juvenile white (Carcharodon carcharias, coastal California) sharks is consistent with the diversity of habitats encountered throughout life. Initial analyses of bull shark teeth show high δ13C variation (-17.7 to -10.0‰) and lower δ15N variation (9.8 to 12.4‰) expressed across the jaw. We also observed isotopic shifts across teeth, from older to younger, possibly indicating habitat transitions between pelagic and coastal environments. These and related findings using the dentine component of teeth will support novel assessments of functional plasticity in both modern and historical contexts given the potential application to museum specimens.
2188: Accurate measurements are critical data for managers in the study of wildlife. Measuring animals in the wild, such as  marine megafauna can be difficult, especially for species that cannot be directly measured without invasive capture techniques, this includes the giant manta ray (Mobula birostris). The Florida Manta Project aims to assess and compare different measurement methods: 1) underwater laser photogrammetry, 2) aerial photogrammetry, and 3) visual estimation by trained researchers. This study compares the precision of these methods by analyzing measurements of 20 mantas collected during small boat surveys. The primary objective is to identify potential discrepancies in size estimates between the methods and assess the variation in measurements. These findings will provide insights into the reliability of these commonly used methods and contribute to refining measurement protocols for marine megafauna research. Ensuring the precision of size measurements will enhance the understanding of manta ray life history traits, such as size at maturity, supporting more effective population models and conservation strategies.
2189: Streams are important habitats for amphibians in Northeastern Pennsylvania, which are reliant upon these water sources for their larval development and adult survival. Prescribed fire, a practice that is used to manage forest undergrowth, often occurs in regions where there are streams. Whereas direct stream habitat may not be burned, runoff from burned habitat could likely impact streams. This study was done to determine how prescribed fire affects the water chemistry of various stream habitats and biodiversity of salamander species. Changes in the water chemistry and biodiversity were documented in six streams within burnt, and unburnt, lands located in Northeastern Pennsylvania. pH, turbidity, and total dissolved solutes were recorded at each of the streams. Three 100-ml water samples were collected from each stream and analyzed in a laboratory for heavy metals, particularly lead, cadmium, arsenic, copper, and zinc. The high heat of a fire could release heavy metals from bound states in the soil humus and plants in the form of ash runoff. Salamander biodiversity at each stream was determined by conducting time-constrained surveys over the course of several months. Alpha and beta biodiversity were compared among burned and unburned sites using population data collected from each survey. Differences in water chemistry were determined between burned and unburned sites. Our results will help determine if prescribed fire has any impact on the water chemistry or salamander biodiversity of streams
2190: Lamniformes (Elasmobranchii) is a relatively small but diverse shark order, consisting of seven families, ten genera, and fifteen species. Although the dental morphology of these sharks is well known, the morphological range of their jaws has been poorly investigated. In this study, we quantitatively examined the jaw curvatures of the fifteen lamniform species based on radiographic (X-ray and computed tomography) data using two-dimensional geometric morphometrics. Our study shows that, whereas Alopias spp. exhibit a wide range of jaw curvatures with seemingly no specific pattern, plots of species belonging to the genera Odontaspis, Pseudocarcharias, Carcharias, Lamna, Isurus, and to a certain extent, Mitsukurina are clustered closely together in one morphospace and are characterized by tightly curved jaws. On the other hand, plots of the remaining taxa, Megachasma, Cetorhinus, and Carcharodon, are more widely distributed in another morphometric region and are characterized by broad, gently curved jaws. The former cluster is characterized by conventional piscivorous taxa with narrow, non-serrated piercing-type teeth, whereas the latter is represented by taxa with either large, broad, and serrated cutting-type teeth (Carcharodon, which its gently curved jaw presumably promotes the ‘sawing effect’ of its teeth) or diminutive teeth due to planktivory (Megachasma and Cetorhinus). Phylogenetically, our study indicates that tightly curved jaws are plesiomorphic, and more gently curved jaws are apomorphic. Although the exact reason is unclear, the broad plot distribution for Alopias spp. may be related to their unique hunting strategy using their elongated tail where their jaw curvature may play little role in their feeding.
2191: Sand tigers, Carcharias taurus, are mackerel sharks with a disjunct global distribution in tropical and temperate seas. In the Northwest Atlantic, sand tigers migrate along the coast of the eastern United States from the Gulf of Maine to Florida and occupy structurally complex benthic habitats. The long-term, underwater camera installation, SharkCam, at Frying Pan Tower, off Cape Fear, North Carolina, USA, sits atop an expanse of hard bottom reef frequented by sand tigers. The citizen-science platform, Spot A Shark USA (SAS USA), uses images of sand tigers to identify and track individuals. This study utilized image encounters from SAS USA (n=1,359) and SharkCam (n=3,846) to glean information about sand tiger relative abundance, site fidelity, seasonality, and fish associates off the coast of North Carolina. To investigate site fidelity of sand tigers, SharkCam encounters were entered into SAS USA (n = 545). Sand tiger seasonality, sex, and relative abundance at Frying Pan Tower were tracked from 2014–2021. SharkCam and SAS USA encounters were used for identifying fishes associated with sand tigers. At Frying Pan Tower, 44 individual sand tigers were resighted up to 15 times over multiple years, with some females possessing visual markers of pregnancy. There was a total species richness of 17 fishes behaviorally associated with sand tigers. This study contributes to existing evidence that coastal North Carolina is important for sand tigers throughout their lifetimes, while the understanding of fish associates provides additional insight into interspecific interactions within the food web.
2192: Brevetoxins, the toxins produced by the harmful algal bloom known as Florida Red Tide (Karenia brevis), and their incorporation into elasmobranch tissues is greatly understudied. The only study to date found a correlation between the frequency of red tide blooms and the average concentrations of brevetoxins in elasmobranch tissues collected from animals who experienced a Red Tide-induced fatality (Flewelling, 2010). We utilized competitive ELISA analysis in samples of Blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) collected between 2019 and 2024 within Sarasota Bay, Tampa Bay, and Manatee River using bottom longlines and gillnets to further investigate brevetoxin concentrations in blacktips not currently experiencing an active Red Tide bloom. Preliminary data suggests there is a difference between brevetoxin concentrations in tissue types, as well as variation existing between individuals. There is also evidence of a correlation between the time post-bloom and the concentration of brevetoxins. The build-up and elimination of these toxins at sublethal doses in elasmobranchs requires further study, and this project seeks to provide a better understanding of this topic and the impacts of Florida Red Tide on sharks.
2193: The Baja Coachwhip (Masticophis fuliginosus) is a large colubrid restricted to the Baja Peninsula (Mexico) and southern California (USA). Understanding the processes that have led to the current patterns of biodiversity throughout the Baja Peninsula has been the focus of many studies, yet the evolutionary history of this species is poorly understood. Previous work within Baja has suggested that sea level rise, mountain uplift, and desertification have resulted in genetic divergence across codistributed species. Here, we have collected 73 specimens from across the distribution of M. fuliginosus as well as the closely related M. piceus in southern California. We used low-coverage whole genome sequencing to assemble complete mitochondrial genomes. These data were used to construct phylogenies using maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference to infer the evolutionary relationships among whipsnakes and assess the influence of potential geographic barriers on the genetic structure of M. fuliginosus across Baja. Our findings support previous hypotheses regarding the strong influence of allopatric divergence on creating genetic diversity in the southern Baja Cape region; however, we find no population structure throughout the central and northern regions of the peninsula. These data can inform patterns of isolation by distance and environment, which is a key to disentangling the evolutionary history of this species. By using low coverage genome sequencing, we have documented the drivers of diversification within the Baja Coachwhip and suggest that similar patterns may be found in other codistributed squamate reptiles.
2194: Minorities in Shark Sciences (MISS) is collaborating with community members in North Carolina to investigate how sharks use coastal and inland waters in and around Pamlico Sound. This project originated through the efforts of the community-driven Instagram page, Encounter NC, where local shark enthusiasts shared encounters and fostered curiosity about local shark populations. Recognizing the need for deeper scientific understanding, Encounter NC partnered with MISS to explore these sharks more extensively. Pamlico Sound, previously overlooked, has now been identified as a potential northernmost nursery for bull sharks along the U.S. Atlantic coast, extending beyond the previously known boundary of the Indian River Lagoon in Florida. The project also offers a unique opportunity to study the impact of climate change on shark populations. Understanding these shifts is essential for conserving these populations. By integrating community science, satellite tracking, and self-reported encounter data, this project will support local efforts to co-manage Pamlico Sound and the surrounding area and ensure the protection of shark populations, particularly bull sharks, highlighting the crucial role of community engagement in marine conservation. We will present preliminary data from this project as well as the inclusive conservation framework we will employ for the project.
2195: Biofluorescence occurs when an organism absorbs shorter and then emits longer wavelengths of light. Most studies on biofluorescence focus on documentation, rather than on its possible evolutionary function. This study examines the potential ecological significance of biofluorescence in larval Gray Tree Frogs (Dryophytes chrysoscelis/versicolor). Tadpoles in this group develop large, orange-red tails to deflect invertebrate predators. Their tails also fluoresce in the orange-red spectrum. If biofluorescence in tadpoles varies with the predator community, then it could function in signal enhancement for predator deflection. We quantified fluorescence, the invertebrate predator community, and the underwater light environment experienced by tadpoles. We tested 47 tadpoles for fluorescence in response to blue (440 - 460 nm), cyan (490 - 515 nm), and green (510 - 540 nm) light. We used both spectrometry and digital photography to quantify fluorescent emissions and the proportion of the tail fluorescing in the orange-red spectrum, respectively. Biofluorescence varied across individuals. Blue and cyan light, which are present in the water column, produced striking orange-red fluorescence. Proportionally, this fluorescence contributed approximately 0.24 to total brightness under blue and cyan excitation. For some individuals, nearly 45% of the lateral surface of the tail fluoresced orange-red. We use linear models to explore the relationship between site-dependent variables, such as predator diversity, on the orange-red fluorescence of tadpole tails. Our work adds to a limited pool of knowledge regarding biofluorescence in larval amphibians and provides insight into another possible function of biofluorescence in these vertebrates.
2196: Blacknose sharks (Carcharhinus acronotus) and sandbar sharks (C. plumbeus) are two endangered shark species found within the Western North Atlantic Ocean, including in the waters near Miami, Florida.  This study assessed the reproductive biology of mature blacknose (n=56) and sandbar (n=42) sharks captured in the Miami area between December 2019 and December 2024.  We examined plasma concentrations of testosterone (“T”), progesterone (“P4”), and 17β-estradiol (“E2”), and compared those hormone levels to catch date, catch location, season, and gravidity (determined via ultrasonography).  In addition, this study scored mating wounds identified in sandbar sharks using a four-stage wound healing analysis to determine the wounds’ apparent age and compared results of mating wound analysis with location, hormone, and ultrasound data to provide a more complete picture of sandbar shark mating and reproductive activity in the Miami area. Via these components, seasonal variations in levels of T and E2 were identified in blacknose sharks, and circulating E2 levels were correlated with gravidity.  In sandbar sharks, seasonal shifts in T and P4 were identified, as well as a possible relationship between the presence of mating wounds and levels of P4.  These findings provide insight into blacknose and sandbar reproductive biology and seasonality in waters near Miami, Florida.
2197: Spatial capture-recapture is a promising method for estimating population vitals and has been used in many studies on population dynamics. These studies are important because they improve understanding of how species respond in different environments. The eastern red-backed salamander, Plethodon cinereus, is a terrestrial, lungless salamander that is common in Eastern North America and parts of Canada, ranging from Quebec to North Carolina. Plethodon cinereus is small in size and can be easily found and studied in forest ecosystems. This species will defend their territory through aggressive behavior and are known to be territorial. However, the extent of territoriality of males and females, and how salamanders spatially disperse has not been thoroughly examined in Pennsylvania. The goals of this study are to (1) estimate population density and (2) describe differences in (a) spatial distribution and (b) movement patterns between males and females of P. cinereus in central Pennsylvania. We used spatial capture-recapture methods to address these goals and test the following hypotheses. We hypothesized that (1) males have larger foraging areas than females and (2) both sexes display site fidelity by staying within the same plot and area within plot. Our study location included 6 plots of 50 coverboards each in central Pennsylvania where this species has previously been found. Individuals were marked with a unique four-color code through injection of Visible Implant Elastomer tags.
2198: Road salt intrusion and invasive honeysuckle are increasing ecological concerns in freshwater habitats. Amphibians are sensitive to these stressors due to their permeable skin. Salinization can lead to increased mortality, behavioral changes, and reduced growth. Invasive honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii) has been found to cause mass mortality in amphibians. Road salt and honeysuckle are likely to overlap in habitat near ephemeral pools, such as disturbed and edge habitats, which are utilized by amphibians. If these stressors were to synergistically interact, it could lead to a higher increase in mortality and behavioral changes. These negative impacts could ultimately lead to a shift in amphibian community dynamics. We investigated the synergistic effects of road salt and honeysuckle on the predator-prey interactions of small-mouthed salamanders (Ambystoma texanum) and gray treefrogs (Hyla versicolor). Larval A. texanum (predator) and H. versicolor tadpoles (prey) were placed in cattle tanks with a control, honeysuckle, salt, or combined treatment. Half of the cattle tanks contained only A. texanum larvae and the other half contained both A. texanum larvae and H. versicolor tadpoles. Survivorship of H. versicolor tadpoles and A. texanum was monitored along with A. texanum body length, mass, and time to metamorphosis. We found that road salt and honeysuckle did not significantly impact metamorphosed A. texanum life history traits. However, we found that road salt significantly impacted some life history traits of larval A. texanum. Additionally, A. texanum predation ability was not impacted by road salt or honeysuckle.
2199: The role of progesterone (P4) in elasmobranch reproduction has long been under question, as P4 is generally not elevated during pregnancy, unlike in mammals, reptiles, and amphibians.   Numerous previous studies on elasmobranch reproduction, including previously presented results on the bonnethead shark (Sphyrna tiburo), have confirmed that E2 stimulates the production of vitellogenin (Vtg) in the liver during follicular development, but the role of P4 in this process remains undetermined.  This study specifically looked at the potential role of P4 in regulating Vtg production in S. tiburo.  Immunoblotting was used to detect the presence of Vtg in S. tiburo plasma, while chemiluminescent assays analyzed plasma P4 concentrations.   Immunohistochemistry was also conducted to look for E2 and P4 receptors in S. tiburo liver.  Receptors for both E2 and P4 were detected in S. tiburo liver, suggesting both hormones play a role in Vtg production.   High concentrations of plasma P4 were found during the late spring months, when Vtg presence in plasma samples was declining.  These preliminary results suggest that P4 may bind to receptors in the liver and trigger the slowing or termination of Vtg production and follicular development in S. tiburo.  Further investigation of this potential role is needed, perhaps by examining in vitro and/or in vivo effects of P4 treatment.
2200: Tooth morphology and arrangement are widely used in paleontological and ichthyological field guides to identify sharks in the order Lamniformes. The size and shape of tooth crowns and the presence or absence of lateral cusplets on either side of the central tooth crown are among the more commonly referenced morphological odontological characters. These characters are also the focus of renewed scrutiny with respect to phylogenetic and taxonomic importance. Here we document the teeth and dentition of an adult Porbeagle Shark (Lamna nasus) exhibiting an atypical number of tooth cusplets and tooth files. We present and comment on the morphological variability of teeth within a single tooth file and illustrate the presence and developmental sequence of a putatively aberrant symphyseal tooth file. Collectively, these observations highlight the importance of understanding natural intraspecific variation in morphological dental features if they are to be used in taxonomic identification or as phylogenetic characters.
2201: Biological invasions by anurans are increasing. It is critical to understand the global patterns of these introductions to develop conservation interventions. Our goals were to describe the taxonomic, spatial, and temporal patterns of anuran invasions. We determined the anthropogenic transport pathways of non-native anurans and evaluated the frequency of occurrence of these pathways through time and space. We also assessed the geographic sources and sinks of anthropogenic anuran introductions and evaluated whether they have changed over time. In addition, we conducted models to determine which predictors most influence the success of anurans in the invasion process. We based our analysis on our collation of a new database of anuran invasions. We found that the pathways of anuran introductions have changed over time from primarily intentional introductions to mostly accidental introductions. Despite broad perceptions, non-native anurans are rarely introduced via the pet trade. Spatial heterogeneity exists in pathway usage and the sources and sinks of anthropogenic anuran invasions. Our modeling indicates pathway of introduction is an important predictor of invasion success of anurans. Other predictors, such as life history traits, are less important, but also significant. Further research can expand these analyses to other groups of invasive herpetofauna and can direct action towards the control of transport of non-native anurans.
2202: Ray-finned fishes are one of the largest groups of vertebrates on the planet, having first shown up in the fossil record 480 million years ago. Despite being such a long lived and diverse group, little is known about many extinct genera of fishes, particularly stem actinopterygians from the Early Mesozoic, a time where fish were diversifying into and exploiting empty niches following the End-Permian Extinction Event. Herein we describe recent advances in knowledge regarding actinopterygians from the Upper Triassic Dockum Group of New Mexico and Texas (approximately 230–200 Ma). The Dockum basin contains a distinct assemblages of fishes belonging to the orders Redfieldiiformes (Actinopterygii: “Palaeoniscimorpha”), Scanilepiformes (Actinopterygii: Cladistia), Semionotiformes (Neopterygii: Holostei), and Dapediiformes (Neopterygii: Holostei). Several new species of fishes have been identified from the Colorado City Formation, Dockum Group of western Texas; we describe their morphology and unique three-dimensional preservation. We describe a unique mass mortality of juvenile semionotiforms from the Redonda Formation, Dockum Group of eastern New Mexico. We compare this assemblage to the similar but distinct assemblage found in the Upper Triassic Chinle Formation of Utah, Arizona, and Colorado, and discuss evolutionary relationships among stem actinopterygians.
2203: Quantitative analysis of animal kinematics is critical for advancing our understanding of marine locomotion, yet traditional manual annotation of video data is labor intensive and error prone. We present an automated framework that leverages machine learning to rapidly extract wing beat frequency in manta rays from aerial drone footage. Fifteen short video sequences were annotated using a custom event labeling tool to generate precise ground truth timestamps for each wing beat, enabling rigorous evaluation of our system. The framework computes three distinct features per frame: the inter‐wingtip distance (wing span) with 91% accuracy, the polygonal body area (pixel count of the detected shape) with 88% accuracy, and the bounding box aspect ratio (length divided by width) with 76% accuracy. These features yield sinusoidal curves over time, whose local extrema reliably correspond to individual wing beats, with the wing span measurement demonstrating superior robustness. Although the present study detected wing span or disc width of a pelagic ray, the flexible feature definition framework supports diverse measurements for utilization on different elasmobranchs. The system nearly reaches real-time processing, supports continuous operation for hours, and can track multiple individuals in parallel, achieving a 90‐fold acceleration in data extraction compared to manual methods. Occasional discrepancies highlight areas for further algorithmic refinement. This study demonstrates that integrating advanced object detection, pose estimation, and versatile keypoint-to-feature mapping within a unified system can transform kinematic analysis in marine biology by enabling rapid, automated movement metric extraction that facilitates biomechanical and behavioral research.
2204: Dragonfishes and their allies (Stomiiformes) are a species-rich lineage of marine pelagic fishes frequently found in deep-sea habitats where they have evolved adaptations, such as bioluminescence, for living in this environment. Dragonfishes are distributed throughout the world’s oceans, with some taxa exhibiting broad distributions across multiple oceans and others having more restricted distributions to specific regions. In this study, we are investigating the biogeographic patterns of dragonfishes over time. We infer these biogeographic patterns with a phylogenomic perspective on stomiiform evolutionary relationships that is time calibrated based on the fossil record. We use this temporal phylogeny in combination with our study on stomiiform distributions to investigate the biogeographic patterns of dragonfishes.
2205: Formalin is used to preserve specimens by creating cross-links that prevent bacterial decay and effectively preserve them. However, there is evidence of shrinkage occurring during preservation by a small amount ( ~ 1-3%). This shrinkage could affect our ability to accurately measure preserved specimens. We quantified the change in shape in geckos/anoles before and after preservation. 23 anoles (16 Anolis carolinesis and 7 Anolis sagrei) and 9 Phelsuma laticauda were collected in Hawaii in 2018. We photographed their toe pads, collected morphological measurements, and then euthanized them. After euthanasia, they were preserved in formalin for 12-24 hours and then kept in 75% ethanol until March 2023. They were then rephotographed and remeasured. Measurements were taken externally using calipers. Toe pad shape and area were measured using three programs: TPSDig, ImageJ, and R. TPSDig was used to record landmark coordinates on our toe pad photographs. ImageJ was used to record the area of the lizard's toepads. Lastly, R was used to compare toe shape and area of the pre and post preservation toepads, and generate plots to visualize our results. Results will be used to dictate if a change in preserved specimens is significant enough to impact future studies using preserved specimens.
2206: Air breathing and the use of lungs are synonymous for the vast majority of tetrapod vertebrates. Amphibians, however, have evolved a diverse set of respiratory adaptations over their evolutionary history, from air breathing, to retaining larval gills, to losing lungs and relying on integumentary and buccopharyngeal respiration. Comparatively, the respiratory diversity of larval amphibians has been generally overlooked. Frog larvae, i.e. tadpoles, are remarkably diverse however, including both lunged and lungless forms, as well as gill and skin specializations in various lineages. We present evidence that larval air breathing has re-evolved in tadpoles of the African red toad (Schismaderma carens): the first known independent evolution of air breathing in any tetrapod. We combine photographic and anatomical evidence to show that S. carens tadpoles frequently surface to gulp air bubbles that are then swallowed into their spiral intestines. S. carens tadpoles are best known for their unique, vascular headcrest that has been suggested to serve as a respiratory organ. We suggest that gut breathing has evolved in this group to facilitate buoyancy control and use this crest, given they lack inflated lungs. Following metamorphosis, froglets begin to breathe air into their lungs, meaning that larval and adult S. carens perform two evolutionarily distinct forms of air breathing. This study highlights the diversity of respiratory adaptations in larval amphibians, hints at the decoupling power of metamorphosis, and provides a counterexample of non-respiratory air breathing to be compared against the commonly supposed story of a respiratory origin for vertebrate air breathing.
2207: Advanced bioimaging techniques, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), provide opportunities to advance our understanding of neuroanatomy non-invasively, minimizing the risk of damaging rare samples. Considerable inter- and intraspecific variation in the peripheral nervous system (e.g., inner ear) and patterns of brain organization (i.e., the relative size of major brain regions) has been documented in cartilaginous fishes. These patterns are often linked to ecological differences, suggesting behavioral and sensory variation between species and across ontogeny. However, less is known about nervous system morphology in endangered species, leaving a gap in our understanding of brain evolution in this group. The Critically Endangered smalltooth sawfish, Pristis pectinata, has experienced significant declines throughout its Atlantic range, with the U.S. population being primarily restricted to southwest Florida, prompting research to better understand its biology and ecology. Further, recent mortality events of P. pectinata in South Florida suggest neurological impairment, prompting an immediate need to better understand brain morphology in this species. This study aims to develop and optimize protocols for T1-weighted, contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain of opportunistically collected P. pectinata to non-destructively characterize variation in both inner-ear morphology and brain organization. These data can be contextualized to inform behavioral and sensory specializations (a) in comparison to ~40 other batoids and (b) throughout ontogeny in this species. This study is one of the first attempts to gain an evolutionary perspective on the neuroanatomy of these unique rays and can serve as a baseline to investigate neuro-compromised individuals in the future.
2208: Anthropogenic land-use changes are a global driving factor in amphibian declines. Land-use changes have been found to disrupt the skin microbiota of amphibians in a variety of ways, which could lead to increased susceptibility to diseases like chytridiomycosis. However, the spatial scale of land-use has been understudied in assessing its effects on the microbiome. Thus, we aimed to assess the effects of immediate and whole watershed land-use on the skin microbial communities of a fully aquatic salamander, the common mudpuppy (Necturus maculosus). We captured common mudpuppies across a land-use gradient in Wisconsin, USA using trapping, snorkeling, and nighttime surveying methods. Skin microbial diversity was analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing and Bd-load was quantified using qPCR. Preliminary results suggest that developed landscapes correlate with a decrease in skin microbial alpha diversity, while agricultural landscapes correlate with an increase in alpha diversity. Bd prevalence ranged from 70-100% and fungal loads were high across all sampled sites, suggesting no correlation between land-use and Bd in common mudpuppies. Data is being further analyzed to distinguish the effects of aquatic habitat characteristics from those of land-use and will be discussed in further detail.
2209: The production of single-use plastics has risen significantly since the early 1900s, with over 400 million tons produced annually. An estimated 70% of these plastics end up in landfills or the environment, where natural processes break them down into microplastics (<5 mm) and nanoplastics (<1 µm). Acute exposures to these particles have been linked to adverse health effects in both in vitro and in vivo models, including humans. Many studies use plastic concentrations much higher than those found in aquatic ecosystems. This study aimed to examine the effects of environmentally relevant concentrations of plastic particles on Lithobates [Rana] pipiens tadpoles. Specifically, we assessed the impact of micro- and nanoplastics on feeding behavior, gut transit time, and gastrointestinal (GI) morphology. Tadpoles were exposed to either no plastic, 1 µg/L of microplastics, or 1 µg/L of nanoplastics. After three weeks, feeding behavior was observed using fluorescent food, gut transit time was recorded, and microdissections were performed to measure GI tract landmarks. Results showed no significant effect of plastic particles on feeding or gut morphology. As plastic pollution continues to rise, research like ours is essential in determining potential long-term effects and broader ecological implications regardless of the significance of our results.
2210: The Fenwick lab has been studying population genetics of Mediterranean geckos (Hemidactylus turcicus) since 2014. 1,622 samples have been collected from various sites including the University of Central Oklahoma (UCO) and the University of Oklahoma (OU). However, there were over 400 samples yet to be analyzed as of last fall. In an effort to cut down on this backlog, we programmed a liquid distribution device called the Biomek to expedite PCR liquid set up. A few years ago, the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation donated the Biomek to UCO. As of early spring, we were able to complete ten plates of PCR, compared to a yearly average of six plates. This has reduced the amount of samples backlogged by using the Biomek, as well as reduced chances of contamination and error. We have also completed a manual on how to use the Biomek for liquid distribution across a variety of procedures and parameters to expand its uses.
2211: The effects of dam construction on fish populations have been well-studied. Although several studies have documented the effects on species abundance or single species response, few have focused on functional trait variation in response to construction of dams and subsequent reservoir formation. In this study we determine the effects of building a dam on three integrative functional traits — morphology, trophic niche, and condition factor (K)— across three riverine characiform species: Astyanax lacustris, Galeocharax gulo, and Leporinus friderici. In 2012, the São Domingos dam was constructed on the Verde River in the Pantanal region of Mato Grosso du Sol, Brazil, forming a reservoir habitat. We collected specimens in three collection sites from 2019-2023: within the reservoir, upstream from the reservoir, and downstream from the dam. These sites allow for a direct comparison between the native lotic and novel lacustrine environments, allowing us to test for plastic responses in functional traits in an ecological time frame. We utilized geometric morphometrics to model morphological differentiation, stable isotope analysis to model trophic niche variation, and length weight ratios to model variation in condition factor. Each species responded differently to the environmental change; one species (G. gulo) showed no significant variation in any of the three traits over time while A. lacustris and L. friderici showed differing responses in some of the three traits, thus response to construction of the dam and reservoir may depend on the type of trait measured and the focal species.
2212: Rising global temperatures are stressors for many ectotherms, impacting their survival, activity, food acquisition, and metabolism. Oxygen consumption and/or carbon dioxide production have historically been the primary metrics used to measure metabolic rates, but these measures can only be taken in highly controlled lab environments where the animal may be stressed. The ventilation rate, or the number of breaths taken per unit of time, can be used as a proxy for oxygen consumption in wild animals, but few field studies on reptiles have been conducted using this metric. We recorded the resting ventilation rates of wild adult and newborn Prairie Rattlesnakes (Crotalus viridis) using footage from a live-streaming camera at a large rookery in Colorado, where pregnant female rattlesnakes rest and prepare to give birth. We found that neonates had higher ventilation rates than adult snakes, and we noted a negative correlation between the ventilation rate of adult snakes and temperature. Additionally, we often observed snakes of both age classes exhibit breathing bursts, where a given snake would complete several breath cycles in quick succession. These results show that snake ventilation rate differs between age classes, is impacted by temperature, and does not increase with metabolic rate as we predicted. These findings suggest that global warming will likely have varying effects between snake population demographics and that snake ventilation rates are actively regulated in response to temperature changes.
2213: In central Texas, River Carpsucker (Carpiodes carpio) and putative Llano River Carpsucker (C. cf. carpio) are sympatric. C. cf. carpio possess an elongated body with meristic characters and mouth morphology similar to C. cyprinus. The taxon has been identified as a putatively undescribed species by ichthyologists, while the U.S. Geological survey suggests it instead represents C. cyprinus that have been introduced. While phylogenetic analyses and haplotype networks suggest that C. cf. carpio are likely conspecific with C. cyprinus, there are also several shared haplotypes between C. cf. carpio and C. carpio, suggesting that the two may hybridize. We performed genetic distance measurements across mitochondrial and nuclear genes to assess patterns of hybridization between species of Carpiodes across central Texas. Independent Principal Component Analyses (PCAs) on datasets comprising Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) from the mitochondrial CYTB and nuclear IRBP2 genes were created. Our results revealed widespread occurrence of C. cf. carpio mitochondrial DNA in individuals identified as C. carpio. C. carpio of the Colorado and Brazos drainages were found to be genetically identical or minimally distant from C. cf. carpio in the Colorado drainage as suggested by our mitochondrial PCA. Despite this finding, the nuclear PCA revealed C. carpio of the Colorado and Brazos drainages to be genetically distant from C. cf. carpio genotypes. These findings suggest C. cf. carpio readily introgress with C. carpio in the Colorado drainage, while patterns in the Brazos drainage suggest that C. cf. carpio historically were more widespread.
2214: The Sharks and Rays Conservation Research Program at Mote Marine Laboratory has been conducting research on Aetobatus narinari (since 2009) and Mobula hypostoma (since 2013) in the Gulf of Mexico and coastal estuaries near Sarasota, Florida.  During sampling, rays were photographed and evaluated for predatory injuries. Bite marks inflicted by sharks can be used to acquire information about shark size and species, allowing us to gain insight into predator-prey relationships. Bite circumference and interdental distance were measured from photos of 31 M. hypostoma and 24 A. narinari using ImageJ. We evaluated relationships with shark size and species, the location of the bite on the batoid, and batoid size. Preliminary results indicate that for both batoid species, most shark bites occurred on the posterior edge of the wings and the pelvic fins, consistent with field observations of predation events. Most batoids only had evidence of one bite. Based on bite shape, some shark bites are clearly by Galecerdo cuvier, while others can be attributed to various Carcharhinus species. Total length estimates for the various shark species ranged from 0.7 to 3.2 meters. It is important to note that this study examined batoids that have survived predation events, thus we can only make limited inferences about these predator-prey relationships.
2215: Ectotherms are particularly sensitive to changes in temperature and moisture. Most ectotherms exhibit behavior of thermotaxis to balance heat and water retention. Thus, if prescribed burns were to affect the habitat of Eastern Red-backed Salamanders, then the salamander may respond to the changing thermal habitat behaviorally. If prescribed fire creates warmer, drier habitat, then salamanders that prefer cooler, wetter habitat may move away from these habitats. The objective of this project is to determine if there is a difference in thermal preference, critical thermal maximum, and water loss rates of the Eastern Red-backed Salamander from burned and non-burned sites. Preliminary data suggest that there is no difference in the mean of thermal preference between the two groups, but there is less variation within salamanders from burned sites. It is still uncertain whether this means that the salamanders from the burned sites exhibit this behavior because they were the only survivors from the burn or if salamanders that prefer cooler, moister habitat moved out of the warmer site after the burn. These results may also be due to volunteer bias because the salamanders which prefer cooler temperatures may be more fossorial which prevents capture. This study is important because it is imperative to understand the effects of prescribed burns on local wildlife.
2216: Typical skeletal muscle sarcomere structure limits the lengths over which muscle can generate force and power movement, restricting its functional range in most vertebrates. However, chameleons have evolved a unique system of feeding, whereby the tongue is projected out of the mouth at high performance to capture prey up to 2.5 body-lengths away. This extreme elongation is achieved through adaptations to the tongue retractor (m. hyoglossus, MH), which possesses a modified sarcomere structure containing perforated z-discs, allowing increased filament overlap and sustained force production over greater lengths. Hitherto, the MH was the only known supercontracting muscle in vertebrates. We hypothesized that the hyoid retractor muscles (mm. sternohyoideus superficialis (MSS) et profundus (MSP)) which also undergo considerable length change during feeding may benefit from similar supercontractile capacity. To test this, we analyzed length-tension relationship data, performed transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging, and examined embryological origins of muscles of interest. We identified the MSS as the second known supercontracting muscle in vertebrates, exhibiting a similar length-tension relationship to the MH and possessing perforated z-discs. While the MSP also displayed a similarly broadened length-tension curve, its z-discs remained intact, suggesting functional convergence of supercontractile properties through structural adaptations and sarcomere length non-uniformity across muscle fibers. Additionally, both supercontracting muscles (MH and MSS) share a common embryonic origin from occipital somites, which may play a role in the development of their similar sarcomere ultrastructure. These findings reveal important evolutionary and developmental pattens associated with supercontracting muscle and extreme muscle elongation.
2217: The goal of this project is to develop genomic tools, currently lacking in turtles, to advance the use of these non-model taxa (and other reptiles) to study genome-to-phenome mapping, gene function, development, genome architecture, adaptive responses to climate change, and more. To overcome the seasonal reproduction and slow maturation of turtles that hinder their study, we developed gene modification tools in painted turtle fibroblasts by utilizing CRISPR-Cas9 knock-out for gene editing, and RNA interference knock-down for gene silencing. Tools developed in fibroblasts can then be implemented in turtle organoids we have established. Protocols should be applicable to other reptiles. Our growing toolkit for functional genomics using transient transgenic approaches mitigates some of the challenges of studying these long-lived organisms.
2218: Historically, morphology has been an important tool used in taxonomic and evolutionary studies, providing key insights into evolutionary relationships and diversification dynamics. In fishes, morphological characteristics often align with habitat specialization that reflect ecological pressures. Darters are members of Percidae, a highly diverse group of North American freshwater fishes. This family includes several genera with Percina being the only etheostomatine genus that possesses species with functional swim bladders. Limited data exists on swim bladder morphology within Percina, but it is known that some species either lack a swim bladder or possess proportionally large or small swim bladders. Furthermore, some species of Percina previously have been classified as having a benthic life-style, whereas others have been classified as hyperbenthic, suggesting that there may be a relationship between swim bladder morphology and habitat. The aim of this study is to examine variation in swim bladder volume within Percina using micro-computed tomography (microCT scanning). Specimens were prepared following a previously published protocol. Three-dimensional scans of swim bladders from a subset of species of Percina will be presented. We will compare swim bladder morphology and volume for species with benthic and hyperbenthic life-histories.
2219: Vision is a critical sensory system for many animals, directly linking them to fitness through tasks like finding food, selecting mates, and avoiding predators. However, species inhabit diverse light environments, creating selective pressures for visual systems to adapt. At the molecular level, spectral sensitivity can evolve through changes in light-sensitive visual pigments in rod and cone photoreceptors. The most common adaptive mechanism is protein sequence evolution, which can "tune" the wavelength of light pigments are most sensitive to. Our group has collected photoreceptor spectral absorbance and skin reflectance data for ~100 frog species, alongside spectral data from their environments, photoreceptor absorbance data for several frog predators, and ambient light spectra at different times of day. Using a visual modelling framework, we aim to determine the ability of frogs to detect conspecifics, or be detected by predators, against natural backgrounds under varying light conditions, using chromatic and achromatic signals. Within a comparative framework, we will analyze how traits like spectral sensitivity and colouration have evolved across species and identify potential trade-offs between being seen by mates and avoiding predators. For example, how does the reflectance of “green” frogs vary and does this correlate with activity period or predator type? Why do many species have lighter ventral surfaces, but others do not? How might this correlate with aquatic and semi-aquatic vs terrestrial habitats? These findings will be integrated with other ongoing studies to provide a comprehensive understanding of visual and colouration evolution across frogs and improve our understanding across animals more broadly.
2220: The genus Sceloporus, known as blue bellies or spiny lizards, is one of the most conspicuous and abundant lizards in the North American Southwest. Hybridization has been documented between multiple Sceloporus species despite the supposed pre-mating barrier of species-specific throat and belly patches and display behaviors. Sceloporus tristichus and S. occidentalis are sympatric in a small region in southwestern Utah, and some lizards from this zone appear to be morphologically intermediate between the two species. Our work aims to determine whether these intermediates are the result of morphological convergence and/or hybridization owing to the breakdown of pre-mating barriers as observed in other Sceloporus species. Preliminary results based on a mitochondrial and nuclear marker find these intermediate specimens to be S. tristichus. Morphological data show significant differences in patch size and femoral pore counts between S. occidentalis and S. tristichus. Principal component analysis suggests separation between species in the morphospace. While the intermediate specimens patch size falls within the range of S. tristichus, meristic characters place them closer to S. occidentalis. Morphological convergence in this region requires further investigation.
2221: Traditional shark tracking methods, including satellite and acoustic tags, provide valuable data on large-scale movements but lack the fine-scale resolution needed to understand the relationship between swimming kinematics and associated behavior. Some tags incorporate accelerometers, which have been used to infer activity levels. However, they do not provide direct visual confirmation of behaviors, making it difficult to distinguish between different activities such as foraging, schooling, or predator avoidance. To bridge this gap, this study employs animal-borne data logger cameras to quantify the swimming kinematics and behavior of sharks in the wild. The data loggers are temporarily mounted to the dorsal fin of a shark and collect 3-axis acceleration, compass heading, and gyroscopic orientation data simultaneously with a video that records a “shark’s eye view” of the environment. The logger detaches from the shark and is retrieved to download the data. The kinematic data are overlayed on the video to show how the shark moves within each frame. Preliminary trials have shown that the Blacktip shark (Carcharhinus limbatus) exhibits a tail beat frequency (TBF) of 0.909 Hz, consistent with previously reported values for free-swimming individuals observed by aerial drone. This result indicates that the tag package does not seem to impact natural swimming kinematics, validating the approach. This method can reliably reveal how swimming kinematics change with sundry behaviors such as schooling, foraging, feeding, and ascending/descending in the water column. By comparing data across various species, it will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between kinematics and behavior.
2222: Gut contents of juvenile and adult specimens of freshwater Sicydiinae fishes collected globally were examined to catalogue the algal flora ingested by these species.  The algal flora was dominated by benthic stalk forming diatom species.  Diatom taxa represented multiple genera that live in a narrow set of environmental conditions, specifically flow regimes between 0.3 to 0.7 m/s, and dominate during specific stages a successional cycle.   While dental structure varies among the fish species examined, each is an optimal structure for scrapping algae from substrates.  This suggests a highly specialized dietary behavior that depends heavily on continually restarting the benthic algal successional pattern, which appears to be regulated by fish feeding behavior and the hydrological cycles of streams.
2223: The Mississippi Alluvial Plain within northeastern Arkansas has experienced fragmentation and degradation of native wetlands on account of industrial-scale agriculture and other types of habitat alteration. The ACEP Wetland Reserve Easement (WRE) program is a federal initiative that supports land conversion from agricultural fields into wetland habitat for preservation of native species and improvement of landscape functionality.  Amphibians reside in wetlands because of the high availability of food sources and appropriate habitat for breeding and understanding how these species utilize restored wetlands when compared to natural or disrupted lands is imperative for conservation efforts.  We employed a variety of survey techniques uniformly across 40 wetlands that are categorized into three types: (1) Reference, sites over 25 years of age within wildlife refuges that present ideal habitat conditions for amphibians; (2) Control, agricultural ditches that sustain a population of at least one amphibian species; and (3) Restored, parcels under 20 years of age enrolled in the WRE program. Each of the Restored parcels was selected to represent a range of characteristics such as wetland size, age of the easement, and variability in other habitat parameters.  We quantified the richness and evenness of the amphibian community at each site and assessed the relative abundances of different life-history stages of the species present.  We discuss our results in the context of understanding the relationships between habitat characteristics and amphibian diversity, with a primary focus on modeling ecosystem characteristics to optimize conservation efforts in these diverse wetland habitats.
2224: Species reintroduction efforts have historically relied on population demographics rather than genetic diversity to evaluate their success, despite the invaluable information genetic data can provide about the long-term adaptive potential of both the reintroduced and source populations. The genetic evaluations of reintroduction efforts that have been performed for fishes have mostly focused on large bodied, high dispersal species while few evaluations exist for small bodied, low dispersal species such as the Citico Darter (Etheostoma sitikuense). The Citico Darter is a federally endangered fish species native to Citico Creek and Abrams Creek in eastern Tennessee. However, the population in Abrams Creek was extirpated in 1957. In response, the US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and Conservation Fisheries Inc. reintroduced the Citico Darter into Abrams Creek in 1993 and introduced it to the Tellico River in 2003 with continuing population augmentation efforts up until present day. In 2012, the USFWS conducted a genetic assessment of the species in Citico Creek and Abrams Creek using nine microsatellite loci and found low levels of overall genetic diversity and conflicting results regarding population differentiation. Using the same nine microsatellite loci, we will compare contemporary levels of genetic diversity and differentiation in the species to those found in 2012 to evaluate the success of reintroduction and augmentation efforts. We will also generate a contemporary baseline of genetic diversity for all Citico Darter populations using ddRADseq. Thus far, we have collected fin clips from 217 Citico Darters across their entire range and genetic analyses are currently underway.
2225: Fire plays a crucial role in shaping forest ecosystems, yet its effects on small ectothermic organisms, such as the red-backed salamander (Plethodon cinereus), remain understudied. These salamanders rely on cutaneous respiration, making them highly sensitive to environmental moisture and temperature fluctuations, both of which can be altered by prescribed burning. Understanding how fire-induced habitat changes affect their metabolic rate and thermal performance is essential for assessing their resilience to fire management practices. The objective of this study is to determine if metabolic rate differs between P. cinereus in burned and unburned sites. To achieve this, we measured metabolic rates of salamanders from both burned and unburned forest plots at varying temperatures. These physiological traits will be compared to temperatures available in both burned and unburned sites. Preliminary data suggest that metabolic rate may not differ between salamanders in burned and unburned sites. This finding may indicate that salamanders are behaviorally compensating for environmental changes by selecting favorable microhabitats. Additionally, it is possible that metabolic rate is more strongly influenced by intrinsic physiological factors rather than external habitat conditions.
2226: Blue-spotted salamanders (Ambystoma laterale) are primarily found north of the Wisconsin glacial border, where harsh winters are typical; however, the species does not have a cryoprotectant system that allows freezing, and their overwintering behavior is undocumented. This study aims to characterize their overwintering methods and examine if there is any variation between the diploid blue-spotted salamanders (LL) and their triploid-unisexual Jefferson salamander (Ambystoma jeffersonian) hybrids (LLJ). Sixteen PIT-tagged (nine LLJ and seven LL) salamanders were housed outdoors in 10.2 cm x 1.5 m PVC pipes secured together in groups of three to form housing units. Each housing unit was fully buried vertically in the ground, and each salamander-occupied pipe was filled with a soil mix with a leaf litter top layer; an artificial burrow was provided. Salamander depth was monitored via an RFID stick antenna, and salamanders were localized biweekly at noon, with one monthly around-the-clock monitoring. Salamanders remained active throughout the winter, moving deeper during the coldest parts of the season; salamanders moved as deep as 154 cm, well below the frost line. The triploid-unisexual hybrids stayed shallower than their diploid counterparts. There was no observable daily patterning to movements. Our findings suggest that salamanders move substantially throughout the winter, when provisioned with a burrow, and that LL and LLJ salamanders display differences in habitat space utilization. This may relate to habitat partitioning or could be a relict of the origin of the hybrid.
2227: The whitespotted eagle ray, Aetobatus narinari, is endangered throughout the Atlantic and is commonly found in nearshore waters off Florida, where it is considered Least Concern but protected. Previous studies suggest subpopulation structuring in Florida; populations in the Gulf of Mexico exhibit migratory behavior whereas those in the western Atlantic appear to be resident to the Indian River Lagoon. However, the abundance and distribution of A. narinari within the Florida Keys, a critical region for biodiversity, remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study aims to assess the spatiotemporal abundance and behavior of A. narinari in the Florida Keys. Biweekly aerial surveys between Miami and Big Pine Key were conducted in March-June 2023 and 2024-present to document spatiotemporal abundance. Drones were deployed in identified hotspots to track fine-scale movements and record behavior. Preliminary results indicate year-round presence of A. narinari in the Florida Keys, with peak abundance during April and May. Habitats near Key Biscayne and Tavernier Key are hotspots across multiple months, with observed foraging and pre-mating behaviors. These preliminary findings suggest a partial migration through the Keys, highlighting the ecological importance of this region. The continuation of aerial surveys through the end of 2025 and beyond will generate multi-year data on the spatiotemporal abundance and behavior of A. narinari, providing valuable information for the effective management of this protected species, supporting sustainable ray populations and marine ecosystems in Florida.
2228: The Flathead Catfish (Ictaluridae: Pylodictis olivaris) is a widely distributed monotypic species with native populations occurring from the Apalachicola River in the southeast United States, to Texas' Rio Grande basin, and northward through Mississippi River and Great Lake basins. Currently Flathead Catfish are found throughout the United States prolifically along the Atlantic slope, due to introduction. However, with the exception of a single mitochondrial study, little is known about the distribution of P. olivaris genetic diversity. Herein, we conducted a phylogeographic study to examine genome-wide genetic variation across the native range of P. olivaris. To date, we have collected specimens through collaborations with natural resource agencies and university personnel from Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Wisconsin. We used Double-Digest Restriction Associated DNA (ddRADseq) genotyping to gather single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data collected from 30 individuals. The SNP data was analyzed using a suite of population and phylogenetic analyses and our results indicate that there is significant genetic variation across the range of P. olivaris. The implications of these results and the future directions of this study will be presented.
2229: Large sharks are among the few known predators of marine mammals, but remarkably few direct observations of predatory interactions between sharks and marine mammals have been recorded. Here we present aerial observations of two dusky sharks (Carcharhinus obscurus) killing and consuming a gray seal (Halichoerus grypus) in the waters off Nantucket, Massachusetts, USA. Based on additional footage obtained by beachgoers and boaters, at least three other gray seals were consumed by dusky sharks in the area during the summer of 2023. The observations presented here provide new insights into the feeding ecology of dusky sharks, which were previously not known to be direct predators of pinnipeds.
2230: The sexual development of red-eared sliders (Trachemys scripta elegans) is highly influenced by environmental factors. In this species, temperature and steroid hormones alter gonad development, and it is likely that environmental factors influence other organs as well. The kidneys, for example, are near the gonads and oviducts, and are essential for maintaining electrolyte, mineral, and fluid levels as well as waste management, but environmental effects on the development of this organ have not been explored. In this study, we will describe the macro- and microscopic anatomy of the kidneys after temperature and hormone manipulation during embryo development. Eggs were incubated at one of five temperatures (24, 26, 28, 30, & 32ºC), and treated with either estradiol, fadrozole, or ethanol (control). For this species, lower incubation temperatures produce males and higher temperatures produce females. Estradiol is a female producing hormone and fadrozole will inhibit estradiol production. At hatching, each individual was weighed and measured, and their sex will be identified through dissection and histological analysis. After dissection, renal thickness, length, width, mass and volume will be recorded. The control results will provide a basis for the macro and microscopic kidney anatomy, which is poorly described in red-eared slider hatchlings. This study will be one of the first to describe the effects of developmental environments on the kidney, which has critical physiological functions that influence individual performance and fitness.
2231: Microplastics are a pollutant that can be found in every ecosystem on Earth. Despite how widespread these pollutants are, their effects on many species are still unknown. Aquatic species' exposed to high levels of microplastics have had negative impacts when looking at both behavioral and physiological changes. Impacts of environmentally realistic levels of microplastics are less understood. This makes examining bioindicator species, such as tadpoles, a critical step to understanding the effects of microplastics within aquatic ecosystems. This study examined Xenopus laevis tadpoles and the effects of microplastics on the gut morphology of tadpoles post-mortem. Tadpoles were exposed to either no microplastics or 10 ug/L of microplastics. After three weeks of exposure, normality of gut coiling, number of gut coils in the intestines, and gut length were measured. The results showed that Xenopus laevis tadpoles exposed to microplastics had shorter gut lengths and fewer gut coils. These results confirm a change in gut morphology in Xenopus laevis tadpoles exposed to microplastics. More research is needed to determine how this may change digestion efficiency. Understanding the impacts of microplastics on amphibians can provide insights into the effects of plastic pollution in aquatic ecosystems and contribute to global conservation efforts.
2232: Atlantic (Hypanus sabinus) and Bluntnose (Hypanus say) stingrays are two benthic species found in coastal waters in the western Atlantic Ocean, including estuaries and lagoons. While both species appear abundant in their respective ranges, the IUCN evaluated both populations as decreasing. Basic life-history information concerning H. sabinus and H. say is also lacking or incomplete. This project will assess the age, growth, maturity, and reproductive patterns of H. sabinus and H. say stingray populations. Specimens have been collected monthly since July 2023 from the Indian River Lagoon (IRL), an estuarine ecosystem located along the east coast of Florida, via a collaboration with Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s (FWC) Fisheries Independent Monitoring program (FIM). Age and growth models will be developed using vertebral band counts and corresponding morphometric measurements including disk width (DW) and total weight (TW). Stage of maturity for each specimen is assessed based on extragonadal tract development, vas deferens coiling, and clasper length and calcification in males, and tract development and ovarian/uterine tract development in females. Collections to date include 156 H. sabinus (female: n=82, 100 to 316 mm DW; male: n=74, 112 to 379 mm DW) and 134 H. say (female: n=68, 156 to 575 mm DW; male: n=66, 110 to 451 mm DW). The results of this study will increase our understanding of these two species and provide the information required for their increased conservation.
2233: The vast majority of squamate reptiles lay leathery, soft-shelled eggs. Within squamates however, two lineages have evolved calcified eggshells: the relatively small group of legless lizards in the family Dibamidae and geckos (Gekkota). Geckos further stand apart in that three families (Gekkonidae, Phyllodactylidae, and Sphaerodactylidae) lay eggs with a rigid eggshell, while others (Carphodactylidae, Diplodactylidae, Eublepharidae, and Pygopodidae) lay soft-shelled eggs like all other squamates. Moreover, geckos share calcified egg evolution with Testudines, Crocodyliformes, and Dinosauria (including birds). Of the aforementioned groups, the molecular composition of bird eggshells has received extensive attention, with most proteins associated with calcified eggshells having been characterized across several lineages. In this study, we analyzed the molecular composition of the gekkotan eggshell using orthologous genes known to be involved in calcified eggshell formation in birds. The evolutionary implications of this study are discussed with special emphasis on divergence within gekkotans, between geckos and other squamates, as well as convergence between the Archosauria and Gekkota.
2234: The use of eDNA has emerged as a particularly useful tool to document the presence and distribution of species. Standard eDNA metabarcoding analyses rely on the sequencing of short DNA fragments typically less than 300 bp long using the short fragment sequencing platform, Illumina. However, traditional DNA barcoding relies on fragments >600bp long that provide more data for identification of closely related species and other molecular ecology applications. Here, we examine whether there is a significant difference between the use of short and traditional length DNA fragments for detection of target fish species from aquatic eDNA using Nanopore sequencing, a platform capable of sequencing long DNA fragments on a genomic scale. Two experiments were conducted to detect target fish species, one in which water was collected from tanks harboring a lab colony of the Mexican tetra and the other using water collected from Lake Michigan in Chicago, where invasive round goby are abundant. eDNA was extracted from the water, three popular DNA barcoding genes, COI, 12S and 16S, were PCR amplified using primers that amplify either short (~200 bp) fragments or long (>500 bp) fragments and then sequenced using the Oxford Nanopore Minion sequencer. In both experiments, detection of target species was more successful using short fragments and the ribosomal rRNA genes. We recommend using primers that amplify short DNA fragments for eDNA analysis of aquatic communities, even with sequencing platforms capable of sequencing long fragments, and including rRNA barcoding genes to maximize species detection probabilities.
2235: With over 230 taxa in twelve genera, chameleons exhibit an incredible amount of diversity in their morphology, ecology and behavior. While much of their anatomical diversity is evident from their extreme body size variation and diverse external ornamentations, many of the internal structural differences that contribute to their variation has been less well examined. Among the most variable skeletal features in chameleons is the number of presacral and caudal vertebrae, as well as the number of sternal and parasternal ribs. We performed counts of axial skeletal elements from µCT scans of chameleon specimens representing more than 70% of the described species diversity and all genera, and phylogenetic comparative methods to provide insight into the phylogenetic and ecological drivers underlying this variation. We tested for effects of body size and the degree of arboreality on observed variation in axial skeletal element counts, and ancestral state reconstructions to assess where in the phylogeny specific changes in morphology occurred. From these analyses, we show that body size and arboreality are significant predictors of variation in multiple axial skeleton elements. We also document a previously unknown synapomorphy for one of the twelve chameleon genera, which show a reduction in cervical vertebrae and ribs relative to all other genera. These results suggest that both ecological and phylogenetic factors have played important roles in shaping patterns of axial skeleton variation in the Chamaeleonidae. More broadly, these results also provide insight into the morphological evolution of the axial skeleton across disparate ecologies and environments.
2236: Freshwater sculpin in the Pacific Northwest have long befuddled taxonomists and resource managers. Their identification is clouded by a myriad of overlapping morphological characters. Dichotomous keys lead to murky choices based on spurious character states. Recent molecular studies brought forth tantalizing evidence of undescribed diversity, with potentially many new species. We are following up on one such study of the subgenus Cottopsis from Washington, Oregon, and California, which found strong evidence of monophyly of nine recognized species, as well as at least five undescribed clades. Focusing only on the clades from Washington and Oregon, we are gathering morphological data from the same museum specimens used in the molecular analysis that had been identified as four nominal species. We are using traditional morphometrics and meristics, together with micro CT scans, clearing and staining, and 3D morphometrics to elucidate any characters useful for species identification. Using specimens of known genetic affinity removes the bias of misguided taxonomy that has hampered previous attempts at identification. Preliminary results show there may be validity to some traditional characters, e.g. head, mouth, and body width, but many characters show broad overlap between all clades. Subjective characters such as a round vs pointed snout seem uninformative. Palatine teeth, thought to be variable in two of the species, seem to only be absent in Cottus perplexus from the type locality. These data will eventually be combined with similar efforts for the entire Cottopsis clade in hopes of accurately describing the true diversity of this enigmatic group of fishes.
2237: Abstract—The purpose of this poster is to provide an open forum for discussions with the leadership of the American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists (ASIH). What can we do better to (1) grow and support our diverse membership, especially students; (2) foster greater membership involvement and organizational fiscal stability; (3) improve JMIH and Ichthyology & Herpetology; (4) prioritize resources to meet future obligations and goals; and (5) reinforce what we already do well? We can also deliberate the future of ichthyology and herpetology or anything else members wish to discuss with the President, President-Elect, and other members of ASIH leadership. We are here to listen to compliments, critiques, and ideas to improve our Society. We will also share drink tickets with members who stop by to chat!
2238: Ten species of barbs (Cyprinidae, Smiliogastrinae) were examined using vital fluorescent staining (4-di-2-ASP; 2 indiv./sp.) to determine neuromast distributions and SEM to determine neuromast shape and physiological orientation (axis of best physiological sensitivity to flows). A total of 340-2101 diamond-shaped superficial neuromasts (SNs) were found: on the head (up to 668 SNs), trunk (up to 1163 SNs), and caudal fin (up to 236 SNs) among all study species. SNs occur in lines, clusters, and fields on the head, with dramatic variation in SN patterns among taxa.  On the trunk, up to 27 SNs occur in a vertical line on each LL scale (total of up to 377 SNs), and a vertical line of up to 18 SNs occurs on some or all non-LL scales, depending on species. Within each line (on head and trunk), SNs are in a “tip to tip” arrangement, with physiological orientation perpendicular to the line. On the caudal fin, a total of up to 236 SNs are found in 4 to >11 lines in the membranes between fin rays. In contrast to lines on the head and trunk, SNs within lines on the caudal fin are placed “side by side”, with physiological orientation parallel to the line. Organization of the SNs in barbs was compared to that in other cypriniforms (e.g., zebrafish, goldfish, silverjaw minnow, European and Asian minnows) to identify conserved patterns and sources of variation, which should indicate the relative contribution of the LL system to sensory inputs underlying key behaviors among species.
2239: Hybridization plays a complex role in evolution, from influencing adaptations through introgression to shaping species boundaries. Plethodon cinereus and P. electromorphus are two terrestrial woodland salamanders with broad overlapping distributions throughout Ohio. Molecular clocks studies estimate that they diverged approximately 10 million years ago—long enough that hybridization might be expected to be rare. Previous studies have left the extent unclear, as early inferences were based on limited data.
