Our work expanded upon previous research by including temperature treatments in the experimental trials. The trials will be repeated in the Spring 2025 field season. Preliminary results suggest that of all explored variables, the amount of precipitation in the week prior to collection has the greatest effect on their ability to rehydrate after a dehydration event. We predict that this trend will continue into the Spring 2025 field season. The goal of this study is to provide support for the creation and implementation of conservation plans. These findings will be critical for incorporating P. cinereus’ response to changing environmental conditions into such management practices.
2293: Modern technology has vastly increased our access to information. While this access is in many ways beneficial, it has also resulted in a proliferation of misleading work. Understanding how to critically evaluate different sources of information is an important aspect of science education that can help prevent misconceptions and bolster trust in scientific institutions. I designed a seminar course for upper level life-science majors to critically evaluate media sources, while teaching them how to conduct background research using the primary literature. I chose to use nature documentaries in various formats (TikTok, short tv episodes, longer movie-like documentaries) to get students thinking about how they apply their scientific knowledge in their day-to-day lives. The format of this course enabled students to gain a broader understanding of how to critically evaluate media sources while gaining the ability to search and use the primary literature to find trusted information. A theme that unexpectedly emerged throughout the class was how do scientists (and how should scientists) communicate science to a public audience that may have differing levels of interest, knowledge, and understanding of science in order to increase scientific literacy and trust in science. This poster will outline the major assignments used in the course, key take-aways about student learning, and future directions. I will provide some recommendations for those interested in developing similar courses or assignments that engage students using modern media.
2294: The James F. Scudday Vertebrate Collection at Sul Ross State University contains significant coverage of the vertebrate specimens from the Trans Pecos and surrounding area, including notable contributions from Big Bend National Park. Many of the specimens were collected by the late Dr. James F. Scudday, a leader in regional vertebrate research. This collection serves as a vital resource for research focused on the biodiversity and ecology of the region. The collection contains approximately 1,300 amphibians, 6,257 reptiles,1,243 birds, and 2,871 mammals for a total of ~11,671 specimens. This project is actively digitizing the James F. Scudday vertebrate collection and preserving and clarifying the information before it is lost. The digitization is being conducted utilizing a Canon EOS-1DX Mark II DSLR. These high-quality photographs along with their respective identification tag are saved and are available for use by students, community members, and outside researchers. The collection data is cross-referenced as photographs are taken to determine the quality of the specimen and to check if locality data may require some updating. As many researchers know, museum collections before advanced use of GPS devices relied on descriptions of the locations. Many locations are often lost with the passing of the individual that made the collection. We have discussed with local experts who collected alongside our biggest contributor to help clarify some of the specimen localities for the collection. Through this continued effort, we want to encourage people to reach out and utilize the information in our collection.
2295: Batrachochytrium dendrobatis (Bd), the amphibian chytrid fungus, exists in suitable aquatic habitats across much of the United States Midwest and East Coast. Both biotic and abiotic habitat characteristics may help explain the presence of Bd in aquatic systems. While much research has been conducted regarding how environmental factors, such as climatic variables and water quality, as well as amphibian host presence, influence Bd persistence in ecosystems, shocking little work has been conducted to understand how non-amphibian members of ecosystems may interact with this pathogen. This collection of studies aims to identify arthropod species that may be acting as pathogen reservoirs within systems, or acting as fomites which can transmit this pathogen among ponds and wetlands. Using quantitative PCR, our team has identified multiple taxa, including Daphnia, copepods, Notonectid backswimmers, and Chironomid midges, which appear to directly interact with Bd by changing its abundance in controlled experiments. Further, we have demonstrated that water striders from the family Gerridae can transmit Bd on their surface from one location to another. Together this work suggests that complex ecological interactions between amphibians, non-amphibian animals, and Bd may be contributing to the persistence and spread of Bd in aquatic habitats.
2296: The introduction of Burmese pythons in Florida resulted in an ecological disaster for the Florida Everglades, but the scope and extent of the disaster spreads further than range of pythons. Parasites that were introduced to North America from pythons are spilling over into native taxa. The focus of this study is the Asian pentastome, Raillietiella orientalis. The introduced endoparasite now infects at least 18 native snake species of Florida as adults and has been documented as larvae in frogs and lizards. The spread of these parasites has been swift: documentation of the species now extends to the Florida panhandle. This range expansion along with the potential impacts on native taxa requires a thorough examination of the species. In this study, we assess the population genetic patterns present in R. orientalis across three widespread snake hosts: Coluber constrictor, Nerodia spp., and Agkistrodon piscivorus. We compare the genetic patterning of the parasites with respect to the distribution and behavior of their hosts.
2297: Understanding natural variability in population and community dynamics of amphibians is critical to differentiate those dynamics from true population declines. We monitored an amphibian community using a partial drift fence around an ephemeral pond on the Southern Illinois University Edwardsville campus from 2023-2024. We monitored it daily from the start of the amphibian breeding season (~February) until pond drying in each summer. We detected eight amphibian species in each year, with Southern leopard frogs being the most common adult anuran and smallmouth salamanders the most common adult caudate. Most adult movement patterns were tied to rainfall events and in a predictable pattern each year: tiger salamanders arrived first, followed by smallmouth salamanders, Southern leopard frogs, boreal chorus frogs, spring peepers and American toads arriving last. Recruitment differences in each year were driven by hydroperiod. The pond dried in late May in 2023, resulting only two individuals across all species completing metamorphosis. In 2024, where pond drying occurred in early July, tiger and smallmouth salamanders, Southern leopard frogs, spring peepers and American toads all had substantial (> 100 individuals) recruitment. This work highlights the importance of hydroperiod on amphibian population dynamics and sets baseline population and community levels for ongoing monitoring at this study site.
2298: Cryptobenthic reef fishes (CRFs) are small (less than 5 cm) fishes that live in crevices on or near the benthos. CRFs represent at least 40% of all reef fish species, though remain under-described due to their small size, limited mobility, and rapid diversification among niches. Our study examines a species complex within the cryptobenthic dwarfgoby Eviota lachdeberei to determine whether genetic and morphological data support the recognition of multiple species.  Our DNA barcoding data indicate the presence of 4 divergent mitochondrial lineages within the Coral Triangle. We compared morphometric and meristic characteristics of 18 specimens that include our genetic vouchers and type specimens of Eviota lachdeberei and Eviota partimacula, a morphologically similar species. E. lachdeberei specimens came from the Coral Triangle (a region including Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, and the Solomon Islands); E. partimacula specimens came from the Marshall Islands. We conducted a principal component analysis (PCA) to compare morphological traits across all specimens and to compare these groupings with the E. lachdeberei groupings from our COI tree.  Our ongoing molecular and morphological analyses will help clarify the taxonomy of these cryptic species, potentially revealing new patterns in reef biodiversity and speciation within the most diverse marine ecoregion in the world.
2299: Salamanders with biphasic life cycles (aquatic larvae to terrestrial adults) offer a unique opportunity to investigate how eye morphology adapts to ecological transitions, particularly in species that differ in their post-metamorphic use of aquatic habitats. We compare eye structure between two groups: (1) permanently terrestrial salamanders (Dicamptodon tenebrosus and Ambystoma gracile) that abandon water after metamorphosis and (2) newts (Taricha granulosa and T. rivularis) that return to aquatic environments as breeding adults. Using microCT data obtained from MorphoSource and new scans of specimens deposited in the Vertebrate Museum at Cal Poly Humboldt, we test whether these groups exhibit divergent ocular adaptations. Following findings from a recent study on frogs showing aquatic species retain spherical lenses while terrestrial forms develop flatter lenses, we predict that (1) permanently terrestrial species will develop flatter lenses (lower sphericity) as adults, optimizing vision in air, and (2) newts will retain more spherical, larval-like lenses to accommodate both terrestrial and aquatic vision. Our study leverages innovative imaging to link morphological variation with ecological divergence in salamanders, providing a broad comparative analysis of eye structure evolution in this group. Results will clarify how repeated transitions between aquatic and terrestrial habitats shape sensory anatomy, with implications for understanding the plasticity of visual systems across vertebrates.
2300: African pompano (Alectis ciliaris) is an important species in commercial markets and can fetch up to $25/pound. Despite this, nothing is known about their basic biology which is often used when making management decisions. We sought to fill this gap and describe the age, growth, diet and reproduction of the African pompano from Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina. Following collection by fishermen, basic morphological variables were measured and gonads, guts and otoliths were removed. We found that this species is a rapidly growing fish reaching 5.5 kg in their first two years. The oldest individual analyzed here (9 years) weighed 17.7 kg. Though most stomachs were empty, we found that this species feeds primarily on cephalopods including squid and octopus. Fish parts were infrequently found inside the guts. Finally, reproductive capacity was highly variable among individuals. We found a positive relationship between the relative weight made up by the gonads and total weight. Furthermore, we found a positive relationship between female fecundity and age. Surprisingly, there was no relationship between fecundity/egg condition and date collected suggesting that these fish spawn all summer rather than preparing for a massive spawning event. With this research we reveal some important basic biological features of the African pompano. Additionally, this information can be used by managers worldwide to create science backed management policies.
2301: Recent phylogenetic studies have reshaped our understanding of the genera Noblella and Psychrophrynella (Anura: Strabomantidae). Inferred relationships based on molecular data revealed that, despite their similar morphology, species of Noblella actually belong to two non-sister clades. One clade ranges from northern Peru to Ecuador and southeastern Colombia, while the other one, which is paraphyletic with respect to Psychrophrynella, extends from southeastern Peru through northeastern Bolivia and into adjacent regions of Brazil. Recent studies provided new genetic data through the rediscovery and sequencing of the type species of those genera, N. peruviana and P. bagrecito that led to the synonymization of Psychrophrynella with Noblella. However, the assignment of the name N. bagrecito to a population did not rely on name-bearing types. To test this assignment, we extracted and sequenced DNA from a formalin-fixed paratype of N. bagrecito. The resulting sequence is genetically identical to an unnamed clade that was not recognized as N. bagrecito, suggesting that current taxonomic assignments may not reflect the original type designation. Our findings demonstrate the critical role of obtaining molecular data from name-bearing types to ensure taxonomic decisions are anchored to their original definitions. They also illustrate the value of museum collections in clarifying taxonomic uncertainties.
2302: We used three decades of long-term amphibian data for three species (Pseudacris maculata, Lithobates sylvaticus and Ambystoma mavortium) and a Bayesian occupancy modeling framework to estimate changes in occupancy, colonization, and persistence of amphibians across Rocky Mountain National Park and explore mechanisms (e.g., precipitation, drought, visitor use) behind observed changes. Our results indicate that the probability of colonization of previously unoccupied catchments is low, the probability of persistence is declining for all three species; and that occupied catchments are increasingly isolated. A higher proportion of popular trails in a catchment affected initial probability of occupancy negatively, and increasing visitor use negatively affected the probability of persistence of amphibians. In contrast, increased complexity in vegetation was associated with increased persistence and colonization. This information provides a perspective across time in a protected area where change may be less obvious or occur more slowly than in unprotected areas and is useful in planning and implementing appropriate management and conservation actions.
2303: Science illustrations are accurate and informative visualizations created for the purpose of communicating science. They can be a powerful tool to support scientific research by visually explaining and enhancing the accessibility for the viewer. Biological research including evolution, ecology, genetics, physiology, pathology, systematics, conservation etc. concerns intangible or invisible processes. Visual aids can help conceptualize the idea, and can be useful for visualizing 1) the morphological traits of the specimen, and 2) the mechanisms of phenomena. First, illustrations allow the artist and researcher full control over the presentation of visual information. For example, a subject could be rendered with neutral lighting to depict accurate colors, or in an idealized posture for comparisons across taxa. This can be especially important in herpetology and ichthyology because of their highly diverse interspecific and intraspecific variations. While photography is a great tool for documentation, a photo will always be affected by the quality of the light source and a subject's irregularities or imperfections, which may be difficult to capture sufficient detail alone. Second, the ability to visualize mechanisms or processes through abstraction is another strength of illustration. The artist can choose how to simplify findings to deliver information most efficiently in a diagram, graph, or through data visualization. For example, graphical representation can better communicate the phylogenetic relationships, physiological reactions or its role in the ecosystem. The poster would highlight a variety of science illustration methods which can support research and enhance viewer understanding and participation in various ways.
2304: The majority of marine biogeography and biodiversity studies have focused on the tropics, especially ‘biodiversity hotspots’ like the Coral Triangle and Caribbean. However, recent work suggests that speciation rates are higher at high latitudes, likely associated with greater physiological adaptation required by colder and deeper waters. One high-latitude area of interest is the 1.5 million square miles of waters surrounding Alaska, which supports high biodiversity and biomass, fueling booming commercial fisheries that average $4.5 billion/year. This vast area encompasses multiple biogeographic regions, including the temperate Gulf of Alaska, the diverse Aleutian Islands, the productive Bering Sea, and the ice-influenced Arctic. Each area has been sculpted by a dynamic geologic history of glaciers, sea level changes, land bridges, ice cover, and currents. Here we investigate how complex geologic and oceanographic history has driven speciation in the region, creating a high-latitude biodiversity hotspot, using both phylogeographic analyses (population genetics, time calibrated trees, and ancestral range reconstruction) and population ecology (hierarchical clustering, alpha-, beta- and gamma-diversity metrics). Specifically highlighting evolutionary relationships of fish species complexes that span these regions and share similar phylogeographic histories. Utilizing contemporary biodiversity data from the Alaska Fisheries Science Center groundfish surveys we model species distributions, investigate patterns of species richness, and examine current biogeographic region boundaries. Our findings may help refine management units to ensure conservation of both species and genetic diversity and showcase why cold waters deserve just as much focus as the tropics.
2305: The field of herpetology has been an inspiration for many individuals and continues to allow for an intersection of multiple fields of research to converge on the Class Reptilia and Amphibia. Study of herpetology is increasingly important given that many species are experiencing declines. Historically, systemic barriers have limited participation in the field, particularly for individuals from underrepresented backgrounds. The Herpetologists’ League (HL) is committed to addressing and dismantling these barriers to actively build community by fostering community, supporting equitable access, and expanding opportunities for engagement at all career stages. Through new initiatives, we seek to magnify connections across geographical space and foster new collaborations throughout the field. With ongoing efforts, including a student mentoring program, a free student membership drive, the revitalization of the student committee, and efforts to broaden participation through travel support, virtual resources, and recorded professional development workshops, the HL Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Committee remains committed to supporting and building community among current and future herpetologists. We share current initiatives and seek feedback on new and creative efforts to promote access to the field of herpetology.
2306: Amphilius, a genus of mountain catfishes, native to African freshwaters, represent a fascinating group for studying biodiversity and evolutionary relationships. These fishes tend to radiate into clades of morphologically similar species, presenting challenges for accurate identification and highlighting the importance of integrating morphological and genetic analysis to uncover cryptic diversity within this group. This pilot study combines preliminary mitochondrial COI gene sequences with traditional morphometrics and radiograph-enabled meristics to explore the diversity and relationships within Amphilius in the West Central African country of Gabon. Our results revealed seven distinct mitochondrial lineages within the samples, several of which may represent species previously unknown to science. These findings suggest that the current taxonomy of Amphilius in this region underestimates its true diversity. The analysis set the stage for future exploration of landmark-based geometric morphometrics to evaluate variations in body shape and microCT scanning to generate detailed 3D reconstructions of skeletal structures. These investigations will assess whether there are multiple, distinct species that have not been recognized or described due to their morphological similarities and if these species are genetically distinct, representing separate evolutionary lineages. The findings from this preliminary study will lay the groundwork for the development of accurate taxonomic keys and a suitable framework for species identification.
2307: Understanding the immune system of wild vertebrates is essential for assessing the health of populations, including both survival and reproductive potential. Reptile immune performance, and how it is affected by the natural environment, has been historically understudied. Our study examined the relationship between parasitism and immunocompetence in a population of red-sided garter snakes (Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis) in Manitoba, Canada, specifically focusing on males that display overt signs of parasitism. Some males in the population have shortened, swollen ("stubby") tails caused by trematode infection (Alaria mesocercariae) that confers a significant fitness deficit by reducing mating competitiveness. We therefore asked if parasitized males may exhibit altered immunity compared to non-parasitized males. During the spring breeding season (May 2024) at a well-studied hibernaculum, we opportunistically collected stubby (n=25) and normal males (n=311). All snakes were weighed and measured and the data log-transformed to obtain body condition (linear residuals). From the plot, each parasitized male was then size-matched with a similar control male (n=25) to control for any condition effects. Blood samples were then collected to create smears and obtain plasma for performing bacterial killing assays (BKA). Total cell counts were conducted per slide via Ilastik (AI-based software) and ImageJ, and immune cell types, including heterophils, lymphocytes, and monocytic cells (monocytes and azurophils), were counted manually. We saw no effect of overt parasitism on any aspect of the immune cell counts, and after combining the stubby and control male datasets we found that the proportion of monocytes/total leukocytes was negatively correlated with both lymphocyte and heterophil proportions. Further, lymphocyte proportion was negatively correlated with male body size, corroborating studies in multiple groups of vertebrates. Our study is unique in that all males were actively courting females at the time and had recently emerged from long-duration brumation (~8 months), indicating that the immunity patterns we observed may represent a biological optimum for sustained, high-endurance activity.
2308: Among Lake Malawi cichlids, feeding behaviors span a continuum from suction to scraping, likely influenced in part by cranial morphology. To investigate this relationship, we used geometric morphometrics to assess shape variation in the neurocranium of wild-caught cichlids from four rock-dwelling genera—Labeotropheus, Tropheops, Petrotilapia, and Maylandia. We then conducted a principal component analysis (PCA) which revealed interspecific variation in the vomer, a bone at the anterior tip of the neurocranium, with angles ranging from acute to obtuse (relative to the parasphenoid). To test functional implications, we recorded feeding strikes (i.e. suction and scraping) in lab-reared individuals of the same genera using high-speed video (550 fps). Fish were fed Daphnia to elicit suction behavior, and preliminary analyses suggest a relationship between vomer angle and jaw movement. Individuals with acutely angled vomers, such as Labeotropheus and Tropheops, tend to rotate their jaws ventrally during strikes, while those with more obtuse angled vomers, such as Petrotilapia, and Maylandia, project their jaws anteriorly. Fish were given an algal mat to elicit scraping behavior, where we note an association between vomer angle and body orientation. For example, at the extremes, we observe Labeotropheus consistently feeding with a shallow body angle (~45°) relative to the substrate, aligning with its ventral jaw protrusion. In contrast, Petrotilapia feeds nearly perpendicular (~90°) to the substrate, using its anteriorly projecting jaws to graze. Together, these data aim to clarify how variation in vomer morphology influences feeding behavior and contributes to differences in ecological specialization among closely related cichlid species.
2309: The genus Agama is a group of highly conspicuous diurnal, insectivorous lizards with striking sexually dimorphic coloration. Despite their abundance and nearly universal presence in the region, a high degree of morphological conservatism, incomplete taxon sampling, and inadequate geographic coverage has resulted in uncertainties with respect to species boundaries and the validity of certain taxa. Existing work on southern African ground agamas has historically emphasized patterns within South Africa, but the ranges of two highly widespread taxa (A. anchietae, A. aculeata) extend well beyond its borders. In this study, we utilize more representative geographic coverage across their ranges (chiefly by the inclusion of specimens from Angola and Namibia) and increased gene sampling to generate robust molecular phylogenies in maximum likelihood and Bayesian frameworks using a combination of two mitochondrial genes (ND4, 16s) and three nuclear genes (PDKREJC, PNN, SETX). We uncover reciprocally monophyletic, previously undescribed deep divergences within A. aculeata and A. anchietae with geographical significance. We have obtained and annotated low-coverage genomic sequences for most taxa, which represent the first genomic data available for the genus Agama.  Mitochondrial gene order is generally considered to be highly conserved, especially within vertebrates. Currently, only 112 incidences of mitogenomic rearrangements have been confirmed within all of Lacertilia. Whole mitochondrial sequences in all sampled taxa of southern African Agama share a mitochondrial gene rearrangement previously undescribed in any other vertebrate, which lends credence to the growing notion that the conserved nature of mitochondrial gene order may be overstated due to poor sampling.
SSAR Siebert - Conservation, Evolution and Systematics
2310: Gender equality remains a major issue globally. Though progress has been made, the number of women is lower than that of men at all career stages, and data shows that representation decreases as the career stage increases. Societal structures, cultures, norms, and traditions have been identified as factors contributing to gender inequality. However, exposure to diverse role models and broader representation within STEM have a positive effect on the recruitment and retention of students and early-career biologists, especially from underrepresented groups in STEM. To increase the visibility of women in herpetology across disciplines, regions, and cultural backgrounds, we formed the Global Women in Herpetology Project and gathered herpetologists from 50 countries and regions. Collectively, we published “Women in Herpetology: 50 Stories from Around the World,” which contains short stories in which each herpetologist shares a personal narrative that intersects their gender, cultural background, and professional journey. We then used the profits of the book to establish a conference scholarship for female students in underrepresented regions around the world. Through this initiative, we hope to promote further opportunities for collaborations and mentorships for women in the field of herpetology and to engage more people to join our efforts. The next phase of this project is to widely translate the “Women in Herpetology” book into different languages, starting with Spanish and Chinese. Through this initiative, our aim is to collectively place a spotlight on the diversity of women in our field and encourage more young people to enter the field of herpetology.
2311: For many nocturnal animals, moonlight—the primary source of natural nighttime illumination—is a key determinant of predation risk. Nocturnal prey often rely on non-visual senses and have poor dim-light visual acuity, whereas visually oriented predators typically experience improved hunting success under brighter conditions. As such, non-visual prey are generally expected to suppress activity during moonlit periods to avoid detection. Because the moonlight cycle varies in a complex but predictable manner, some nocturnal species may anticipate moonlight timing  via an endogenous circalunar rhythm. However, this has rarely been demonstrated. We document a striking case of moonlight avoidance in the electric sand knifefish (Gymnorhamphichthys rondoni), which inhabits Amazonian streams where visual predators are common. These fish rely on active electroreception to forage in darkness, but its short range (<10 cm) is ineffective for predator detection. Using custom field loggers to detect electric signals, we monitored their activity across a lunar cycle alongside moonlight illuminance measurements. Sand knifefish tracked the shifting timing of moonlight, hiding in the sand during moonlit periods and sacrificing ~25% of their foraging time over the lunar cycle. An increase in electric discharge rate during the afternoon—an indicator of readiness to emerge that night—was observed on days when the moon was due to rise after sunset. This anticipatory increase was significantly reduced during full moon and two days prior, when bright moonlight was already present after sunset. These results suggest that sand knifefish anticipated moonlight conditions hours before nightfall while still buried during the day.
2312: Traditionally, baited hoop-nets and fyke nets are the primary means by which aquatic turtles have been detected during surveys, but when the goal is to map distributions, capturing turtles is a time-consuming excess compared to a birding-derived approach called digiscoping. Nets cannot be deployed in rivers during flood conditions, especially when the water is full of debris. Moreover, where we work, in Kansas, nearly all rivers are privately owned, so public access is limited to rights-of-way along roads at bridges. Riverine turtles are, thus, relatively rarely encountered and documented by museum herpetologists or on iNaturalist.com. Digiscoping opens that frontier. We survey ~150 m up and downstream at bridges with a spotting scope and photograph turtles at 80–300´ for vouchers. Prior to our visual surveys, Graptemys geographica was known in Kansas from 9 specimens collected 1911–1952 in 6 counties, went unrecorded 1953–1989, was rediscovered in 1990–1991 through extensive trapping that yielded 10 individuals in 4 counties, went unvouchered 1992–2016, and was found in 2017–2019 with laborious trapping that yielded 8 individuals. In fall 2018, we started digiscoping and, via modest efforts through early 2022, found 135 individuals at 79 locations (including 9 new county records). Consequently, Graptemys geographica was recently removed from state-threatened status. Digiscoping also yielded many other Emydid (6 taxa), Trionychid (2 spp.), and Chelydra serpentina records. Only Sternotherus odoratus went almost undetected. Graptemys geographica aside, we now average 0.67 new county records and 2.7 new drainage records within counties per field day.
2313: Alligator mississippiensis populations have recovered throughout so much of their range that regulated harvest now occurs in all but one state. The northwestern range limit of A. mississippiensis extends to southeastern Oklahoma, and little is known about the status of the population there. To better inform future management actions, we conducted surveys for alligators at 39 water bodies across 6 counties in southeastern Oklahoma. We also monitored reproductive effort at Red Slough Wildlife Management Area (RSWMA) by conducting nest and hatchling surveys. We documented sources of mortality by monitoring nests and dens with game cameras and direct observations. Alligators were detected in 4 counties, but detection rates were very low in 3 of those counties. The vast majority of detections occurred at RSWMA. Alligator surveys conducted at RSWMA several years prior reported much lower detections than we found in our current study. Data from nest and hatchling surveys indicate an overall increase in reproductive effort, but the number of nesting females remains fairly low. Major sources of mortality were predation of eggs, primarily by raccoons, and death of young alligators during freezing events. Predation by raccoons in 2024 resulted in 100% mortality of known nest sites at the WMA. Our results indicate that the alligator population is relatively small and primarily concentrated in one area of the state. Populations there would potentially benefit from actions that mitigate mortality in early life stages.
2314: Deep reefs fishes are a poorly studied community due to their depths exceeding recreational SCUBA limits. This has severely limited the amount of knowledge that exists regarding the trophic relationships among deep reef fishes and their shallow-water counterparts. Most of what is known about these species is inferred from behavior based on comparison with shallow water sister taxa. This study seeks to examine the percentages of δ15N and δ13C in four common deep reef fishes and to start to map trophic relationships for the ecosystem. δ15N acts as a proxy for determining trophic position while δ13C serves to track carbon sources and estimate trophic plasticity. The specimens were collected from four species that occur exclusively on deep reef reef slopes in Curacao using the submersible Curasub: Pronotogrammus martinicensis (Serranidae), Chrionema squamentum (Bembropidae), Symphysanodon beryi (Symphysanodontidae), and Epigonus sp. (Epigonidae).  These species are some of the most common fishes present on deep reefs and therefore should serve as a good baseline to which further work studying food webs can amend. Samples will be taken from various tissue types to have a broader time range of stable isotope measurements as the tissues chosen have distinct cell turnover rates. These values will be compared with samples from invertebrates and primary producers as well as fishes collected from shallow reefs to build a comprehensive food web of the ecosystem.
2315: Some amphibians have developed a close relationship with bromeliads, utilizing them for moisture, prey, shelter, and reproduction. This association has been so extreme that some species entirely depend on this microhabitat, also known as bromeligenous species. The environmental change hypothesis posits that shifts in species distribution are associated with temporal variation in environmental factors. Amphibian selection of suboptimal microhabitats,  such as ground bromeliads, can be ecologically important, possibly increasing disease risk. Amphibians may avoid bromeliads that maintain low moisture levels. In contrast, bromeliads that maintain high moisture conditions may attract amphibians but also promote pathogen transmission. We tested whether the frequency of occurrence of Phyllodytes gyrinaethes, a bromeligenous treefrog endemic to the Brazilian Atlantic rainforest, increases (1) with canopy cover, (2) during the rainy season in suboptimal microhabitats such as ground bromeliads, and (3) is associated with higher chytrid fungus infection in ground bromeliads and other suboptimal microhabitats shared with other amphibian species. We sampled 131 bromeliads for P. gyrinaethes presence. The frequency of occurrence of P. gyrinaethes increases during the rainy season, at high pH, and with large numbers of bromeliad leaves. The prevalence of chytrid fungus, but not infection loads, varied seasonally in ground bromeliads during the rainy season.
2316: The Dusky Gopher Frog (Lithobates sevosus) is one of the most critically endangered frog species in the United States. One major threat to their persistence is habitat loss and fragmentation. To prevent further species loss, the Memphis Zoo spearheaded the establishment of a captive population to both serve as an assurance colony in the event of species extinction in the wild and to be a source population to help boost wild populations. The first important step for the program was establishing a reintroduction site in Southern Mississippi. Under the guidance of the USFWS and Memphis Zoo, this site underwent significant habitat restoration by the Army Corp of Engineers. From 2017-2024 the Memphis Zoo and collaborators released a combined 10,738 zoo-bred tadpoles and juvenile frogs. As a result of these efforts, we are now at a turning point for this recovery program, where assessment of the establishment of this population is urgently needed for the program to advance. To monitor the status of the reintroduced population we are implementing camera traps using a version of the AHDrift method. We have fully enclosed the pond with a drift fence, with trail cameras in upside-down buckets with openings serving as entrances to and from the pond. These cameras will capture movement of both adults and metamorphs during and after the breeding season. With these images we will determine population estimates and recruitment of juveniles. This will allow us to determine if this population is self-sustaining and where to direct future reintroduction efforts.
2317: Anolis scriptus, also called the Silver Cay Anole, is widespread across the southern Lucayan Archipelago, including the Inaguas, Plana Cays, and Mayaguana of the Bahamas, as well as the Turks and Caicos Islands (TCI). It thrives in diverse habitats throughout this range, from dense tropical dry forests to pine savannas and small vegetated cays. Phylogenetic studies place A. scriptus within the Puerto Rican Anole radiation, closely related to species like A. cristatellus, A. desechensis, and A. ernestwilliamsi. Despite its resemblance to A. cristatellus, A. scriptus likely dispersed from Puerto Rico to the TCI around the beginning of the Pliocene. This migration may have occurred via over-water dispersal aided by currents and hurricanes or by island-hopping across the now-submerged Silver, Mouchoir, and Navidad banks. Potential biogeographic boundaries exist on each of these island banks within the range of A. scriptus. For example, the Turks Bank and the Caicos Bank are separated by the ~20km Turks Island Passage and were never connected. I sequenced 38 individuals at a ~1200bp mitochondrial locus, including individuals from two islands on the Caicos Bank and three islands on the Turks Bank. I then aligned these sequences and conducted phylogeographic analysis using the package ape in R. Despite drastic phenotypic differences, I found no evidence of distinct Turks Bank and Caicos Bank lineages. Rather, there are northern and southern lineages that cross the Turks Island Passage. These data will be important as additional systematic and population genetic work is done on this species elsewhere in its range.
2318: Pacific salmon migration from the ocean to freshwater to spawn impacts a number of species that consume live and dead adult salmon.  We examined trends in the spawning migration timing of Auke Creek pink (Oncorhynchus gorbuscha), coho (O. kisutch), and sockeye salmon (O. nerka) since 2011.  By observing their migration patterns, we were able to determine changes in migration timing, run duration, and relationships between migration timing and stream flow. Consistent with analyses prior to 2011, we found that sockeye migration timing has not advanced, but coho and pink salmon continue to spawn earlier in the year in this warming stream. The duration of spawning migration has a high variance over recent years for all three salmon species with no significant trends.  We explored residuals in the run timing trend for each species to determine whether abiotic variables could explain annual variation in the spawning migration.
2319: Tetracheilostoma carlae was first described by S. Blair Hedges sixteen years ago from Barbados. It is the smallest species of snake currently known, with a total length of 104 millimeters at maximum and a maximum snout-vent length of 98 millimeters. In this study, we use high-resolution computed tomography of two specimens, the holotype (USNM564819) and the paratype (USNM564818), to study the cranial and axial skeletal anatomy of this species. The morphology of the snout is narrow but expands at the neurocranial region. The antero-medial process of the parietal wedges between the frontals. The nasals, rather than being perforated by multiple foramina as in other Typhlopoids, are solid and have an opening in the lateral side of the nasofrontal suture. Each dentary bears five procumbent teeth, and no teeth are present in the premaxilla or maxilla. Compared with Typhlopoids of similar size (Antillotyphlops grantii), the posteromedial border of the parietal is rounded rather than transverse, and the supraoccipital bones are absent. We will continue investigating the individual cranial elements to produce a detailed description of the cranial morphology.
2320: Painted turtles (Chrysemys picta) are famous for their supercooling ability and for surviving long periods of anoxia without further damage in tissues and organs, making them an ideal model for ecology, evolution and biomedicine. For years, turtle research has been hampered for their slow maturation, seasonal reproduction, and the difficulty of having them in captivity. To overcome these difficulties, our lab recently developed the first adult stem cell-derived turtle organoids from liver. Organoids are 3D structures that recapitulate the microanatomy and physiology of their tissue of origin allowing for in vitro testing and experimentation without constantly harvesting donor tissue and screening offspring. Here we present the isolation and characterization of hepatic organoids from three different turtle species: painted, snapping and soft-shell turtles. The isolation of multiple turtle species organoids demonstrated that our protocol is suitable for the generation of organoids in chelonians, allowing the development of most needed tools that are currently missing to study these emerging models.
2321: The marine hatchetfishes (Sternoptychidae) are one of the largest deep-sea families with 10 genera and 79 species. Species in Argyropelecus, Polyipnus, and Sternoptyx have anteriorly deep and posteriorly shallow bodies that resemble a hatchet in lateral view, while the seven remaining genera have a more uniform, slender body. These two morphologies have typically been recognized as the Sternoptychinae and Maurolicinae, respectively. All previous molecular studies have failed to recover the family or every genus as monophyletic. We investigate the evolutionary relationships of the Sternoptychidae using  415 mitochondrial and nuclear loci (including ultraconserved elements) and 149 morphological characters. We will present the results of our combined phylogenetic analysis that recognizes a monophyletic Sternoptychidae, paraphyletic Sternoptychinae, and polyphyletic Maurolicinae. Further all genera represented my multiple species were recovered as monophyletic.
2322: The NSF Bio-LEAPS Advisory Board has outlined recommendations to improve accessibility and inclusivity at the Joint Meeting of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists (JMIH) conference. A key suggestion is the introduction of a separate accommodations survey during the registration process, allowing attendees to request child care, dietary accommodations, language support, and more. Additionally, the formation of an accessibility team, trained to manage these requests, is recommended to ensure smooth implementation during the event. The Board also advocates for clear visa letters for international attendees, detailing their accepted abstracts and participation. The Advisory Board emphasizes the importance of a user-friendly conference app with accessibility features, alongside providing physical maps and announcements to ensure equal access to information. The inclusion of opt-out options for attendee names on registration lists is also recommended to respect privacy. In terms of conference venue and logistics, the Board urges JMIH to select accessible locations with public transport options, safe environments, and ADA-compliant hotels. Conference rooms should be accessible, with adequate space for mobility devices, accessible bathrooms, and multiple food options that cater to dietary restrictions. The use of microphones, captions, and accessible podiums for presentations is recommended, along with the creation of sensory-friendly spaces for those with sensory sensitivities. Further suggestions include offering affinity and language badges to foster community, ensuring free access for caregivers, and providing affordable childcare. Finally, the Board stresses the importance of ensuring safety through clear guidelines on photography and videography, and a review of the Code of Conduct during the opening ceremony.
2323: The ringed salamander, Ambystoma annulatum, is a species of mole salamander that is endemic to the Ozark Plateau regions of the Midwest in the United States. They are found in and near ponds during their fall breeding season and lay eggs in the wetland, with larvae overwintering in ponds until the following spring. There are few studies conducted on the population dynamics of this species, and because of its small geographic range, it is considered a species of concern for this region. This study aims to assess the presence or absence of ringed salamanders in areas where urbanization is encroaching. Secondarily, I will also examine occupancy patterns of other species to explore which taxa may be less susceptible to the negative effects of urbanization. I will sample up to ninety ponds across varying habitats during two seasons surrounding St. Louis, Missouri. Dip netting will occur in all accessible areas near the bank and encompass all potential microhabitats at each pond. All captured individuals of all species will be identified and released, and their life stage, species, and sex (if apparent) will be documented. Candidate models will be compared using locally recorded and spatial factors using Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC) to determine which factors affect the occurrence and implemented into a GIS software map. I predict that study sites that have an increase of fragmentation, are in closer proximity to roads, and have had recent increases in forest clearcutting will negatively affect amphibian populations, therefore decreasing A. annulatum occurrence and abundance.
2324: Stable isotopes of carbon and nitrogen are commonly used to examine food web structure, diet composition, and resource use within communities. In many cases, the whole organism is homogenized to obtain isotope ratios from bulk-tissue, or muscle samples from carcasses are used. Often, non-lethal subsamples, including fin, toe, and scale clips, are preferred for logistical, conservation, or animal welfare reasons. Firstly, we compare δ13C and δ15N values of nonnative Cuban treefrogs (Osteopilus septentrionalis) and African jewelfish (Hemichromis bimaculatus) to determine if non-lethal sampling methods (toe clips for anurans and fin clips for fish) give an equivalent isotope measure to that of bulk-tissue. Preliminary results show that δ13C values are similar among tissue types. δ15N values of anuran toe clips and bulk-tissue samples are similar, and thus non-lethal samples may be substituted for lethal samples. For fish, bulk-tissue samples are depleted in δ15N values compared to fin clips, which may be due to the fast metabolic rate of muscle. Due to variation in δ15N values, it is important to compare “like with like” when measuring relative isotopic niche space by keeping the use of lethal or non-lethal samples consistent within species. Secondly, we conduct a meta-analysis to determine the combined effects of preservation methods on stable isotopes of museum specimens. Although changes to δ13C and δ15N values of alcohol-preserved specimens have been documented, they are predictable and can be corrected for. We validate the use of non-lethal samples as a less-destructive means of sampling museum specimens for long-term food web studies.
2325: Will County is the most herpetologically rich county in northeastern Illinois and is home to a diverse community of anuran species. Although the Forest Preserve District of Will County safeguards an extensive network of local habitats, the county has also been experiencing significant urbanization. Given the strong link between amphibian breeding and recruitment with environmental conditions, there is a growing concern about how land-use change, such as urbanization, may impact anuran species. From 2022 to 2025, we conducted resurveys of forest preserves in Will County to understand how the herpetofauna survived, thrived, or were displaced since the last comprehensive compilation was published in 2015. We examine how calling phenology, a proxy for breeding phenology, varied across species and sites. We used passive acoustic monitoring to record anuran calling activity in wetlands of five forest preserves. To identify calls to species, we analyzed the audio data with a machine learning algorithm, which yielded a higher performance for some species than others. For species in which the algorithm allowed us to classify calls with a high confidence, we describe phenological patterns and determine how environmental and habitat factors affect variation in phenology. Calling activity exhibited species and site-specific variation. Understanding the drivers of variation in phenology across species and localities is increasingly important in the context of global change, as it can inform conservation strategies and management practices aimed at preserving biodiversity in rapidly changing landscapes.
2326: As rapid population growth, urbanization, and landscape alteration continue to increase, so too will anthropogenic inputs to ecological systems across spatio-temporal scales. Reptiles and amphibians, among Earth's most imperiled taxa, are particularly sensitive to these changes and, as such, exist at the center of the human-nature intersection. This increasingly shifting condition of their existence threatens to compromise the pivotal roles these species enact in the maintenance of biodiversity and ecosystem functioning. Responding to these challenges will require a methodological praxis which accounts for the social, political, economic, and cultural aspects involved in socio-ecological systems. This will necessitate the engagement of new, interdisciplinary approaches and epistemological frameworks, as well as increased collaboration and reflexivity in our research. Moreover, it will require the deconstruction of systems of oppression which contextualize and pervade our field in addition to interrogation of the roles we play in reifying them. A growing body of scholarship is elucidating the ways these structures, such as settler colonialism and racial capitalism, have historically operated -- and continue to operate -- to the detriment of ecology and natural history, including herpetology. In addition to upholding barriers to participation and perpetuating exclusivity and inequity in the field, these systems also affect our scholarship -- not just shaping who performs herpetology, but how it's performed and what it produces. This poster gives an overview of some of herpetology's oppressive history, offers examples of its implications, and proposes strategies and tools for systemic dismantling, embodying more critical approaches, and identifying potential areas of intersect.
2327: Crotalus ravus (Cope, 1865) is an endemic mountain rattlesnake that ranges across the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt (TMVB). This region is located between the Nearctic and Neotropical biogeographical realms and is recognized as a center of diversification in many taxa due to its environmental heterogeneity and relatively recent geologic origin. C. ravus has undergone several taxonomic changes throughout its history, and a recent phylogeographic study revealed previously unknown genetic diversity in populations across an east-west axis. Here, we present an integrative taxonomic approach incorporating different lines of evidence with the aim of evaluating whether the reported genetic diversity is reflected in morphology and environmental preferences, specifically through traditional morphology (meristic and mensural characters), hemipenial morphology, geometric morphometrics of head shape, and ecological niche overlap. None of the morphological lines of evidence showed significant differences between both lineages, while an ecological niche similarity test showed low overlap between lineages. Although our results suggest bioclimatic conditions differ across the distribution of C. ravus, these do not seem to influence the morphological characteristics considered. This study also suggests cryptic diversification processes in a species with a highly conservative morphology, highlighting the importance of carrying out integrative studies that incorporate genetic, morphological, and ecological data with the aim of understanding the evolutionary history of species distributed in biogeographically complex regions.
SSAR Siebert - Conservation, Evolution and Systematics
2328: The Hell Hollow Slender Salamander (Batrachoseps diabolicus) is a species of plethodontid salamander that occurs in the lowlands of the Sierra Nevada foothills in California. This lungless salamander occupies one of the most fire-prone regions of the state—one that is also rapidly growing in terms of human footprint.  At the time of description in 1998, this species was noted to encompass staggering genetic diversity, with extremely divergent populations found in the central portion of the species’ range. Our work uses modern molecular approaches and expanded sampling to describe how populations of this data-deficient species interact with each other and exchange genetic information. Specifically, our study examines the range-wide population structure and phylogenetic relationships of this species complex at a genomic scale to assess genetic diversity and the conservation status of this species. Through several years of fieldwork, we have more than doubled the elevational range that this species was thought to occupy and have discovered populations in novel habitat types. As a result, we have greatly expanded the extent of samples for divergent populations in the center of the range of B. diabolicus, with 10x the quantity of samples from this region included in our study as compared to prior publications, helping add context to the evolutionary history of this divergent lineage. Overall, this work has produced new insight into habitat preferences, range extent, and population genomic diversity for a member of an at-risk salamander group.
SSAR Siebert - Conservation, Evolution and Systematics
2329: Several species of barbs (Cyprinidae, Smiliogastrinae) were examined using vital fluorescent staining (4-di-2-ASP) and scanning electron microscopy to examine the distribution, shape, and physiological orientation (axis of best physiological sensitivity to flows) of the neuromast receptor organs of the mechanosensory lateral line system. As neuromasts were studied in detail, other structures were found in the skin on the head, trunk and tail in scanning electron micrographs. Breeding tubercles were found on the head and caudal fin of some species and taste buds were identified on the lips and barbels in some species. However, multicellular structures similar to taste buds, with what appear to be short microvilli, were also found in the epidermis on the head and overlying the scales, but also along the posterior edge of scales and, most surprisingly, in a ring around the entire circumference of the corneal epithelium. At least some of these structures are likely to be taste buds (given reports of wide distribution of taste buds in cyprinids), but the identity of the others remain enigmatic.
2330: Tooth morphology reflects the relationship between a fish and its prey, with different teeth suited for different tasks like piercing, slicing, and crushing. However, dental function is mediated by replacement (i.e. polyphyodonty) and damage to teeth (loss, breakage, blunting, etc). This study investigates tooth replacement patterns and damage across four species of prickleback (Stichaeidae), Xiphister mucosus, Xiphister atropurpureus, Phytichthys chirus, and Anoplarchus purpurescens, a group of fishes exhibiting ontogenetic dietary variation and differences in jaw and tooth morphology/mechanics. We assessed patterns of tooth replacement and damage across species and ontogeny. Our results indicate that replacement patterns and proportions are conserved across species, suggesting a phylogenetically controlled mechanism despite morphological differences. Species display differences in tooth damage, as fish that have a crushing morphotype incur more damage than fishes with a piercing morphotype. Finally, we compared replacement and damage over ontogeny, and found evidence of changes in tooth count, replacement, and damage over ontogeny for some of the species. These findings suggest that, while tooth replacement remains consistent, tooth damage reflects the forces placed upon teeth during feeding.
2331: Global declines of reptiles are caused by factors such as habitat degradation and invasive species. Understanding the impacts of nonnative cichlids and other tropical aquarium fishes in the southeastern USA is multi-faceted because these fishes probably act as both prey and competitors of aquatic reptiles. We surveyed abundance and diversity of native and non-native fishes, amphibians, and reptiles in southwest Florida wetland ecosystems using minnow trapping and asked how the presence, abundance, biomass density and diversity of prey might drive watersnake occupancy, capture rates, and prey selection. Non-native fishes made up the vast majority of biomass and of watersnake stomach contents. However, the proportionally greater relative abundance (amphibians were 3.5% of captures but 14% of stomach contents) and larger relative prey mass of amphibians in snake stomachs (max 11% for fishes vs. 31% for frogs) suggests that despite their low availability, amphibian prey are likely preferred when selection is possible. Overall, understanding how prey availability impacts snake and other predator populations can help guide conservation and decision-making efforts for these important species.
2332: We present a database to aid in the identification of the presently recognized 625 genera and 4260 species of snakes from around the world using scale characters. There are numerous snake genera for which morphological data and keys are not available, even to professional herpetologists. This compilation is based upon 1) examination of many thousands of museum specimens, 2) published scientific and lay literature, and 3) unpublished data from colleagues and museum collections, all collated by V. Wallach. Searchable characters include number of dorsal scale rows, ventral and subcaudal counts, scale carination, and head scalation. Filtering by global region, elevation, higher taxonomy, and body size is implemented. The database was recently published by DeepScience and a companion ShinyApp was developed by J. Williams and A. Durso. This resource should be of value to any herpetologist seeking to identify snakes based on their scale counts.
2333: Nearly 50 years ago, in 1976, Joseph S. Nelson published the first edition of Fishes of the World. That modest work built on a foundation laid by L.S. Berg and others, and attempted to summarize the diversity, classification, phylogeny, and characteristics of all the world’s fishes. Since that time, four more editions have been published. During recent decades, our understanding of fish evolution and systematics has changed dramatically, owing to the efforts of researchers, the advent of molecular phylogenetics, and the application of morphological tools such as µCT scanning, 3-D virtual reconstruction, and multivariate morphometrics. The pages of Fishes of the World record many dramatic changes in fish discoveries and phylogenies. The new 6th Edition of Fishes of the World, with publication scheduled in 2026, will incorporate new ideas proposed during the past 10 years about fish relationships. This poster focuses on three areas of fish evolution where relationships have been controversial and in flux. One is the phylogeny and classification of chondrichthyans, both extant taxa and their numerous fossil stem-group relatives. A second area is the controversial relationships of the basal-most extant acanthomorphs, including lampriforms, paracanthopterygians, trachichthyiforms, beryciforms, and holocentriforms. A third focus of discussion is the dramatically altered composition of the percoids relative to earlier volumes, and the placement of key taxa among a predominantly scorpaeniform radiation. The purpose of this poster is to invite the conference community to offer input, comments, and suggestions about these and other groups that are under active discussion.
2334: Amphibians are the most threatened vertebrate group on the planet and have been seen as harbingers of the Sixth Mass Extinction. It is with this alarm call that AmphibiaWeb was founded in 2000 and has been operating uninterrupted since then. AmphibiaWeb (amphibiaweb.org) is a non-profit initiative whose mission is to connect people around the world by synthesizing and sharing information about amphibians to enable research, education, and conservation. We do this by providing up-to-date scientific information on amphibian natural history, conservation, taxonomy, and global decline. The website amalgamates information from scientists and experts with the latest in biodiversity informatics. Features include: up-to-date tracking of newly described amphibian species, expert-based species accounts for over 30% of the world’s amphibians, some in multiple languages; dynamic species range and occurrence mapping; detailed pages on amphibian declines and its causes with ongoing literature updates; community- contributed multimedia files (sound, video and photos); and a community of scientists responsive to the latest taxonomic and research developments in amphibian biology and conservation to any inquiries from the public. Here we will provide a guide to how to effectively use this amphibian resource and outline how herpetologists like you can contribute and share your knowledge and photos! Please come visit our poster and meet members of the AmphibiaWeb steering committee!
2335: Fragmentation of natural landscapes disrupts individual movement and population connectivity. With continued anthropogenic change, it is increasingly important to understand how specific landscape features impact populations. The Northern Red-legged Frog (Rana aurora) is native to the Pacific Northwest and is a designated surrogate species for other riparian-associated species. We investigated how particular landscape features influence genetic diversity and connectivity among populations in the Portland, Oregon Metropolitan Region. Genomic data (RADseq) were generated for 158 individuals sampled across the region. We characterized the environmental conditions and land-use features within and between breeding sites. With a reference-aligned RADseq dataset and geospatial data, we estimated standard population genetic metrics, developed gravity models, and conducted a Maximum Likelihood Population Effect (MLPE) regression analysis to determine relationships between landscape features and population connectivity. Given the natural history and ecology of this species, we hypothesized that forested habitat, wetland corridors, and cooler, wetter climates would increase connectivity while human-modified features would decrease connectivity. We found evidence for a genetically distinct site suggesting possible human-assisted migration. At-site features did not affect gene flow among sites. Both gravity models and MLPE analyses indicated that wetland and deciduous forest corridors facilitate connectivity consistent with our expectations. These findings help us understand how human-altered landscapes affect amphibian movement and also contribute important data for improving habitat connectivity in the region for this and other species.
2336: Cryptobenthic fishes are small-bodied, short-lived inhabitants of reef habitats around the world. Recently, our understanding of the ecological importance of cryptobenthic fishes has increased, with their taxonomic diversity and varied ecological roles of particular note. However, there is relatively little detailed information on the anatomy of these fish, especially in comparison to their diversity, to allow for in-depth investigations into their adaptations to such specialized lifestyles. Here we present CryptoVert, a digitization project led by the Department of Ichthyology at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, in support of the openVert project (oVert). This project digitizes at least one species per genus for each cryptobenthic fish family through macro-photography, and two µCT scans: one to document the skeletal anatomy and a second using contrast-enhanced CT scans to examine soft tissue anatomy, including muscle, digestive, circulatory, and nervous systems. In total, over 400 scans have been made across 12 families of cryptobenthic fishes. These scans have been uploaded to MorphoSource and are freely available for download. We anticipate these scans will support research into general trends in vertebrate anatomical evolution associated with body size and will be a valuable resource for the development of new questions and hypotheses in a variety of scientific disciplines. Additionally, we showcase educational models created from these scans that will be useful for classrooms ranging from high school biology to graduate-level ichthyology courses.
2337: Desert reptiles exhibit numerous adaptations, such as high blood osmolality, high operative temperatures, and low cutaneous evaporative water loss (CEWL) to survive drought. It is well known that between closely related squamate species, those inhabiting hotter and drier habitats tend to exhibit more extreme versions of those adaptations than relatives in milder climates. However, very little is known about whether these adaptations vary intraspecifically. The Yellow-backed spiny lizard (S. magister uniformis) conveniently inhibits a transect of increasing aridity and temperature from the San Joaquin to the Mojave Deserts in California. I hypothesized that lizards sampled from hotter and drier sites will exhibit higher operative temperatures, higher blood osmolality, and lower CEWL than those sampled from cooler and wetter environments. I established six field sites across this gradient and sampled 20 lizards each for blood osmolality and CEWL measurements. A subset of 10 more lizards per site were outfitted with light-level geolocators (GLS) to determine their voluntary thermal maximum in combination with operative temperature models placed in full sun, shade, and burrows. The use of GLS is particularly exciting as these devices are extremely lightweight (<1g w/o harness) and can provide high accuracy temporal measurements of thermoregulatory behavior without labor intensive direct observations. My project will still be ongoing by the time of this conference, but I will have presentable preliminary data by June. My project will add to our understanding of desert reptile physiology overall and inform landscape-scale conservation measures targeting species experiencing a diverse array of climatic conditions.
2338: Different environments have distinct light characteristics that place evolutionary constraints on vision. Over time, evolution under these constraints has resulted in the dynamic and specialized photosystems visual systems seen across various animal groups. Environments where light is limited or absent are expected to relax the effects of selection on vision-related genes, resulting in evolutionary regression of the visual system as other sensory systems are favoured. Many aspects of visual system regression have been well studied in fossorial mammals but remain understudied in fossorial amphibians and reptiles. Caecilians and several independent lineages of fossorial squamates have convergently evolved similar morphological adaptations to their fossorial lifestyles, but the molecular underpinnings of the changes to their visual systems have not been studied. We predict that vision-related genes will show convergent patterns of regression across independent evolutionary transition to fossoriality. However, in addition to regression, we hypothesize that a subset of genes will show evidence of adaptation, where those genes, and their proteins, have been selected for alternative functions within the fossorial light environment. To test these predictions, we supplement existing amphibian and squamate genomic resources through the sequencing of additional genomes from fossorial taxa. Vision-related genes from fossorial and non-fossorial taxa will be compared to determine the extent of gene loss across taxa and molecular evolutionary models will be used to estimates selection pressures included test for relaxed and positive selection. Preliminary results suggest many fossorial taxa maintains many more vision-related genes than expected suggestion potential adaptive evolution or co-option for non-visual functions.
SSAR Siebert - Conservation, Evolution and Systematics
2339: The Atlantic cownose ray (Rhinoptera bonasus) is a highly migratory batoid occurring along the eastern coasts of North and South America and throughout the Gulf of Mexico (GoM), frequently observed in large schools. Although R. bonasus possess an extremely vulnerable life history and has historically been targeted in directed fisheries, a formal stock assessment has never been conducted, inhibiting management and making it difficult to assess population fluctuations. Cownose rays have been frequently documented using estuaries during reproductive and young-of-year (YOY) life stages, increasing potential anthropogenic interactions during delicate life stages. While cownose ray movement behavior has been extensively described on the US East coast, movement data in the GoM is limited. In this study, 36 cownose rays (mature and YOY males and females) were acoustically tracked in Apalachicola Bay, Florida. Both life stages used the estuary extensively, with mature females making unique, directed movements to specific seagrass-dominated areas after parturition/mating. A large proportion of mature individuals exhibited seasonal residency in the Apalachicola Bay system, with mature females demonstrating the strongest fidelity to the estuary and mating area. Tagged animals remained in the bay for durations of weeks to months, primarily using mud habitat near the river mouth during the spring and summer. Sporadic winter detections on the eastern side of the system and near inlets suggest that cownose rays do not migrate great distances after departing the system. This study provides a novel assessment of habitat use, seasonal residency, and mating behavior of cownose rays in the GoM.
2340: The Atlantic sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae) is the most abundant shark species found in the coastal waters of the Gulf of Mexico (GoM). Due to their relatively small size, they have developed life history strategies such as rapid growth and maturation, to counteract various pressures. Understanding the diet of young-of-year (YOY) individuals is crucial for assessing maternal influence on early feeding behaviors, which play a key role in promoting rapid growth. This study examined YOY diet composition in St. George Sound, FL, using a combination of gut-content analysis and stable isotope analysis (δ13C and δ15N). Diet composition was quantified using the Index of Relative Importance (%IRI), incorporating the percent number of prey (%N), percent weight of prey (%W), and percent frequency of occurrence (%O) to assess dietary significance of different prey taxa. Preliminary results indicate that of the YOY sampled (n=167; n= 67 empty), guts were dominated by Teleostei (n=75; %N: 53.9, %W:69.6, %O: 62.5, %IRI: 84.05), followed by Malacostraca (n=31; %N: 26.5, %W: 9.6, %O: 30.2, %IRI: 11.89). Unidentified animals made up 12 of the contents (%N: 10.3, %W: 2.3, %O: 11.36, %IRI: 1.57), then Cephalopoda (n=9; %N: 7.7, %W: 15.5, %O: 9.4, %IRI: 2.4) and Sipuncula (n=2; %N: 1.7, %W: 3.1, %O: 2.1, %IRI: 0.1).These findings align with previous studies completed in the northeastern GoM, further supporting the role of teleost fish in the species' diet. Future results will explain isotopic shifts across fork length (cm) in conjunction with gut-contents, providing further insights into ontogenetic dietary shifts.
2341: Skates are an important, yet poorly studied taxonomic group, with multiple species often co-occurring in space and time. We compared the relative abundance of three species of skate to examine trends in phenology compared to oceanographic conditions and explore niche overlap using a fisheries independent survey. Three of the most abundant skate species in the Mid-Atlantic Bight (MAB) are Clearnose Skates Rostroraja eglanteria, Little Skates Leucoraja erinaceus, and Winter Skates Leucoraja ocellata. We found that off of New Jersey, peaks of Clearnose Skate abundance occur at higher temperatures compared to Little and Winter Skates (center of temperature distribution for Clearnose Skates = 17.6°C, Little Skates = 11.3°C, Winter Skates = 10.3°C). Correspondingly, Little and Winter Skates abundance peaked in the early spring. In addition to variance in seasonal occurrence, interspecific variations were documented in terms of spatial habitat occupancy in the coastal oceans off the coast of New Jersey. Clearnose Skates displayed a more southerly center of distribution compared to Little Skates, and Winter Skates. Notably, the centers of distribution for all three species occurred at higher latitudes during summer months suggesting a seasonal north-south migrational life history strategy. Additionally, we found inter and intraspecific depth distributions for each species. Overall, our results demonstrate the occurrence of niche partitioning between these species based on differences in habitat occupancy and create a foundation upon which future investigations into skates in the MAB can build upon.
2342: The Guana and Tolomato Rivers provide essential habitat for several ecologically and economically important species and serve as nursery habitat for a variety of Atlantic coastal shark species, including scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini), sandbar (Carcharhinus plumbeus), and bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas). Spanning the northeastern Florida coast, the rivers are home to over 50 endangered or threatened species and host several habitat restoration projects due to their ecological significance and proximity to development along the coast. The effects of human influence and pollution, and specifically toxic metal mercury (Hg), has not been well studied in this system. Mercury is known to biomagnify through the food web, therefore posing significant health risks to high level consumers that possess elevated concentrations, such as elasmobranchs. Therefore, this presentation will highlight the completed first section of my master’s thesis, investigating the presence of mercury in fishes and elasmobranchs of the Guana and Tolomato Rivers and its movement through the food web. Mercury concentrations were analyzed in elasmobranchs and their prey species, using the current federal guidelines for safe mercury concentrations in fish as set by the EPA (0.3 mg/kg/ of wet-weight) and the FDA (1.0 mg/kg of wet weight). Additionally, trophic levels were determined through stable isotope analysis to better illustrate the transfer and magnification of mercury within this system.
2343: The lemon shark, Negaprion brevirostris, is a large-bodied inshore species of shark that is well documented in tropical waters of the Western Atlantic. Until 2019, this species has been largely absent from coastal surveys in Georgia. In 2019, a potential lemon shark nursery was identified for the species on Little St. Simons Island (LSSI) – a first for the state. The lemon sharks around LSSI were determined to have a strong selectivity for surf and inlets, which likely offered shelter at high tides. In this study, we hypothesized that lemon sharks were also present on other Georgia barrier islands. Using aerial imagery, we selected habitats with similar characteristics to the lemon shark nurseries on LSSI and sampled them using the same methods used previously on LSSI. In 2021–2022, we documented 108 lemon shark captures, including 28 recaptures, in surf and inlet habitat on Little St. Simons, Ossabaw, and St. Simons islands. Additionally, juvenile lemons were observed in 2022 on St. Catherines Island but were not successfully captured during sampling. These results suggest nursery habitats may exist in those additional locations, and that Georgia has an underassessed presence of juvenile lemon sharks. The documentation of these novel nurseries provides important information about habitat preference and the geographic extent of nursery habitat for this species, which is critical to the proper management of these highly migratory sharks.
2344: The Brassy Jumprock (Moxostoma sp.) is a known yet undescribed species of freshwater fish that has long remained in taxonomic uncertainty. Initially discovered in 1956, the species was erroneously diagnosed as Moxostoma robustum, a species originally described in 1870 but unseen since. However, the subsequent rediscovery of a population matching the original description of M. robustum in 1992 clarified the identity of M. robustum, leaving the Brassy Jumprock without a valid scientific name. Herein, in the effort to compose a formal description for the species, morphological and meristic characters from a total of 215 Brassy Jumprock specimens were examined, representing every major river basin where they are known to occur. Furthermore, 154 specimens of comparative material were examined consisting of coexisting, morphologically similar congeners sympatric with the Brassy Jumprock. These analyses were able to identify a suite of characters that can be used to distinguish the Brassy Jumprock as a unique species. In conjunction with formalizing a description, we sought to examine the population structure of the species. A series of historical geographic records from museum collections and state agencies was used to define a precise distribution range for the species.
