Population structure was then examined via RADSeq data from individuals throughout the geographic range to determine the degree of population connectivity between drainages and to search for any unrecognized cryptic diversity. This comprehensive approach provides the foundation for the formal recognition and description of the Brassy Jumprock.
2345: Unionid mussels have severely declined, and reintroduction represents a valuable conservation tool. Fishes serve as hosts for early life stages of mussels (glochidia), and recolonization is dependent on the ability of fish hosts to disperse to suitable mussel habitat. The Mission Reach of the San Antonio River is an urban reach with ‘flashy’ hydrology, and restoration has involved the construction of 31 erosion control structures across an eight-mile (12.8 km) segment. These structures have not been evaluated for fish passage. Although juvenile mussels have been reintroduced, natural recolonization by sexually mature mussels that persist has not been documented. One hypothesis for the lack of recolonization success is that movement by fish hosts may be limited by installed structures or hydrologic variables, thereby reducing connectivity between mussel populations and suitable rearing habitat. Our objective was to determine whether fish are passing erosion control structures and evaluate predictors of passage. We used passive integrated transponder (PIT) tags to evaluate movement across seven structures within the Mission Reach. We PIT tagged 1,140 individuals representing 20 species and used a mobile antenna system to redetect individuals. We redetected 229 individuals and documented 22 passage events. Passage was correlated with fish length, Julian date, and several structure-specific characteristics, indicating that larger individuals pass structures more frequently and that some structures may pass fish more efficiently than others. Our results will inform future mussel reintroduction efforts and indicate that structures comparable to those in the Mission Reach do not represent complete barriers to movement by fishes.
2346: Aphredoderus are a widespread genus of lowland freshwater fish native to the Eastern United States. Along the southeastern coastal plain, Aphredoderus exhibit widespread sympatry with little to no evidence of admixture between sister taxa. Using biogeographic, genomic, and temporal data we evaluate relationships between sympatric species of Aphredoderus. We find incompatibilities between spatial and temporal data of one Aphredoderus species, and evidence of pervasive ancestral introgression in both allele-frequency and haploid sequence data. Our data support extensive early-to-mid Pleistocene introgression and reticulation within the phylogeny of Aphredoderus.
2347: In central Texas (CTX), there is evidence of a potentially undescribed catostomid, the Llano River Carpsucker (Carpiodes cf. carpio). C. cf. carpio possess a more elongated body compared to sympatric River Carpsucker (C. carpio), with meristics and mouth morphology similar to C. cyprinus. While the U.S. Geological Survey suggests C. cyprinus were introduced to CTX, the earliest non-native record of C. cyprinus match the original collection of C. cf. carpio from the Llano River. Considering this, the relationship between C. cf. carpio with recognized species of Carpiodes is unknown along with its native status. The objective of this study was to assess genetic differences between C. cf. carpio and Carpiodes across their distribution using traditional molecular markers and phylogenetic techniques. Tissues collected from 260 Carpiodes specimens inhabiting Brazos, Colorado, and Guadalupe drainages of Texas were compiled with museum requested tissues representative of the distribution of Carpiodes. We extracted DNA from tissues, amplified the mitochondrial cytochrome b (CYTB) and nuclear IRBP2 genes, and sequenced data for each specimen. Our phylogenetic analyses revealed that potentially undescribed species of Carpiodes species exist within the southeastern United States which are currently listed as C. cyprinus. Furthermore, C. cf. carpio of CTX were closely related to C. cyprinus inhabiting Mississippi, Great Lakes, and Hudson Bay drainages yet possessed CYTB haplotypes that were unique among our sampled distribution. Our work suggests C. cf. carpio are native locally adapted C. cyprinus which has crucial implications for the conservation and management of native fishes in Texas.
2348: The macroevolutionary drivers of morphological diversification are varied, ranging from genetic mechanisms, developmental processes, and ecological and environmental pressures. Life history strategy, which optimizes growth, sexual maturation, and reproductive output, may also drive morphological evolution. Because morphological traits, such as body size, are linked to life history strategies, variation in life history may influence phenotypic diversity patterns. Lampreys have three remarkably different life history strategies: anadromous-parasitic, freshwater-parasitic, and freshwater-nonparasitic, each evolving repeatedly across the lamprey phylogeny. In this study, we explored the role of life history strategy in structuring morphological evolution in lampreys. We analyzed 14 traits that capture morphological variation across 35 lamprey species using a suite of phylogenetic comparative methods. Our preliminary results reveal patterns of phenotypic divergence among life history strategies, with the strongest divergences among traits linked to feeding. Additionally, we find that body size is the primary axis of divergence and is most strongly associated with migration. Our study emphasizes the importance of life history strategies in driving morphological diversification and adaptation.
2349: Spotted Gar (Lepisosteus oculatus, Winchell 1864) is widespread with a disjunct population in the Great Lakes Basin found from Michigan south to Louisiana, southwestern Texas, and the western Florida panhandle. The primary area of its range comprises the Mississippi River Basin and neighboring drainages. A disjunct northern and southern population sets L. oculatus apart from other gar species which have more contiguous ranges. Despite their external appearances being little changed since the Jurassic, there appears to be more diversity within gars than once expected. Here we compared differences in body shape using traditional and geometric morphometrics across the distribution of Spotted Gar. We also collected tissue samples from across the distribution for population genetic analyses using ddRADseq. Significant population structure was discovered in L. oculatus. Spotted gars from the northern disjunct population were not genetically distinct from neighboring populations in the Mississippi River Basin, likely due to the recency of their Great Lakes colonization after the Last Glacial Maximum. Sampled Florida gars (L. platyrhincus, DeKay 1842) were nested within a larger clade with samples of Spotted gars from their zone of sympatry in the Florida panhandle. These results have significant taxonomic implications given the prevalence and ease at which gars can hybridize.
2350: The behavioral displacement hypothesis posits that competition and behavioral interactions drive niche divergence, making these interactions potential determinants of invasive species success and distributions. House Geckos (Hemidactylus spp.) are widely distributed human-commensal invasive lizards. Over the past century, Mediterranean House Geckos (H. turcicus) have established populations in the southern USA, followed by Tropical House Geckos (H. mabouia) in southern Florida, and Sri Lankan House Geckos (H. parvimaculatus) in southern Louisiana and Texas. These species are ecologically similar, leading to speculation of competitive displacement of H. turcicus, which no longer occurs in southern Florida and is increasingly rare in southern Louisiana. Yet, no study has documented competition among these species. Our goal is to determine if the gradual disappearance of H. turcicus from previously occupied regions can be attributed to competition with congeners. Specifically, we are ascertaining the competitive dominance hierarchy among these three species. To determine this, individual H. turcicus were randomly paired with geckos of both competitor species (n = 3/species) and a conspecific control. Fasted pairs were introduced to arenas where behavioral interactions were night-vision video recorded for 45 mins. Predefined behaviors were quantified and categorized to assign dominance ranks that will be compared via GLM to determine the dominance order among species. Data indicate H. turcicus is submissive to H. mabouia yet evenly matched against H. parvimaculatus. Competitor sex did not matter, but body size may. Our findings will broaden our understanding of the role of behavior as a mechanism of competitive displacement among co-occurring invasive species.
2351: Habitat loss and fragmentation lead to the breakdown of important spatial processes that determine population and metapopulation persistence. For example, the decline of the longleaf pine-wiregrass ecosystem has led to the imperilment of many species, especially endemic amphibian species that breed in geographically isolated wetlands. In Georgia, Gopher frog (Rana capito) metapopulations and populations now exist on relatively small, isolated, and highly fragmented landscapes. Very few of these landscapes support more than one or two breeding wetlands. Thus, little is known about the factors that determine connectivity between breeding sites and how they affect Gopher frog population dynamics. I used an Individual-Based Model (IBM) to simulate how landscape features influence the patterns of breeding site occupancy and the genetic structure of Gopher frog populations on one of the few remaining landscapes that support multiple breeding wetlands in Georgia. Based on field and experimental studies, the model integrates frog behavior and breeding site population projection models. This technique creates a realistic, mechanistic model to evaluate how natural and human-driven variation in soil and land cover type affects metapopulation processes and persistence. The model can be used to evaluate management scenarios, including spatially explicit habitat management and translocation decisions, to maximize Gopher frog persistence in this and other managed landscapes.
2352: Invasive species are one of the largest contributors to global biodiversity loss, especially on islands. Novel interactions from introduced taxa including predation, competition, habitat loss, dietary shifts, and hybridization often cause population decline and extinction in native species. Despite the potential severity of threats, little research has focused on large scale impacts of invasive species on native lizards. Our goals are to identify the relative impact of invasive species as a threat to native lizards, the major species and threat types (e.g., predator, competitor) affecting native lizards, and the geographic patterns in invasive species occurrence and native lizard decline. We compiled data for over 600 lizard species with invasive species identified as a major threat. For each lizard species, we identified their invasive threat, their invasive threat type (e.g., mammal predator), other threats to the species, range type (island, continent, both), range midpoint, habitat, lizard body traits (e.g., average mass, length), and lizard extinction status (e.g., least concern, endangered, etc.). We used these data to assess which threats and conditions may be linked to high lizard extinction risk and which may be most conducive to native-invasive coexistence. The results of this research will be the first cohesive review of the threat of invasive species on native lizard species. Our work will provide valuable information that is immediately applicable to conservation strategies for lizard species across the globe.
2353: The niche concept has been widely reviewed by ecologists since its introduction by Grinnell in 1924 and by Elton in 1927, who described the spatial niche and functional role niche, respectively. In Florida, the impact of invasive species on the niches of native species remains uncertain. The vacant niche hypothesis states that nonnative species, upon arrival to a new area, will occupy a niche which is “unused” by native species, whereas the niche competition hypothesis states that nonnative species will occupy an overlapping niche, resulting in a shift or alteration of the niche composition of native species over time. We use δ15N and δ13C stable isotope analyses to test the vacant niche hypothesis and the niche competition hypothesis within the aquatic vertebrate community of Rainey Slough in Glades County, Florida. In the 1970s, Rainey Slough hosted high amphibian and reptile biodiversity and biomass, but drastic herpetofaunal declines have occurred over the past 50 years, likely driven by competition and predation from nonnative fish species, Cuban treefrogs (Osteopilus septentrionalis), and island apple snails (Pomacea maculata). Preliminary data from museum specimens collected in 1969-1979 and samples collected in 2024-2025 may determine if nonnative species occupy a niche space which either (1) is unused by native species, or (2) displaces native species. It is important to determine how community structure and diversity affects invasibility (susceptibility to invasion) in relatively undisturbed habitats as nonnative species continue to spread throughout Florida.
2354: Many lizards, like most other herpetofauna, are vastly understudied, and some of Southwest Florida’s invasive lizards are no exception. Understanding the ecology of invasive lizards and how they use their new environment is essential to not only determining their impact on our ecosystems but can give us a better idea about their ecology in their native range. This study sought to assess the habitat characteristics of vegetation used by Chamalaeo calyptratus (veiled chameleons) and Anolis equestris (knight anoles) in Southwest Florida. Nocturnal visual surveys were conducted to locate lizards, and all trees in which lizards were found were tagged to be measured later. Vegetation surveys were then conducted on all transects during daylight hours, where both trees used by individual lizards and randomly selected trees were identified to the species-level and measured for height, diameter at breast height, canopy cover, and stem number. Both C. calyptratus and A. equestris were found more often in taller trees and A. equestris was found more often in trees with higher canopy cover. Lizards were found using six of the seven most common woody vegetation species available (cypress, pine, colicwood, dahoon holly, wax myrtle, and cabbage palm), but were not found in the fifth most common species (silverling), suggesting that overall, these lizards may not have strong preferences for vegetation type. These data can support further research on the ecology of these lizards and inform potential management implications in the future.
2355: Raillietiella orientalis is an invasive pentastome parasite introduced to southern Florida by the Burmese python. This parasite poses a conservation threat for native snakes in the southeastern United States, as infections are associated with morbidity and mortality. Little is known about its life history, impacts on native snake species, or the extent of its spread. To address this, the Snake Lungworm Alliance and Monitoring (SLAM) organization was established to conduct opportunistic surveillance of infection. We performed dissections on collected roadkill and snakes found dead in habitat, examining the respiratory tract and viscera for R. orientalis adults. We assessed infection prevalence across Florida, comparing natural and anthropogenic land cover types, and analyzed infection rates among 30 native snake species. A generalized linear model with snake genus as a random effect found no significant difference in infection odds between natural and anthropogenic areas (OR = 1.24, p = 0.61, 33% vs. 28% probability). Compared to central Florida, odds were 91% lower in northeast Florida (OR = 0.09, p = 0.002, 3% probability) and 97% lower in northwest Florida (OR = 0.03, p < 0.0001, 1% probability). Southern Florida showed a non-significant trend toward higher infection probability (OR = 2.13, p = 0.1), with a predicted probability of 45%. Region was a significant predictor of infection likelihood. Chi-square analysis showed significant variation in prevalence among species. Several areas of Florida remain underrepresented in surveillance, highlighting the need for more data to fully understand the spread and impact of R. orientalis.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
2356: Prairie Rattlesnakes (Crotalus viridis) can gather by the hundreds to hibernate and give birth, making them an exceptional candidate for studying reptile social behavior. Why do snakes gather in these impressive aggregations and how are their social relationships maintained? Much of our historical knowledge of wild rattlesnake behavior has been confounded by the disturbance caused by human presence, leaving many unobserved behaviors and unanswered questions about social groupings among these mysterious and feared animals. Through the umbrella organization Project RattleCam, we used camera trap photos processed through the community science platform Zooniverse and the first 24-7 live-streaming camera on a den of wild reptiles to monitor interactions among snakes throughout the active seasons of two populations. While painted rattles identified individual snakes in the camera trap photos, community scientists named and tracked snakes based on unique scale patterns in the livestream. Our project has revealed group-level trends in activity as well as individual personalities among rattlesnakes. Social networks reveal that females are highly connected, and some males remain at rookeries throughout the summer. We continue to investigate the social dynamics of communicative head twitching behavior and drinking behavior from the livestream footage. Community scientists have been instrumental to this project’s success through the processing of photos, identification of individual snakes, and reviewing video footage. From dozens of dedicated volunteers to our growing YouTube subscriptions, this project has fostered a global community to deepen our understanding of snake behavior that could ultimately change how people perceive and interact with snakes.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
2357: Non-native species can pose significant threats to native biodiversity, especially once established in novel areas. We evaluated the effectiveness of ten years of removal effort in a recently established population of invasive non-native Common Watersnakes, Nerodia sipedon, introduced to Roseville, California. We used aquatic minnow traps to capture and remove snakes from 2015–2024. We estimated annual abundance using the Leslie depletion method and examined relative mass of snakes annually. We removed 110 snakes from 2015–2019, with none captured after 2019. Estimates from Leslie depletion models showed abundance declined annually during removal, with initial estimates of 55 snakes in 2015 and 41 snakes in 2016, followed by a decrease to 4 snakes in 2017, 7 snakes in 2018, and 8 snakes in 2019. Estimated abundance and relative mass of snakes were decreasing before removal began, possibly due to a drought, but relative mass increased after removal began, suggesting possible competitive release. Our results suggest the population was successfully eradicated, with no snakes seen since 2019. Drought conditions likely aided eradication, but the increase in relative mass of snakes as abundance declined highlights possible risk of compensatory growth and population rebound if removal effort had ended earlier. Our analysis highlights the value of targeting removal effort to coincide with environmental conditions that are challenging to non-native species, while revealing the risk of populations recovering from density-dependent releases if removal effort ends before successful eradication.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
2358: Blackside Dace (Chrosomus cumberlandensis; BSD) is a federally threatened leuciscid endemic to the upper Cumberland River system in Kentucky and Tennessee. BSD have been extirpated from numerous streams within their home range due to anthropogenic disturbances such as agriculture, logging, and surface coal mining. Streams within this system are characterized by low levels of background conductivity (<100 uS/cm); however, these anthropogenic activities are linked to elevated conductivity levels with impacted streams often exceeding 1000 uS/cm. BSD populations do not persist in streams over 340 uS/cm but the direct impacts of elevated conductivity to their physiology is unknown. Prolonged physiological stress from abiotic factors such as alterations in water chemistry can impact growth, feeding, and behavior of fishes. Elevated conductivity does negatively impact growth rate on the more widely distributed congener Southern Redbelly Dace (Chrosomus erythrogaster). Therefore, we hypothesize elevated conductivity directly impacts growth, feeding response, position in water column, and recovery to disturbance. We subjected shoals of three adult BSD to either the control treatment (<250 uS/cm) or high treatment (700 uS/cm) for four weeks. To test impact on growth, we measured total shoal weight before and after exposure. We assessed latency to feed, position in water column for a five-minute observation period twice per week during the trial period, and on the final day, we assessed time of recovery from disturbance. Impacts on growth and behavior are non-lethal, but likely contribute to reduced fitness of individuals when exposed to chronic levels of elevated conductivity.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
2359: In 2011, the IRL underwent a regime shift because of an intense harmful algae bloom (HAB) that fundamentally changed ecosystem conditions to favor phytoplankton over seagrass. We wanted to determine if this regime shift is reflected in fish community dynamics, including mass mortality events, in the IRL. We analyzed long-term data sets of fish kills and of population fluctuations of 10 fish species of interest. HAB events correlate with the frequency of fish mortality events, perhaps caused by hypoxia and exposure to toxins produced by certain algal species. It is conceivable that the 2011 regime shift may coincide with a decline in young-of-the-year (YOY) abundance and distribution for the fish species of interest, perhaps due to the loss of essential nursery habitat because of the regime shift. This situation underscores the impacts of human activity on the IRL and the importance of proactive environmental management to protect this vital ecosystem.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
2360: Ocean warming poses an ongoing threat to many species. To anticipate how populations will respond over multiple generations, we need to understand the genetic capacity of thermal responses to evolve and the processes that promote genetic variation. One potential source of such variation is local adaptation to environmental conditions. For example, if individuals inhabiting cooler waters tend to have cold-tolerant genotypes and individuals inhabiting warmer waters have warm-tolerant genotypes, then local adaptation could promote genetic variation in the population as a whole. We tested for local adaptation of thermal sensitivity in populations of California Grunion. We collected the gametes of Northern, Central, and Southern populations of Grunion and reared their embryos and larvae in a common laboratory environment. Larvae were reared across temperatures reflecting their natural range and we measured growth and mortality. The Central population exhibited a higher capacity for growth under higher temperatures than the Northern and Southern populations. Mortality was lowest at intermediate temperatures, but the Southern population exhibited peak survival at a significantly higher temperature than the Northern and Central populations. When examining the effects of temperature on biomass production (combination of survival and growth), we found that Southern populations indeed have a higher thermal optimum than northern populations. Grunion experience gene flow at large spatial scales and our results suggest that adaptation to local temperature conditions can increase overall heritability in thermal sensitivity by 25 to 75%. Local adaptation may thus increase the population-wide capacity for evolutionary adaptation to climate change.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
2361: Climate models predict that environmental conditions will change, exposing long-lived freshwater fish to novel climate patterns. To determine how the vital rates of long-lived freshwater fish species respond to climate change, we modified the environmental variation in a previous stochastic matrix model on June suckers (Chasmistes liorus) and used that model for comparison. We evaluated the demographic responses to four likely climate scenarios over a 200-year period: (1) increased stochasticity in river flow, (2) a 0.5 m decline in lake level due to a megadrought, (3) increased lake level amplitude from 1 m to 1.5 m, and (4) shortened climate cycles from 30 years to 8 years. We also performed combinations of scenarios to assess the relative strength of effects. We found that increased stochasticity in river flow and declining lake level had negative effects, while greater amplitude in lake level and a 12-year climate cycle had positive effects. In addition, we observed that different combinations of scenarios had varying effects on population growth. These results suggest that stabilizing lake levels and maintaining a 12-year climate cycle could promote positive population growth in June suckers despite ongoing climate change.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
2362: The warming world may shape food webs in different ways. Rising temperatures may strengthen top-down effects by increasing consumption of prey by predators or may dampen top-down effects if temperatures exceed predator tolerance limits. We investigated the effects of predatory amphibians and temperature on three aspects of a forest floor community: plant survival, invertebrate abundance and leaf decomposition rate. We used outdoor pens that contained either four or zero wood frogs and were either warmed with a greenhouse chamber or experienced ambient temperatures. In each pen we planted two common blue violets and two eastern red columbines. The plant species exhibited different responses to the treatments. Greenhouses decreased survival of violets, but their effects on columbines were contingent on the presence of frogs. With greenhouses, survival of columbines was increased when frogs were present. At higher temperatures within tolerance limits, frogs may consume more herbivorous invertebrates that would otherwise consume more columbine tissue. Without greenhouses, survival of columbines was decreased when frogs were present. Frogs decreased the abundance of springtails, detritivores that enrich the soil with nutrients. Although greenhouses decreased leaf decomposition rate, there was no effect of frogs on decomposition, suggesting that frogs did not affect plant survival by consuming detritivores. Our results provide mixed support for the hypothesis that rising temperatures strengthen top-down effects of amphibian predators on forest floor communities: frogs increased survival for one plant species when warmed, but frogs and warming did not interact to affect the other plant species, invertebrate abundance, or leaf decomposition.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
2363: Seasonal changes manifest variation in environmental cues, such as dial period and temperature, that can signal physiological and behavioral changes. Most terrestrial ectotherms reduce activity and metabolic rates during the winter to conserve energy when resources are scarce, which can result in changes in body condition and blood metabolites. Reproduction can produce drastic changes in body condition and energetic state in many animals. As infrequent eaters and capital breeders, snakes provide a model for analysis of interseasonal energy storage and allocation. Our study quantified variation in body condition and blood metabolites in two species of natricine snakes, with the expectation that values for both variables would be lower following brumation. During 2011-2015, we collected Thamnophis sirtalis and Thamnophis elegans from three sites within a montane valley wetland habitat and measured parameters of body condition, blood metabolites, and steroids as a function of year, sex, and season. We conducted radioimmunoassays to determine the concentrations of corticosterone and testosterone. Glucose and triglyceride levels were determined using standard assays. We found that body condition, but not corticosterone level, varied by season. Additionally, we detected changes in blood metabolites between Spring and Autumn. These results provide insight into how snakes store and allocate energy at a molecular level during energetically demanding events.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
2364: The lower jaw is toothless in all frogs, with the notable exception of Gastrotheca guentheri (Guenther’s marsupial frog), a species that re-evolved true mandibular teeth. Frogs evolved a spectrum of dietary preferences, with some species specializing in hunting small insects like ants and termites to larger species that are opportunistic predators of small mammals. Such vast dietary variation could possibly drive the morphology of lower jaws. Frogs also occupy diverse ecological niches. For example, tree frogs from South America spend their entire lives in the upper canopy of trees, species of African aquatic frogs spend the majority of their life underwater, and some desert frogs live entirely underground, only coming to the surface to breed. Microhabitat differences may also influence jaw shapes due to variability in the types of prey available. A few frogs have tooth-like bony projections on the lower jaw called odontoid fangs. Some of these fanged frogs are among the largest anuran species and known to prey on other vertebrates. Additionally, some fanged frogs take part in male-male combat during the mating season, using their odontoids to bite one another. Currently, it is unknown if the lower jaw morphology of frogs is influenced by diet, microhabitat variation, or presence of odontoid fangs. Our study uses micro-computed tomography data and three-dimensional geometric morphometrics to quantify shape diversity of the lower jaw from 150 frog species. Using phylogenetic comparative methods, we are testing if jaw shape is correlated with diet, microhabitat, fang presence, and body size to understand the factors driving lower jaw morphology across living frog diversity.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
2365: The relationship between organisms and their climate is complex, and it is influenced by hydrothermal physiology, behavior and evolutionary history. Microclimatic variation at a local scale provides a variety of conditions that animals can select, influencing selective pressures that act on physiology, particularly for small ectotherms such as anurans. One of the major sources of microclimatic variation in forested environments is provided by trees because temperature and humidity vary vastly along the ground-to-canopy axis. Therefore, arboreal habits and microhabitat selection will influence the selective pressures that act on physiological traits. To investigate how vertical microhabitat use mediates the evolution of physiological traits, I have collected detailed eco-physiological data of frogs in five localities across four years in the Amazon and Atlantic Forest of Brazil. I obtained critical thermal limits, dehydration and rehydration rates for multiple species of frogs and used phylogenetic comparative methods to investigate how arboreality mediates the evolution of physiological traits to different climatic regimes.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
2366: Organophosphorus pesticides were created with the intent to inhibit the nervous systems of insect pests, to decrease their numbers from impacting agriculture or spreading disease. Due to their widespread use, pesticides can be found in nature at varying concentrations including the habitats of many amphibians. Malathion is a common organophosphorus pesticide that causes seizures, nausea, and even death in non-target organisms exposed to acute concentrations. However, exposures to low and more environmentally realistic concentrations are less well studied. In this study, we wanted to better understand the impacts of environmentally realistic concentrations of organophosphates on amphibians after a chronic exposure. To do this, we exposed Northern Leopard Frog (Lithobates [Rana] pipiens) tadpoles to either a vehicle control. 1 μg/L of malathion, or 10 μg/L of malathion for approximately three weeks in a blind, controlled laboratory study. We found changes in behavior, brain morphology, and gut morphology in tadpoles exposed to the organophosphates. By gaining a better understanding of how environmental pollutants impact tadpole development, we may be more likely to improve how we apply pesticides and help conserve herpetofauna worldwide.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
2367: An unexplored dimension of biological invasions is the impact of acoustic interference among invasive and native anurans. Vocalizations by invasive frogs may result in attraction by heterospecifics if there are acoustic similarities to their conspecific signals. To gain insights into consequences of interactions between native and invasive species’ calls, we conducted field experiments in playback arenas that focused on acoustical overlap between calls of invasive American Bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana) and native Chiricahua Leopard Frogs (Rana chiricahuensis). We found both female and male R. chiricahuensis showed positive phonotaxis to calls of R. catesbeiana. When given a choice, both sexes of R. chiricahuensis chose their conspecific call over the heterospecific call. However, their frequency of positive phonotaxis towards their conspecific call decreased when exposed to both heterospecific and conspecific calls simultaneously rather than sequentially. Female R. catesbeiana expressed mostly random movements in the phonotactic arena. However, male R. catesbeiana did express a phonotactic response to vocalizations of R. chiricahuensis. The attraction to the invasive bullfrogs’ calls could increase encounters between R. chiricahuensis and R. catesbeiana. This may in turn increase the native frogs’ susceptibility to predation by the invasive species. Reproductive costs to R. chiricahuensis, such as wasted energy or changes in mate choice, are other potential consequences. Thus, our findings may be one mechanism behind the pattern of extirpation of R. chiricahuensis following the arrival of R. catesbeiana.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
2368: Squamates show tremendous variation in precloacal vertebral number, ranging from just 14 in Brookesia chameleons to nearly 400 in some snakes. Some evidence suggests that both ecological and developmental-genetic factors might influence vertebral counts, but the relative importance of these and other drivers of this variation across squamates remains poorly known. We tested how body size and habitat may explain variation in vertebral number between and within squamate clades. We predicted that vertebral counts within elongate clades would largely be explained by body size. In contrast, we predicted that vertebral number would be largely conserved in non-elongate clades, with changes associated with ecological differences or drift. We counted vertebrae from radiographs of museum specimens and supplemented these data from the primary literature to compile vertebral numbers for 2,360 species spanning the squamate phylogeny. Phylogenetic history explained a large proportion of the variance in vertebral number within clades, more so in lizards than in snakes. Size and habitat also explained a small proportion of variance in elongate clades, although there was still considerable unexplained variance. Vertebral number in amphisbaenians and blind snakes differs from patterns observed in other elongate clades, showing little influence of body size or phylogenetic history. Miniaturization or greater reliance on tunnel concertina locomotion may explain the decoupling between vertebrae and body size in these groups. Taken together, our results indicate a surprising complexity to vertebral evolution and we find little evidence that any single factor affects vertebral variation consistently across all squamates.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
2369: Introduced species often occur within habitats similar to those of their native range (i.e., niche conservatism), but invasive populations occasionally exploit novel portions of their fundamental multidimensional niche space. The plasticity of an organism’s realized niche (i.e., niche divergence) tends to be more common among aquatic and semi-aquatic invasive species, and seems to occur independent of an organism’s lifespan and time since introduction. Spectacled Caimans (Caiman crocodilus) are unique among crocodilians in that they have established populations outside of their native range, and can frequently be encountered in Cuba, Puerto Rico, and Florida. The objective of our research is to determine whether the climatic niche of Spectacled Caimans within their introduced range has diverged from that of their native populations. Incorporating long-term climatic data associated with verified localities of native and introduced Spectacled Caimans, we used multidimensional hypervolume analysis to determine the degree of overlap and/or divergence (a) between native and introduced populations of caimans and (b) among the three areas where Spectacled Caimans have established outside their native range. By identifying whether this plastic species exhibits climatic niche conservation or divergence within areas of establishment, we can validate habitat suitability models that predict areas within the southeastern USA that might be vulnerable to establishment of additional crocodilian species.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
2370: Overfishing, coastal habitat degradation, and climate change are altering marine food webs and interfering with ecosystem function. The declining abundances of preferred prey species may force predators to adopt increasingly generalist consumption strategies and incorporate novel resources. Tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) are a circumtropical coastal apex predator with a reputation for being indiscriminate generalists despite morphological adaptations specialized for preying upon sea turtles. We investigated tiger shark diet around Biscayne Bay, Florida, USA—where sea turtles are afforded protection under the Endangered Species Act—using DNA metabarcoding of minimally invasive cloacal swabs and opportunistically sampled regurgitated stomach contents. We identified a diverse assemblage of prey species with high taxonomic resolution and confidence belonging to at least 7 teleost families (Scombridae, Carangidae, Sphyraenidae, Mugilidae, Tetraodontidae, Haemulidae, and Echeneidae) and one elasmobranch genus (Carcharhinus). We also identified one species of seabird, the double-crested cormorant (Phalacrocorax auritus). Cloacal swabs yielded fewer taxa than stomach contents but proved a successful minimally invasive method of collecting prey DNA from large-bodied sharks. Overall, these results support the classification of tiger sharks as generalist predators that feed across a range of trophic guilds and coastal habitats. This consumption strategy may initially have been driven by historic declines in sea turtle populations but potentially now confers an evolutionary advantage in the face of anthropogenically destabilized coastal food webs.
2371: The use of nursery habitat by many elasmobranch species improves the growth and survival of juveniles, including young-of-year (YOY) bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas). Identification and proper management of nursery habitat are essential, as sharks support healthy marine ecosystems through top-down effects and nutrient transport. Systematic frameworks for defining shark nursery habitat have been established in the literature; however many areas suspected as nursery habitat remain unevaluated according to such frameworks. Further, studies demonstrate that increasing water temperatures have altered the habitat ranges of many shark species, including the locations of historical nursery sites. The Alabama Gulf coast is home to Mobile Bay, a suspected bull shark nursery experiencing increasing annual water temperatures. Here, we employed a long-term fisheries-independent dataset to assess the entire coastline of Alabama, which includes the eastern Mississippi Sound, Mobile Bay, and western Perdido Bay, as YOY bull shark nursery habitat across multiple timescales (i.e. from 2004-2023 and in 5-year-increments). From 2004-2023 and 2014-2018, the entire Mobile Bay region of the coastline satisfied nursery habitat criteria. However, only lower Mobile Bay satisfied all nursery habitat criteria in 2009-2013 and only upper Mobile Bay did so in 2019-2023. From 2004-2008, no portion of the Alabama coastline satisfied all criteria. As changing habitat conditions persist, these results showcase the spatiotemporally-dynamic nature of nearshore bull shark nurseries and may be useful for understanding distributions of future shark populations.
2372:
The diverse reproductive strategies of elasmobranchs pose an unknown cost to pregnant females from the 1) provisioning of nutrients and 2) physiological and physical changes throughout gestation. Matrotrophic elasmobranch species that secrete lipid histotroph invest greatly into the post-fertilization and pre-parturition period.

Seventeen mature female Hypanus sabinus (220-320 mm) were collected with seines the first week of April 2024 along the Florida State University Coastal and Marine Laboratory coastline (IACUC PROTO20230000004). Pregnancy was confirmed through ultrasonography (PAL HD3 Phased and Linear Array). Specimens were housed in Florida State University Coastal and Marine Laboratory facility tanks for five months at 26°C (±1) and trials conducted every three to four weeks (N = 13). Dissolved oxygen was recorded over a 24-hour trial period then converted to average standard metabolic rate (SMR). Preliminary analysis shows a rapid drop in SMR from late-stage gestation to parturition and significant differences in SMR between the late gestation and post-partum period. Full analysis will be presented in full to test for an energetic and physical cost to lipid histotrophic gestation and identify the most vulnerable gestational stages.

Gravid H. Sabinus were also collected between April and August 2023 and euthanized (IACUC PROTO20230000004). Histotroph samples (N = 43) were collected through the puncture of uterine cavities with a sterile scalpel and fluid removed using a 0.5 mL syringe and stored at -80°C. Total protein and total lipid content were quantified through Bradford Protein Assay and Folch Modified Protocol. Total Energetic Content was quantified through Chemical Oxygen Demand Assay Kits. Fatty Acid Species and Protein components were identified through LC-MS to identify key biochemicals that contribute to embryonic development in matrotrophic species. This comparative study will compare biochemical contents of intrauterine fluids that support embryonic development in species with various reproductive strategies and identify how biochemical content changes through gestion in one individual. Overall, both studies will assess the cost of supporting a successful pregnancy while identifying how this varies inter- and intra-specifically.
2373: Intertidal reef flats serve as communal nurseries for juvenile stingrays, where they perform important roles as mesopredators and ecosystem engineers; however, contributions to ecosystem processes can vary among species. We investigated the foraging behaviours of three stingrays: the cowtail stingray (Pastinachus ater), mangrove whipray (Urogymnus granulatus), and pink whipray (Pateobatis fai) at Pioneer Bay, Orpheus Island. Individual rays were followed using drones for 7-18 minutes (mean = 13.5) at heights of 3-5 m, and details were recorded for each feeding event. Analysis of 96 behavioural tracks revealed distinct foraging tactics among the three species. Cowtail stingrays and mangrove whiprays fed more frequently at low tides than high tides, which may reflect changes in prey availability across the tidal gradient or increased predation risk with depth. Cowtail stingrays and pink whiprays preferred foraging on smooth sand using nondisruptive feeding behaviours, although cowtail stingrays also used intense excavation feeding more often than other species. In contrast, mangrove whiprays showed greater preferences for coral rubble substrates and alternated between surface and suction feeding. Although findings support resource partitioning and species-specific functional roles, further works are needed to effectively link diets, prey distributions, and specific foraging behaviours, and to quantify functional outputs at the species level.
2374: Recently, there has been increasing use of baited remote underwater video (BRUV) surveys for assessing shark and fish populations in marine ecosystems. This approach may provide a non-destructive, non-extractive, and cost-effective alternative to traditional fishing-based methods. However, to date, most studies using BRUVs have focused on their use in high-visibility ecosystems, such as tropical reefs. Furthermore, few studies have compared results from BRUV surveys with those obtained using traditional methods to evaluate the efficacy of this approach. Therefore, the goal of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of using BRUV surveys to assess shark and fish populations in low-visibility ecosystems. This goal was addressed by conducting BRUVs and bottom longline surveys in the Tolomato River, a northeast Florida estuary that has been shown to serve as a communal nursery habitat for juveniles from multiple coastal shark species including sandbar (Carcharhinus plumbeus) and scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini). Surveys were compared using metrics of both abundance and diversity. Results of this study found that BRUV and longline surveys sampled different portions of the community and BRUV surveys were able to detect a greater number of species, including some that are not sampled using a longline survey in this system. However, longline surveys produced greater sample sizes, greater abundance estimates, and provided more information on shark populations, compared to BRUV surveys. While BRUV surveys did not provide similar data to longline surveys, especially regarding abundance estimates, they may work as a useful tool to provide insight into community ecology.
2375: The Rainbow characin is a freshwater fish endemic to western Ecuador and northern Peru, comprising two species: Rhoadsia minor and R. altipinna. Due to their morphological similarity, these species are primarily distinguished by geography: R. minor in northwestern Ecuador and R. altipinna in central and southern Ecuador and Peru. Previous analyses revealed genetic distinctiveness corresponding to these distributions, along with evidence of admixture and within-species population structure using twelve microsatellites and two mitochondrial genes. While these markers have proven effective in population genetic studies, they represent only a small fraction of the genome, potentially introducing bias into the results. We used Restriction-site Associated DNA Sequencing (RADseq), which analyzes thousands of genomic markers, to reassess the species status and population structure of the Rainbow Characin in western Ecuador. Our results were largely consistent with earlier findings, including evidence of admixture at the species range boundaries. However, low phylogenetic resolution for separation from the inferred maximum likelihood tree casts doubts on the separation of the two species. Further exploration is needed to clarify their systematics, including ecological differences, breeding compatibility, and potential reproductive preferences.
2376: The relative contributions of spatial and temporal scales to ecosystem variation is an area of focus in ecology. Most stream fish monitoring programs rely on data from single snapshots (e.g., one year) taken during a single time of year. Whether or not these snapshots are reflective of broader temporal variation is rarely tested. We surveyed stream fish assemblages at longitudinally distributed locations in the San Saba River and the Llano River multiple times at two temporal scales. Surveys included annual samples of each site during the summers of 2021, 2023, and 2024 (i.e., annual scale), and season samples of each site during March, May, June, July, and November of 2024 (i.e., seasonal scale). We used standardized seining protocols during each survey, and we identified and counted all fishes collected. We used permuted multivariate analysis of similarity and square root-transformed abundance data to test for temporal differences in assemblage structure at the annual and seasonal scales. Results revealed no significant difference in assemblage structure among years or seasons for the six sites included in the analysis. These findings suggest that inference gained from a single survey is representative of broader seasonal and annual time scales. Our results support loose equilibrium theory that fish assemblages remain within some bounds around a central tendency with temporal fluxes in species abundances. However, we identify potential directional change which may eventually push assemblages outside of loose equilibrium. We suggest long-term monitoring programs be established in regions where future change is expected.
2377: The Polochic-Cahabón Area of Endemism (AoE) is located in northern Central America, and comprises seven river basins across eastern Guatemala and southern Belize. It includes a large lake system, and numerous rivers, showing environmental heterogeneity in habitats and freshwater connectivity. Notably, the assemblage of freshwater fishes is not homogeneously distributed across the AoE. To assess the relationship between distribution of freshwater fishes and environmental heterogeneity across the Polochic-Cahabón AoE, we took a comparative approach in which we focused on the families Cichlidae and Poeciliidae, which dominate the regional species pool. We hypothesized that beta-diversity is higher for poeciliids compared to cichlids, as the former has a higher number of endemics for this AoE. To test our hypothesis we used species distribution models to understand the patterns in distribution of species richness and turnover across the AoE. A total of 16 species of poeciliids, and 13 cichlids are recorded from the area. Our results highlight contrasting distributional patterns between the two families. For cichlids, the highest species richness was predicted in the lowest reaches of rivers and shoreline of Lago de Izabal. Conversely, the predicted distribution of the species richness of poeciliids recovered a widespread distribution in the area, tightly associated with riverine habitats. Beta-diversity shows that species turnover correlates to habitat transitions. However, we found a greater assemblage turnover when comparing headwaters to the lake shorelines, with a larger effect in Poeciliidae. Present-day distribution of freshwater fish diversity in the Lago de Izabal basin responds to environmental factors.
2378: The luring apparatus of anglerfishes and their allies (Acanthuriformes: Lophioidei) comprises the esca, illicium, and associated pterygiophore, all derived from modifications of the first dorsal fin spine. These structures, used for prey attraction and potentially interspecies communication, exhibit remarkable diversity in size, morphology, and function across the infraorder. Our phylogenetic character state reconstruction revealed that the common ancestor of the Lophioidei possessed a purely mechanical lure, with chemical lures evolving independently twice and bioluminescent lures evolving once. Taxa inhabiting pelagic environments and those with bioluminescent lures exhibited significantly larger luring structures and higher diversification rates compared to other luring types. Our results suggest that bioluminescent lures, which are widespread among deep-sea anglerfishes, may serve dual purposes: attracting prey and facilitating sexual communication with parasitic male counterparts. Additionally, we identified habitat-related variation in the rotational range of lures: taxa from shallower waters (≤200 m) and extreme depths (3000–6000 m) showed restricted rotational ranges, while midwater taxa (200–3000 m) displayed more diverse ranges. These patterns may reflect ecological adaptations, such as optimizing lure visibility in deep-sea environments or enabling species-specific communication among ceratioid anglerfishes. Despite limitations in directly observing luring behaviors in anglerfishes and their allies, this study demonstrates the utility of museum specimens in investigating evolutionary transitions and inferring behavior. Our findings highlight the need for further observational and experimental research, particularly on deep-sea taxa, to refine our understanding of the functional and evolutionary dynamics of anglerfish luring mechanisms.
2379: The Neotropics have been recovered as a single biogeographic unit for freshwater fishes in global studies. Several analyses have identified subregions of biogeographic significance within the northern Neotropics and the core Neotropical region in South America. In contrast, the Neotropical islands of the Greater Antilles (GA), have received less attention. Building on the assumption that the islands of the GA do not function as single independent biogeographic unit, we test whether: 1) each island do possess a unique fish assemblage, 2) biogeographic structure can be identified within the GA at the scale of river basins, and 3) if patterns of community assemblages and genetic structure are congruent within islands. Our analyses support our hypothesis that the region is not a single biogeographic unit. Instead, it consists of multiple subregions of biogeographic significance, where river basins from the same island are more similar to each other than to basins from other islands, with Hispaniola as the only exception. Additionally, our analyses identified various areas of endemism within Cuba, Hispaniola, and Jamaica. A tight interplay between the region’s geological history and a diverse array of life-history traits, colonization events, and in-situ speciation events likely contributed to the observed patterns. Our research provides the first fine-scale analysis to help understand GA freshwater fishes' biogeographical patterns in over three decades, compiling the largest dataset on the distribution of this group to date. Altogether, we aim for these efforts to inform conservation planning and management actions in these biologically rich yet vulnerable islands.
2380: Body shape is a fundamental metric of functional diversity among taxa across the tree of life. For aquatic animals, body shape and size strongly affect physiology and behavior, and are excellent predictors of many ecological and life history traits, evolutionary patterns, and conservation threats. Fishes represent excellent materials to study how whole-body phenotypes, like shape and size, affect ecological dynamics, spatial distributions, and conservation decisions. Here, we applied 3D photogrammetry, PCA, and geometric morphometrics to study shape variance in freshwater fishes. We created digital 3D models representing 645 (72%) species and 105 (92%) families from 26 river basins of North and Central America. We then created a 3D morphospace to quantify body-shape disparity across taxa, basins, and climate zones. All the top PCs are complex, including shape variables from several landmarks. The major trends are elongation and flatfish asymmetry on PC1, body depth on PC2, and body width across several top PCs. Shape differences due to preservation artifacts are minimal due to the effective unbending and preparation of digital models before PCA. The morphospace margins are delimited entirely by Marine-Derived Lineages (MDLs). The morphospace taxonomic composition at the species and genus level is dominated by Mississippi Basin Fauna (MBF), and peripheral basins have a higher proportion of endemic and MDL taxa. Species composition and morphospace occupation are correlated with geographic distance from the Mississippi Basin center of diversity.   These data support the concept of an “MBF vacuum,” contributing to the structure of body shape disparity among North American fishes.
2381: Family Alestidae constitutes the most species-rich clade of African Characiformes. Therefore, understanding the phylogenetic relationships within this family is critical for advancing our knowledge and the conservation of biodiversity in African freshwater ecosystems. This study describes a new genus in Alestidae and explores speciation in the Kouilou and Ogooué rivers, offering novel insights into the historical biogeography of West-Central Africa. Using 1,759 nuclear ultraconserved elements (UCEs) and complete mitochondrial genomes of 38 representatives from all alestid lineages, we conducted likelihood and species tree inferences, as well as Bayesian time-calibrated and parametric biogeographical analyses. Our molecular phylogenetic analyses support the polyphyly of Brachypetersius and Nannopetersius, revealing that certain species classified within these genera form a novel clade (genus): referred to here as the ‘Brachypetersius’ gabonensis clade. Morphometric, meristic, and microcomputed tomography (µCT) analyses of 139 museum specimens further distinguish it by having more outer dentary teeth than Brachypetersius and fewer predorsal scales than Nannopetersius. Additionally, molecular data and µCT scans identifying three novel morphological traits support the revalidation of subfamily Clupeocharacinae, comprising eight genera from West and Central Africa. Time-calibrated analyses reveal that the new genus diverged during the Early Miocene (23–15 mya), suggesting the influence of geological events and potential river captures between Lower Guinea and Lower Congo drainages. Ancestral range reconstruction further elucidates the biogeography of this genus, highlighting how the geological history of the Kouilou and Ogooué rivers has influenced speciation. These findings enhance our understanding of the evolutionary processes shaping alestid diversity in coastal West-Central Africa.
2382: Color polymorphic species, where multiple color morphs coexist within the same interbreeding population, are extremely common in nature. In the salamander genus Plethodon, at least ten species exhibit a striped/unstriped color polymorphism, while closely related species are fixed for either morph. In a single species, the Eastern Red-backed Salamander (Plethodon cinereus), previous work has indicated that morphs may diverge in climatic niche space. However, the magnitude and direction of color morph-climate associations has varied across studies. Further, little research has examined the relationship between climate and color morph in the nine other color polymorphic Plethodon. Here, I scored color phenotypes from >65,000 web-based georeferenced community science images of color polymorphic Plethodon. With this extensive color morph dataset, I quantified the climatic niche of each species and their color morphs when applicable and utilized a comparative approach to examine patterns of climatic niche overlap, niche breadth, and potential responses to future climate change.
2383: Biofluorescence has recently emerged as a widespread phenomenon in amphibians, including the most speciose family of salamanders (Plethodontidae). Modified granular glands (MGGs), a distinct type of skin gland, have been hypothesized to be the source of biofluorescence in woodland salamanders (genus Plethodon), but this has yet to be confirmed and the function of biofluorescence remains unknown. In this study, we used a variety of microscopy and behavioral techniques to evaluate the morphology and function of biofluorescent skin glands (BFGs) in the red-legged salamander Plethodon shermani. We found that BFGs are synonymous with MGGs and are concentrated mainly in the ventral trunk and tail. BFGs are sexually dimorphic in size, with males having larger glands than females, but not in number. Further, BFGs resemble antipredator granular glands in their morphology, possessing a continuous myoepithelial sheath surrounding syncytial secretory compartments. Confocal microscopy revealed that BFGs possess a histologically-distinct sub-compartment and that the intensity of emitted fluorescence is not sexually dimorphic. Finally, BFGs did not appear to play a visual role during courtship and did not secrete during scent-marking or in response to electrical stimulation. Our results provide the first dedicated morphological and functional evaluation of biofluorescent skin glands in salamanders and reveal that the function of BFGs may be elusive and nuanced. We propose that BFGs may no longer serve a secretory role, instead serving as an honest signal of individual quality or as nutrient-storage organs. Our results also establish BFGs as a complex glandular system in need of further study.
2384: Traditional mark-recapture methods, though valuable for estimating population size, survival rates, and movement patterns, often rely on invasive techniques that may harm the animals being studied or affect their natural behaviors. To address this, non-invasive alternatives such as photo-recognition software have been developed, particularly for large mammals. However, in recent years, its use for smaller more cryptic species has been investigated, though mostly in the lab. This study investigates the efficacy of photo-recognition on small cryptic species in a field setting using Hotspotter, a photo-recognition software, and the lesser siren (Siren intermedia) across three manmade ponds. Using Passive Integrated Transponder (PIT) tags as redundant marks, we analyzed the software’s ability to match individuals over two seasons (2023 and 2024). False Acceptance Rate (FAR) and False Rejection Rate (FRR) were calculated to assess the accuracy of HotSpotter across different ponds. Results demonstrated a strong matching ability, with overall FAR at 1.6% and FRR at 5.5% with the majority of the false rejections occurring in a single pond. However, matching accuracy decreased over time, particularly for individuals recaptured after extended periods. Our findings suggest that while HotSpotter is a promising tool for short-term studies, time between captures can impact its long-term reliability. The integration of redundant PIT-tag marking provided an effective solution to mitigate these limitations. This study highlights the potential of photo-recognition software as a non-invasive alternative for mark-recapture studies of small cryptic species, offering a cost-effective and ethical method for population monitoring.
2385:
Oviposition site selection plays a crucial role in offspring survival and, consequently, adult reproductive success. While this behavior has significant conservation implications, the specific factors influencing oviposition site selection in many amphibian species remain poorly understood. In this study, we examine the role of habitat and microhabitat characteristics in shaping oviposition site selection in Indosylvirana indica, a stream-dwelling ranid frog endemic to the central Western Ghats of India.

To assess whether site selection is non-random, we conducted field surveys across three streams in Sirsi Taluk, Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka. We compared habitat and microhabitat features between 64 plots containing egg clutches and 91 plots without clutches. Our findings indicate that I. indica shows a preference for oviposition sites in streams bordered by forested patches rather than those adjacent to plantations or agricultural areas. Among the environmental variables analyzed, water depth, distance from the stream edge, and water temperature significantly influenced site selection. However, factors such as water velocity and substrate composition did not have a notable impact.

Our results suggest that I. indica females exhibit selective oviposition behavior, preferring warm, shallow waters away from the stream margins, particularly in areas with intact forest cover. These findings provide valuable insights into the reproductive ecology of I. indica and highlight the importance of conserving riparian forest habitats to support amphibian populations. Understanding the environmental factors driving oviposition site selection can aid in the development of more effective conservation strategies.
2386: The southeastern Coastal Plain has experienced widespread loss of pine savanna habitats, including the degradation of seasonal geographically isolated wetlands (GIWs). While previous management efforts have primarily focused on restoring upland habitats, this approach may only partially benefit species that depend on wetlands to complete their lifecycles. GIWs are crucial habitat for the reproduction of many common and rare amphibians including the State-threatened Gopher frog (Rana capito). Recently, agencies are focusing resources on restoring the plant community composition and structure, hydrology, and disturbance regimes of GIWs for priority species. We used acoustic recording devices and dipnet surveys to conduct post-restoration amphibian monitoring of 53 restored and non-restored wetlands among four managed landscapes in Georgia. Vegetation monitoring data was used to characterize pre- and post-restoration conditions. We used an integrated Bayesian community occupancy model to estimate amphibian occupancy probability across varying wetland restoration conditions. We predicted that amphibian occupancy would generally increase with canopy openness and emergent herbaceous abundance but vary among species. Among restored wetlands, we predicted that those managed with canopy thinning and prescribed fire would have the lowest woody plant cover, highest herbaceous abundance, and highest amphibian occupancy and richness. Additionally, we expect occupancy to have a time lag after restoration depending on wetland isolation, terrestrial habitat abundance, and vegetation management intensity. Our results will highlight the importance of integrating species-specific management strategies into restoration efforts, informing the need for additional management actions like animal translocations, while emphasizing the application of adaptive management and monitoring principles.
2387: Antipredator traits are often the focus of studies of the impact of urbanization on wildlife, yet this global threat likely has impacts on other fitness-relevant traits, including those that may contribute to variation in escape behavior itself. We addressed these considerations using adult ornate tree lizard (Urosaurus ornatus) populations across six sites in Tucson, Arizona, representing low, mid, and high levels of urbanization. We measured escape behavior (flight-initiation and flight distances), sprint performance (maximum speed and speed variance), and morphology (body size, limb lengths, and toe lengths). On the surface, while urbanization appeared to affect morphology and performance, antipredator behavior remained unchanged across the gradient. To further explore the impact of urbanization on underlying trait relationships, we used path models for each urban level. At low-urban sites, morphology, performance, and behavior were all positively linked: effectively, larger lizards sprinted faster and exhibited greater escape distances. At mid-urban sites, however, morphology and performance were unlinked, and faster lizards exhibited shorter escape distances. And, at high-urban sites, only morphology and performance were positively associated, supporting that larger lizards were faster, but these relationships were not tied to their escape behavior. Collectively, our results suggest that urbanization alters how morphology, performance, and behavior interact, not just behavior (or the other traits) alone. Our findings contribute to growing evidence that urbanization produces complex, sometimes hidden effects on wildlife. They highlight the need for more integrative approaches to understand how urban environments shape organisms beyond antipredator responses alone.
2388: Floating aquatic vegetation and algal blooms are expected to increase with climate change, reducing UVB exposure and vitamin D synthesis in freshwater turtles. Vitamin D is crucial for calcium metabolism and reptile health, yet its response to floating vegetation remains unclear. We quantified vitamin D3 levels in the blood of adult female painted turtles (Chrysemys picta) exposed to either high vegetation or clear water outdoors for one month, followed by another month indoors under similar conditions during the Fall. A marginal reduction was observed in the vegetation treatment by day 60 but disappeared after multiple corrections, suggesting that adult females are robust to the effect of floating vegetation. However, further research across various seasons, sexes, and age groups is warranted to determine painted turtles’ resilience in their vitamin D levels affected by floating vegetation. We also examined how floating vegetation influences turtle habitat preferences. We hypothesized that turtles would avoid areas with vegetation cover, preferring clearer waters that maximize basking duration for vitamin D synthesis. To test this hypothesis, we assessed female habitat preferences exposed to an artificial pond partitioned into clear-water and high-vegetation sections and later in tanks indoors at two temperatures. Results revealed that turtles prefer vegetation-covered habitats, suggesting that the benefits of floating vegetation may outweigh the costs of reduced UVB exposure. These findings provide new insights into turtle habitat selection and highlight the complex interplay between habitat features and environmental change, offering valuable implications for conservation management.
2389: Cryptic polymorphism can bias tests of phenotypic variation across space and time. Because many colors exist outside the range of human perception, color variation is not always easily detected even when it plays an important role in organismal biology. In lizards, ultraviolet (UV) color is often associated with aggressiveness and resource acquisition, but its dynamics across space and time are less well known. To test among factors structuring UV color variation, we captured 771 wall lizards (Podarcis erhardii), a color polymorphic species, across 35 islands in the Greek Cyclades and examined how UV traits vary across habitats, predator communities, and lizard densities. We discovered new evidence for a cryptic, low-UV phenotype whose presence varies from absent to being fixed within several islands. We did not find any correlation among predator presence, island-wide environmental variables, and UV phenotype. However, we did find that on islands with mixed-UV phenotypes, higher-UV individuals are more likely to occupy greener, moister areas. Evidence for microhabitat partitioning in mixed-morph populations suggests that UV phenotypes may be under natural selection at the local scale. We also found that lizards on low-UV islands are significantly larger than in mixed- and high-UV populations. Our results suggest that the presence of a cryptic UV morph may have novel ecological implications for our understanding of wall lizard social dynamics and evolution.
2390: The mechanisms allowing the coexistence of cryptic species have long puzzled ecologists. Cryptic species have nearly identical morphology and, therefore, would be presumed to have high niche overlap and potential for interspecific competition and competitive exclusion when resources are limited. Lowland rivers in South America have hundreds of coexisting fish species, with certain congeneric species having nearly identical functional morphology. Here, we compare key niche dimensions of Cichla cataractae and C. ocellaris, piscivorous cichlids that have nearly identical morphology and coexist in the Essequibo River Basin in the Guiana Shield region of South America. Data were collected on spatial distribution, habitat use, and diet to estimate niche overlap. Field research was conducted during the dry season when habitat and food resources are most limited, and competition is predicted to be the greatest. The two species were found to have high dietary overlap but negligible overlap in habitat use. Cichla cataractae almost exclusively inhabited rocky shoals located in river channels, whereas C. ocellaris occurred mostly within lentic habitats in the floodplain and near-shore areas of channels. This high degree of niche segregation contrasts with the assumption that phenotypic similarity should yield similar niches.
2391: Human actions are one of the most prominent drivers of local and global ecological change. One of the biggest anthropogenic modifiers of freshwater environments are human-made dams. While dams are a ubiquitous part of human infrastructure, they also significantly alter stream ecology, disrupting lotic environments and imposing barriers to upstream breeding habitats for migrating fish. Studying fish populations in watersheds impacted by damming provides a unique opportunity to ascertain the effects of these ecological changes and understand how anthropogenic actions impact vulnerable populations. We conducted a morphological comparison of anadromous steelhead trout, Oncorhynchus mykiss, along the South Fork Eel River. Utilizing museum specimens, we used geometric morphometric analyses to quantify shape differences across temporal and spatial scales around a human-made barrier, Benbow Dam. We find that lateral body shape varies both temporally and spatially, though shape differences cannot be explained by dam presence alone. Overall trends reveal similar levels of morphological disparity before and during Benbow Dam’s presence (temporal comparison), and differences in head shape between specimens collected above and below the dam (spatial comparison). Current research leverages 3D geometric morphometrics of high resolution microCT data to further understand morphological variation across these comparisons, particularly within the cranial region. A focused 3D interrogation of skeletal regions containing prominent 2D variation—specifically the cranium, orbit, preoperculum, and cleithrum—will allow for a rigorous methodological comparison between a non-lethal, field-deployable method and a more data-rich lab method to quantify internal structure.
2392: The Blunt-nosed Leopard Lizard (Gambelia sila) is an endangered species found in the San Joaquin Desert of California, USA, where much of its habitat has historically been converted for human land use. Remaining desert habitat is often impacted by roads, oil and gas extraction, and non-native grasses, and will likely be threatened with further degradation by climate change. Here, we examined how space use and activity of lizards was associated with drought and non-drought years and differed between a site with ample perennial shrubs and one with no shrubs. We radio-tracked 154 lizards when they were most active from May–July over four years (2018–2021), during which annual precipitation and temperature varied. We calculated minimum convex polygons and autocorrelated kernel densities to estimate space use across all years and at both sites. Males consistently had greater estimates of space use than females, consistent with earlier explanations that mate searching contributes to greater space use in male lizards. Estimates of space use were also greater in non-drought years than drought years (95% MCP of 0.57 ha versus 2.0 ha), and in the shrubbed habitat than in the habitat with fewer shrubs (95% MCP of 1.82 ha versus 0.71 ha), irrespective of sex. We suspect that the need for lizards to manage body temperatures and minimize the risk of over-heating and desiccation likely resulted in reduced activity that led to the smaller estimates of space use.
2393: 30% of North American minnow species engage in nest association, and current hypotheses indicate it is mutualistic with reduced egg predation risk through a dilution effect. While the nests confer safety to the eggs, the conspicuous adults are also susceptible to predation while in mixed species spawning aggregations. The skin of all North American minnows contain club cells that release an alarm cue (Schreckstoff ) which induces anti-predator responses in fish that detect it. Schreckstoff’s composition is species-specific, and while individuals typically have the strongest response to conspecific Schreckstoff, they can respond to heterospecific Schreckstoff. Through interspecific responses to Schreckstoff, nest association may also serve as an alarm system to reduce the threat of predation on adults. To investigate if nest association also serves as predator avoidance mechanism, we exposed spawning aggregations containing nest building Largescale Stoneroller (Campostoma oligolepis) and nest associating Southern Redbelly Dace (Chrosomus erythrogaster) to Schreckstoff from Southern Redbelly Dace and non-native Zebrafish (Danio rerio). We predicted that the nest building and associating species would have similarly intense fear responses to associate Schreckstoff and limited responses to non-native Schreckstoff. However, in our initial trials, spawning fishes did not respond to Schreckstoff, which may indicate a tradeoff between predator avoidance and reproduction. We conducted additional trials in and out of the spawning season to investigate this potential seasonal sensitivity to Schreckstoff. Preliminary findings indicate that non-reproductive aggregations have variable responses to both associate and non-associate Schreckstoff extracts.
2394: Physical armor is among the most widespread, diverse, and successful defensive adaptations in the tree of life. In fishes, thick dermal armor has arisen repeatedly, but is relatively uncommon in extant species. Among the exceptions are the marine family Agonidae (Poachers), featuring heavy coats of modified bony scales. Beyond their armor, many Agonids have noteworthy cranial appendages such as cirri and unusual bony processes. The Rockhead, Bothragonus swanii, features a uniquely strange skull with a large depression in the dorsal surface. This cavity takes up approximately as much cranial volume as the fish’s brain, and contains complex internal structures.
