Through a combination of optical microscopy and micro/nanoCT, we discovered significant innervation of the Rockhead’s cranial pit. This suggests it may function as a sensory organ. We discuss the pit’s purpose and expand on its role countering the tradeoffs of heavy armor in fishes.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
2395: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is a powerful tool proving useful in detecting and monitoring  rare, threatened, and endangered species in both aquatic and terrestrial environments. Developing non-invasive methods, such as eDNA, is crucial for studying sensitive species in environments often difficult to access. The Floridan Aquifer System is home to many vulnerable species, including the Georgia Blind Cave Salamander (Eurycea wallacei), the Dougherty Plain Cave Crayfish (Cambarus cryptodytes), and many other species of conservation concern. These animals are difficult to access due to the need for specialized cave-diving skills or simply the physical barriers of submerged groundwater systems. These barriers leave researchers to rely on citizen diver’s accounts alone regarding the biodiversity residing in these caves. Environmental DNA provides a cost-effective, safer, and more feasible alternative to unveiling broad-scale biodiversity in hard-to-get-to habitats. The goal of this study was to determine if eDNA is a feasible method to categorize metazoan biodiversity, as well as compare active and passive sampling techniques at various levels of cave accessibility. In this study, we performed an eDNA field survey using both active and passive sampling techniques from seven locations within a cave system near Marianna, Florida, sampling at various horizontal distances from the cave entrance, including inside the cave, at the cave vent, and above the vent at the surface. A fragment of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1 (COI) gene was amplified using a metazoan primer set and submitted for Illumina sequencing. Biodiversity estimates, across different cave microhabitats, will be presented.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
2396: Asexual lineages face higher extinction rates than sexual species, suggesting that asexual reproduction incurs significant fitness costs. One hypothesis explaining why sexual species outlive their asexual counterparts is Muller’s ratchet, which posits that without recombination and segregation, harmful mutations accumulate more readily in the genomes of asexual lineages. In this study, we tested Muller’s ratchet by estimating mutation accumulation in the hybrid-origin parthenogenetic lineage, Aspidoscelis tesselatus. We utilized RNAseq data for the parthenogenetic lineages and IsoSeq data for the parental species. Using this data, we constructed subgenomes based on phased haplotypes in A. tesselatus. We then estimated mutation accumulation by calculating dN/dS ratios between the parental and phased subgenomes, along with analyzing structural variants. We observed higher dN/dS ratios in both A. tesselatus subgenomes, indicating that the parthenogenetic species accumulates more nonsynonymous mutations than the parental species. Although the subgenomes did not show significant differences, there was variation in the dN/dS ratios among the haplotypes, suggesting the potential for haplotype-specific divergence. We also identified several indels in the transcriptomes that likely affect protein structure and function. Through functional annotation and mutation effect analyses, we characterized specific biological functions impacted by mutation accumulation, including protein-DNA organization, regulation of apoptosis, and gene expression regulation. Consequently, we found evidence that mutations accumulate in the parthenogenetic lineage, adversely affecting its fitness. This study demonstrates that not only do mutations accumulate in the parthenogenetic lineage, but they also influence protein function and individual fitness.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
2397: Vocal communication, characterized by species-specific advertisement calls, is the primary mechanism of mate attraction in frogs and relies on a complex integration of vocal and auditory systems. However, some species have lost key structures in these systems, raising the question of how they communicate in their absence. We hypothesize that frog species with losses in the auditory and/or vocalization systems will have compensated through enhanced visual systems, specifically through enlargement of the eyes. To investigate this, we analyzed relative investment in eye and corneal size across 253 anuran species spanning all 55 recognized families, testing for correlations with six ecological traits, including for the first time, the condition of the auditory and vocalization systems. Contrary to our expectation that sensory losses would favour larger eyes, we found that increased investment was specific to corneal size, which showed significant enlargement independent of overall eye size, body size, or weight. Enlarged corneas enhance light capture and visual acuity but are expected to have a lower metabolic cost than larger eyes. Larger corneas in frogs with auditory and/or vocalizations loss likely and allow these frogs to rely more on vision for communication, navigation, and social interactions, while at the same time a minimizing metabolic costs in small animals that are already metabolically constrained. Our findings suggest that the visual system may play an adaptive role in response to the loss of auditory or vocal communication and introduce the condition of sensory systems as an important ecological factor shaping anuran evolution.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
2398: Oncorhynchus mykiss is a recreationally and ecologically important salmonid species found along the Pacific Northwest coast, consisting of many genetically distinct subpopulations that can be resident in freshwater or anadromous. Eleven anadromous populations have received endangered species listings under the California Endangered Species Act and hatcheries have made great efforts to increase O. mykiss ocean-going populations. Throughout all life stages, olfaction aids in navigation, feeding, detecting social cues, prey and predators; however, it is particularly implicated in homing, helping anadromous O. mykiss return to natal streams. These behaviors are controlled by a small suite of chemoreceptor cells: ciliated, microvillous and crypt cells, each of which appeared abnormal in our initial studies of hatchery individuals, potentially due to chemical treatments during ontogeny. To distinguish hatchery from wild individuals, the adipose fin is clipped, so it is common practice to anesthetize hatchery-released O. mykiss using tricaine methanesulfonate (MS-222). There is little research on how MS-222 treatments might affect the delicate microstructures and anatomy of the olfactory rosette. I compared gross anatomical and ultrastructural differences between wild and hatchery-reared residents using histological serial sectioning of the olfactory rosette, microCT scanning and Transmission and Scanning Electron Microscopy of the surface and the interior of the olfactory epithelial tissue. Through controlled dosage of MS-222, I also observed the effects of anaesthesia on rosette structures. Determining whether rosette atrophy and immune responses in hatchery fish are due to MS-222 exposure vs. genetic abnormalities may have downstream implications for management of this culturally and economically important species.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
2399: Extreme structural adaptations serve as valuable models to help answer a central question in functional morphology and biomechanics: How do novel behaviors evolve from existing structures? Some organisms have evolved highly specialized anatomical structures which increase the performance of a specific behavior. However, these structures can be co-opted for additional purposes, providing benefits to the organism beyond their primary role. Chameleons have evolved a unique feeding mechanism which allows them to ballistically project their tongue up to 250 percent of their body length to capture prey. Despite this extreme specialization, some chameleon species have been documented directly capturing certain prey items using only their jaws. We compared the feeding kinematics of ballistic tongue projection and direct prey capture in two chameleon species to determine whether direct prey capture is a co-optation of the ballistic tongue projection feeding strategy or if distinct behaviors can be performed despite the extreme specialization of the feeding mechanism. Our results confirm that during direct prey capture in chameleons, the jaw is contacting the prey item before the tongue, however, direct prey capture kinematics varies across chameleon species and prey types. Understanding how highly specialized structures evolve novel behaviors provides insight into the evolutionary flexibility of extreme systems and may illuminate whether the extreme specialization of the chameleon feeding system has necessitated the evolution of a novel feeding mechanism or if the mechanisms underlying the direct prey capture feeding strategy are conserved across iguanian families.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
2400: In fisheries, depredation is the partial or complete removal of a hooked species by a non-target species. Depredation of targeted fish by sharks affects myriad fisheries in the United States (US) and globally. Fishers in the US are demanding action, but shark depredation is not just a US problem. Understanding how shark depredation is impacting fisheries elsewhere can provide important insights into mitigating this interaction in US waters. Building on 10 years of research in Australia, an international team conducted a comprehensive review of methods to mitigate shark depredation via a semi-quantitative ranking process. Using seven criteria (effectiveness, suitability across fishing sectors, cost to implement, impacts on target species, impacts on depredating sharks, impacts on non-target animals and impacts on the environment), ninety mitigation methods were identified and ranked. These methods were then presented to fisheries stakeholders at ten workshops in Western Australia, the Northern Territory, Queensland and New South Wales. Additional feedback regarding fishers’ perceptions, attitudes, and beliefs towards shark depredation was gathered using participatory mapping exercises and a national online survey. Results from this project are an important first step for identifying the mitigation strategies that are most likely to effectively reduce shark depredation and be practically implemented in Australia and beyond.
2401: Despite their reputation for occasional bites and fatalities, California enacted protection for white sharks in State waters in 1994. Since that time, the population has shown considerable signs of recovery likely attributed to a mosaic of environmental and fisheries management regulations. As the population has increased, so have white shark sightings and aggregations along public beaches, raising human safety concerns. The California Shark Beach Safety Program was formed working closely with ocean lifeguards to understand the behavior of white sharks along southern and central CA beaches to assess risk. The research program has focused on understanding movements, habitat use, diet and foraging, as well as quantifying shark-human interactions. Social and economic research has focused on human perceptions (locals and tourists) of shark risk as well as costs associated with safety mitigation. Data from this on-going research is provided to lifeguards and water safety officials and is being used to inform adaptive beach safety management. These data are also used in a variety of public outreach vehicles including in-person informal beach safety education, infographics, PSAs, social media, and comic books. Results thus far indicated that science-based education and outreach is increasing public understanding of white sharks and fostering conservation stewardship and reducing preconceived fears, despite continued shark-human related incidents. This program is being considered as a non-lethal, cost-effective mitigation model for use in other locations where shark bites occur.
2402: Over the last decade, coastal New York has seen notable rises in human-shark interactions, which include both shark bites on water users and perceived increases in depredation in some fisheries. These patterns are often sensationalized by media outlets, resulting in growing cultural sensitivity and proposed causalities lacking in robust scientific evidence. Immediate mitigation measures include strategies that have proven useful elsewhere, such as drone surveillance. However, the paucity of local historical knowledge about shark behavior, coupled with the environmentally dynamic nature of temperate marine environments, risks a decoupling between current response efforts and positive outcomes. Here, we present a brief history of human-shark interactions occurring over the last ten years in coastal New York. We summarize current knowledge of shark assemblage composition and horizontal and vertical habitat use in coastal New York waters gathered by several longstanding research organizations. Growing data volumes highlight diverse shark assemblages, which routinely utilize nearshore beach environments under somewhat predictable oceanographic conditions. Importantly, vertical movement data and limited water clarity suggest that drone surveillance may be largely ineffective at mitigating risk for ocean users. As such, we discuss the need for a broader portfolio of management responses informed by science, placing particular emphasis on addressing human perceptions and expanding educational initiatives.
2403: Scientific and public concern about declining shark populations has prompted the implementation of management plans and protective legislation for many species in recent decades, and some populations are beginning to recover. However, the continued success of such measures depends on an ability to mitigate the potential for increases in negative shark-human encounters, which can undermine public support of conservation policies, as recovering populations return to regions where they have long been absent. Cape Cod, Massachusetts, is a popular tourist destination that has emerged as a seasonal aggregation site for the recovering northwest Atlantic white shark, Carcharodon carcharias, population over the past fifteen years, and negative interactions with humans have been on the rise. This has resulted in progressively dramatic media coverage that has skewed the public’s perception of risk and raised concerns that the presence of the species will negatively affect the region’s tourism-driven economy. In response to these issues, we have been using tagging and drone technologies to better understand the nearshore behavior of white sharks. To mitigate concerns regarding public safety, our scientific results are shared in a timely manner with educators, conservation groups, local officials, and the news media through multiple vectors. This kind of communication and collaboration outside of the scientific community is critical for navigating the complex societal conflicts that arise when and where white shark populations recover, which will likely present the next major conservation challenge for this iconic species.
2404: The Cornell University Museum of Vertebrates (CUMV) has several long-term sampling sites. Of these, Catatonk Creek is the most regularly and longest sampled locality. The first collection efforts concerned with the community of fishes occurred in 1930 and sampling has continued every other year up to and including 2022. This talk will explore an overview for several aspects of a near century of ichthyological sampling including changes in the faunal assemblage, and a look at preliminary results from stable isotopes (C, N, and S) in this community over time.
2405: Mortality and habitat fragmentation associated with roadways are leading threats for freshwater turtles. While road mitigation for wildlife is becoming more common, it is often expensive, and effectiveness for small animals remains understudied. The Minnesota Zoo, in partnership with the Minnesota Department of Transportation and Twin Cities metro counties, spent four years evaluating the effectiveness of barriers and warning signs in reducing turtle road mortality. Our goal was to redirect turtles away from roadways and to existing under-road infrastructure where practicable. We implemented a Before-After-Control-Impact (BACI) study at 25 sites from 2018 to 2021. Starting in 2019, modified chain-link fences, 8-inch corrugated pipe barriers, or wildlife warning signs were installed across 12 different treatment sites. Our results showed that chain-link fencing (with wrap-around end treatments) effectively reduced mortality of adult turtles, but not juveniles. After retrofitting fences with ½-inch wire mesh, we documented a significant reduction in mortality of all age classes at treatment sites (up to 91% over pre-treatment) when comparing treatment with control sites. Although our sample size was limited, 8-inch diameter drainage pipe also appears to be an effective barrier, with mortality reductions of over 50%. The value of wildlife warning signs, however, remains less clear, as preliminary data suggest significant variability in effectiveness among sites. This study provides a framework for measures that can be implemented to mitigate road mortality of turtles, thereby benefitting wildlife conservation and improving safety for drivers.
2406: Will County is the most herpetologically rich county in northeastern Illinois, with 18 amphibian and 25 reptile species known to occur in the county. Will County is also home to the extensive Will County Forest Preserve system, which has grown to cover over 23,000 acres of land since 1927. Between 2022 to 2025, we conducted resurveys of these forest preserves to learn how the herpetofauna of Will County survived, thrived, or were displaced since the last comprehensive compilation was published in 2015.  We have collected tissue and/or vouchers of 14 amphibian and all 25 reptile species, thus contributing hundreds of modern voucher and genetic materials to the collection of the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago for use in research on midwestern herpetofaunal diversity. We present here the results of these surveys, summarizing our observations of the relative abundance and distribution of amphibians and reptiles in comparison to historical datasets. We also discuss the relevance of these updated records to informing land management efforts on their effect on local herpetofauna.
2407: Invading novel habitats can increase ecological opportunity, promoting rapid phenotypic evolution as species adapt to new niches. Conversely, invading homogenous habitats can limit phenotypic adaptation to only a few niches, reducing ecological opportunity and leading to slower rates of morphological change. However, invasion of a novel habitat can limit phenotypic diversity without changing the rate of evolution, if the transition is recent and selection favors only a few highly adaptive phenotypes. We examine body shape diversity in neotropical characiforms across flow regimes and explore the role of time, evolutionary rate, and functional constraints in explaining patterns of morphological diversity. High-flow habitat invasion was rare until the last 60 million years, after which it steadily increased.  Low-flow fishes exhibit greater body shape disparity than high-flow species, though evolutionary rates are similar. Low body shape diversity in high-flow habitats results from a combination of two factors. First, characiforms have occupied high-flow habitats for less time, having recently transitioned from low-flow environments. Second, the body shapes of high-flow lineages are not a random subset of low-flow lineages. Instead, they are restricted to intermediate body shapes and some unusually dorsally flattened and elongated forms, apparently as a response to the mechanical demands of living in fast-flowing water. Higher body shape diversity in low-flow habitats reflects longer occupation, fewer flow-related constraints, and environmental stability over 100 million years. Our study highlights how patterns of phenotypic diversity emerge on broad landscapes through the interplay between habitat-specific environmental factors and evolutionary time.
2408: Terrestrial salamanders function as dominant predators in forest floor communities because of their large population densities and voracious appetites. The impact they have on the community structure of their prey (leaf litter invertebrates) is appreciable. I investigated these relationships in a bottomland hardwood forest where Plethodon mississippi was the prevailing salamander species. An unrestricted field experiment using coverboard arrays and leaf litter collection was used to accomplish this. In light of an unprecedented drought resulting in mass salamander mortality, leaf litter samples were paired with gut content analysis for further comparison.
2409: Urbanization is hypothesized to promote greater overlap in resource use among persisting species. Florida green watersnakes (Nerodia floridana) and brown watersnakes (Nerodia taxispilota) are abundant in freshwater habitats in southern Florida and appear to exhibit distinct dietary preferences, with the former feeding on a variety of fishes and amphibians, and the latter feeding almost exclusively on fishes. The two species are further known to occupy canals in the region which traverse urbanized habitat matrices. Based on previously reported reductions in native amphibian abundance along urban-rural gradients, we hypothesized that populations of N. floridana and N. taxispilota from urban habitats would exhibit greater trophic overlap compared to those from more natural habitat following their exploitation of the remaining prey resources (i.e., fishes). To test our hypothesis, we used stable isotopes to assess trophic overlap by comparing carbon and nitrogen isotope signatures from individuals sampled across three urban transects, with those of museum specimens collected from a more natural habitat in the region. We found significant enrichment of nitrogen in both species for individuals sampled from urban habitats relative to the natural habitat, and significant differences in carbon signatures in N. floridana collected in natural habitat relative to those sampled from the urban habitat, where urban habitat N. floridana exhibited no significant difference relative to natural and urban habitat N. taxispilota. The greater isotopic overlap observed in urban populations of the two snake species indicates a more similar diet, suggesting a prey community constrained by urbanization.
2410: The syntopic coexistence of species with overlapping life-history traits suggests that resources in shared habitats are either partitioned among species or sufficiently abundant to minimize competition.   Resource availability is not static, however, and shifts in the diversity, abundance, and spatial distribution of prey likely influence patterns of dietary overlap among predators.   In wetland ecosystems, both predictable (seasonal) and stochastic fluctuations in hydrology impact prey availability, altering access to key resources and influencing predator foraging dynamics.  Using stable isotope analyses, we examined the diets of five semi-aquatic snake species from three distinct clades that co-occur near the northwestern extent of the Gulf Coast Plain.  By comparing plasma and scale tissues, which differ in isotopic turnover rates, we assessed dietary integration and examined temporal shifts in dietary overlap.  We classified the prey community into seven guilds based on carbon and nitrogen isotope profiles and used Bayesian mixing models to estimate their relative contributions to the diet of each snake species.  Plasma tissue analyses revealed greater resource partitioning among snake species than scale tissue analyses, which reflect a longer dietary history.  This pattern is indicative of seasonal fluctuations in prey availability, particularly the increase in dietary overlap when certain prey resources, such as anuran larvae, become widely available.   As these resources decline, dietary partitioning among snake species becomes more pronounced.  Our findings highlight the role of seasonal prey pulses in shaping niche utilization and the importance of equitable sampling in assessing predator-prey interactions in dynamic ecosystems.
2411: Snubnose Darters compose much of subgenus Simpoperca within the speciose genus Etheostoma. This freshwater genus has more than 250 species across eastern North America from northern Mexico to temperate Canada. Etheostoma species largely spawn during the Spring. My observation of several Snubnose darter species in the southeastern United States has shown them to have marked female skew during reproduction. Theory and observation suggest that sex ratio of adult fishes during reproductive season can reflect genetic or temperature determination during development, or differential survival at maturity as males may be preferred prey items because of coloration and size. Sexual reproduction results in every offspring having one female and one male parent, but does not require equal numbers of males and females among reproducing adults. Snubnose Darters were examined for evidence of female skew in museum holdings of six Snubnose Darter species. All collections were made in the Spring, with at least 20 individuals in a collection. Individual sex was determined by external examination, typically obvious during spawning season. Standard length and mass data were also collected for all individuals. Between 13 and 27 collections were examined for each species. Five of these species – E. coosae, E. duryi, E. flavum, E. ramseyi, E. simoterum – showed female skew in almost all collections, often significant using X2 tests. E. blennioides did not. Males were typically significantly larger than females in all six species. E. blennioides differs in habitat preference, preferring deeper, faster streams with coarser substrate which may explain higher male presence.
2412: Recreational, commercial and subsistence fisheries generally have a disproportionately large impact on the oldest and largest individuals in stocks. Research on diverse vertebrate and invertebrate taxa has demonstrated the importance of old individuals to fundamental biological and ecological processes, including reproduction and recruitment, trophic dynamics, and population resistance and resilience to ecological and anthropogenic disturbances. The importance of old individuals spans taxa ranging from mollusks to fishes, whales, and humans. The benefits of old age are supported by life-history theory and old animal storage effects. Life-history theory explains why old, large, highly fecund fishes can have a strong influence on reproduction and population stability. Gars and buffalos are examples of an extreme periodic (bet-hedging) life history strategy associated with long lifespan, large recruitment variation, and populations typically comprised of several dominant cohorts. Longevity conservation should become an explicitly stated objective for management of long-lived species. This will require methods for detecting and measuring longevity depletion (i.e., age-truncation) when formulating policies for sustainable fisheries and recovery of threatened species. Longevity conservation to reduce mortality of old individuals is feasible using strategies such as age- and size-based harvest regulations, catch-and-release, time–area restrictions, and networks of protected areas. Research and management priorities should include understanding: 1) how old fish may yield storage effects that enhance population resilience and community stability; 2) trophic dynamics of old, large fish and their role in food web structure and function; 3) how behaviors exhibited by older individuals influences migration, habitat use, and survival; and how human alteration of natural patterns of environmental variation impact recruitment of long-lived fish species.
2413: Ectotherms are particularly dependent on temperature effects on the functioning of many physiological processes, including muscle powered movements. Populations, however, are known to adapt to the thermal environment in which they live and acclimate in response to acute temperature changes. Chameleons present an opportunity to assess the extent to which adaptation and acclimation affect performance across a range of temperatures in both elastic recoil-powered and muscle-powered movements. As their ballistic tongue projection is powered by the recoil of pre-loaded elastic elements, performance is largely temperature independent, while their muscle-powered tongue retraction is strongly affected by temperature. We compared temperature effects on tongue projection among species from different thermal environments before and after an acclimation period to a common laboratory setting. Feeding events were filmed for individuals from six species of Bradypodion and Chamaeleo at five temperatures between 15ºC and 35ºC using high-speed video immediately following collection and after a two-month acclimation to laboratory conditions. A significant effect of pre- versus post- acclimation on tongue projection performance was observed but varied in extent across temperatures among species. In all species, however, acclimated performance declined across all temperatures. These results suggest that elastic recoil-powered movements can acclimate to acute changes in thermal environment and that some of the population level differences in thermal performance may be short-term responses to temperature fluctuations rather than evolutionary adaptation. Acclimation to a lab setting, however, may also result in performance declines, perhaps as a result of feeding motivation.
2414: Ecdysis is a defining feature of all squamate reptiles, occurring at least annually in snakes.  Shedding occurs at irregular and unpredictable intervals, inhibiting studies of the importance of ecdysis to life history.  To date, limited information on the endocrine mechanisms controlling ecdysis has been used to induce sheds via endocrine gland removal.  However, whole-gland removal is often lethal, limiting the scope of any conclusions drawn from these studies.  We used data from the literature and reports of the natural timing of shed events in rattlesnakes to design a novel, non-invasive method for inducing ecdysis in the laboratory.  Temperature manipulations following simulated brumation periods were used to induce ecdysis.  Temperature trials were successful in inducing ecdysis in 63% of treated animals (28 of 44).  Efficacy of the induction of ecdysis induction via temperature manipulation was related to body condition and time since previous shed cycle (with high body condition animals that had not shed in the 3 months prior being most likely to shed).  The timing of ecdysis (Immediate or Delayed) relative to temperature manipulation was related to days since last shed but not body condition, with those who had not shed > 5 months prior to manipulations being most likely to shed immediately after warming from brumation temperatures (10⁰C).  Temperature manipulation shows potential for use in the lab-based induction and study of ecdysis, particularly in high body condition animals that have not shed in several months.
2415: Mediterranean geckos (Hemidactylus turcicus) are native to the Middle East but spread worldwide, including regions that should be too cold for survival. Critical thermal limits have been measured for U.S. populations along the Gulf Coast and south Texas, but not points further north. At the University of Central Oklahoma geckos have been found outside in temperatures far below published critical thermal minima, and therefore we have been collecting and measuring thermal limits for over a year. In comparison to published work, we measure not only adults but also subadults, and we have collected geckos across seasons instead of from one time point. Current data suggest the window of critical thermal limits has shifted lower by about half a degree, with persistent differences between subadults and adults. We are now coordinating with collaborators to use consistent methods to evaluate patterns in multiple U.S. locations.
2416: The underlying mechanisms by which organisms are capable of rapidly acclimating to their environments are of particular interest as the global climate becomes more extreme and unpredictable. Squamates are an ecologically diverse group, inhabiting a wide range of environments which fluctuate to varying extents over annual, seasonal, and daily shifts in humidity and temperature. Thermoregulation and hydroregulation are closely coupled mechanisms necessary for survival and both are dependent on the integument which drives transport of heat and water between internal and external environments. We measured acute changes in cutaneous evaporative water loss (CEWL) rates over a 12-hour period (day vs. night) in three chameleon (Bradypodion and Chamaeleo) species from diverse thermal and hydric environments. We evaluated differences in CEWL within and between species from measures taken across the body on field-fresh individuals. We found that some species experience greater shifts in CEWL rates due to daily shifts in temperature whereas others experience greater shifts due to humidity. After chameleons were acclimated to a controlled lab environment, there was reduced variation in CEWL rates based on temperature and humidity. Short-term acclimation effects over a 12-hour period illustrates the chameleon’s ability to rapidly and reversibly change CEWL in response to environmental conditions. Longer-term acclimatization effects to a stable lab environment revealed species differences in CEWL rates which could be a result of phylogenetic, environmental, and physiological effects.
2417: Amphibians are ectotherms, and they can respond to changes in environmental temperatures by behavioral thermoregulation in thermal gradients. Ectotherms thermoregulate to exploit thermally diverse environments while maintaining control of certain physiological processes. Many species regulate body temperature by selecting appropriate microhabitats. In salamanders, thermal biology is still widely unknown as the literature on this topic is sparse compared to other ectothermic organisms. Furthermore, in the few studies focused on salamander thermoregulation, salamanders are exposed to artificial thermal gradient temperatures that extend beyond temperatures found in the field and ectothermic animals often neglect to thermoregulate in artificial settings. In this study, I will investigate the behavioral thermoregulation of the plethodontid salamander Eurycea cirrigera using their thermal preferences as an indication of their thermoregulation and test if these behaviors, like thermal preference, are likely genetically or environmentally derived.
2418: Thermal environments are critical in setting the limits of species distributions for terrestrial ectotherms across broad geographic scales. This is evident for plethodontid salamanders, being lungless, desiccation-vulnerable ectotherms that have low metabolic rates. Despite the ubiquitous impact of temperature heterogeneity on physiology and ecology, there are still many open questions regarding salamander thermal biology at a fine scale. We have yet to distinguish how salamanders utilize localized variation in temperature, how this varies across populations, and the impact of thermal landscape heterogeneity on population dynamics. To address this deficit, we conducted coverboard surveys of Plethodon cinereus (Eastern Red-backed Salamander) across four arrays, spanning two Central Ohio forests. We used infrared thermography to characterize thermal landscapes at the coverboard level, within and across arrays. Utilizing data on activity and salamander body temperature, we tested the hypothesis that Plethodon cinereus exhibits evidence of microhabitat selection based on available temperatures at both the level of a standardized cover object and the wider local environment. Given that Plethodon cinereus behavior is highly seasonal and reliant on environmental conditions, we also tested whether thermal conditions differed when salamanders occurred in close proximity to one another. Characterizing plethodontid thermoregulatory behavior at fine spatial scales will produce valuable insights for generating predictions regarding salamander population dynamics and the effects of anthropogenic environmental change on terrestrial Plethodontid ecology.
2419: The predator-prey relationship between western garter snakes (Thamnophis) and toxic Pacific newts (Taricha) is considered a classic example of arms-race coevolution. However, questions about the mechanisms that promote and maintain this geographic mosaic of coevolution persist. Recent empirical and modeling work suggests that phenotypic tradeoffs may be a key ingredient in geographic mosaics. Indeed, the mutant sodium channels of Th. atratus and Th. sirtalis, though nearly impervious to binding by TTX, suffer major performance deficits. Here, we explore phenotypic tradeoffs in the third TTX-resistant species, Th. couchii. To determine whether their resistance comes at a cost, we measured TTX resistance and assessed performance at three levels of biological organization: cellular, muscular, and organismal. We found that all assayed individuals of Th. couchii carry the same sodium channel mutation, which confers moderate resistance to TTX while having a negligible effect on sodium channel functioning. Muscular performance varied between individuals but showed no correlation to muscle or whole-animal TTX resistance. Organismal performance also showed no relationship to TTX resistance at the tissue and organismal levels. These results suggest that TTX resistance in Th. couchii does not carry the tradeoff observed in Th. atratus and Th. sirtalis. The lack of any clear trade-off suggests other mechanisms are responsible for the geographic mosaic of trait variation in Th. couchii, and shows that even classic coevolutionary systems are shaped by ecological and evolutionary dynamics we do not yet understand.
ASIH Stoye - Physiology & Physiological Ecology / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2420: When introduced species are brought into novel environments, they often encounter dramatically different climates than those in their native environments. With the increasing threat of climate change, introduced species serve as a model for understanding how species respond to rapid environmental shifts. Broadened temperature tolerances may arise by adaptive response or phenotypic plasticity, when a single genotype expresses differently when exposed to novel environmental conditions. Hemidactylus turcicus, the Mediterranean House Gecko, is native to the Arabian Peninsula but is found throughout the United States. While present across a broad climatic range, little work has been done to characterize the genetic basis of temperature tolerance. To investigate the mechanisms behind this thermal flexibility, we conducted physiological trials to test both critical minimum and critical maximum temperatures on 81 individuals from 22 cities spanning a broad climatic range. We found four distinct climate clusters within our data: continental, Mediterranean, subtropical, and arid desert climates. We ran generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) to parse out the importance of climate group, weight, and sex on our thermal tolerance data. We found that climate group was the most important factor in our data. We ran post hoc analysis and found that the continental climate (Midwestern) has significantly lower critical minimum temperatures than other climate groups. These findings suggest that H. turcicus populations are undergoing rapid adaptation, giving broad implications into the understanding of rapid adaptation in the face of climate change.
ASIH Stoye - Physiology & Physiological Ecology / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2421: As natural environments undergo rapid transformation, understanding how environmental changes impact wildlife is essential for assessing the health and stability of individuals and populations. One physiological mechanism that helps wildlife adapt to these changes is the release of glucocorticoids (GCs), which are key hormones involved in the vertebrate stress response that allow organisms to react and adapt to various environmental conditions. We investigated the effects of periodic heating, cooling, and drying on GC stress responses in Incilius nebulifer tadpoles (n=200). We evaluated the impact of variable environmental stressors common to Texas, including temperature fluctuations and water availability, compared to consistent conditions. We measured GC levels on Days 8 and 14, taking samples from baseline, stress-induced, and recovery conditions to assess physiological responses to the treatments. We found a slight treatment effect on mass at metamorphosis and time to metamorphosis, with tadpoles from hot and wet conditions being the smallest and quickest to metamorphose. However, we found few significant treatment effects on GC levels in this species, which is known to be tolerant and outcompete other native amphibians. Future study should investigate how environmental conditions affect the stress response of more sensitive amphibian species.
ASIH Stoye - Physiology & Physiological Ecology / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2422: With the climate crisis causing dramatic changes in the environmental conditions available to wild reptiles, understanding how reptiles respond to the climate is becoming increasingly important for reptile conservation. However, it is still unclear how climate variables like temperature, humidity, and ultraviolet (UV) radiation interact to impact behavior or how their impacts vary across temporal scales. To help answer these questions, I utilized a remote controlled, live-streaming camera to study a high-elevation rookery of Prairie Rattlesnakes (Crotalus viridis) in Colorado, where dozens of females rest over the summer as they prepare to give birth in the fall. I used the live-streaming video camera to take still images of four different preset views of the den every 30 minutes from 8am-8pm MST from June through August of 2024. Our research team processed the images and recorded the number of snakes present and how many exhibited specific body postures and different levels of exposure to sunlight. We used an onsite weather station and operative temperature models to collect weather measurements of temperature, humidity, and UV Index synchronized with the still images. With these data, I am using logistic regression models to predict both the number of snakes active, and the probability of specific behaviors being exhibited as a function of the environmental variables measured at the den. The results from my models will provide insights into the trade-offs snakes must make to maintain homeostasis and help identify potential changes in reptile activity patterns in the face of climate change.
ASIH Stoye - Physiology & Physiological Ecology / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2423: Embryos of vertebrate ectotherms are particularly vulnerable to changes in temperature because they have little ability to thermoregulate. Although much research demonstrates embryonic temperature can alter fitness-relevant phenotypes via developmental plasticity, little research has considered the long-term effects of developmental temperature on ectotherms. The streamside salamander (Ambystoma barbouri) is a Tennessee state endangered species that oviposits in shallow, ephemeral streams which are subject to thermal variation over space and time. The purpose of this study is to determine the long-term effects of developmental temperature during embryogenesis on fitness-relevant traits of adults. Eggs were collected from natural nests, incubated at ecologically-relevant temperatures (5°C, 10°C, and 20°C), and resultant metamorphs have been raised to adulthood to assess temperature effects on morphology (body size, head size, body mass), performance (speed and endurance), and physiology (growth rate). We present preliminary results for salamanders 12- and 20-months post-metamorphosis.  We aim to assess the potential for incubation temperature to influence fitness proxies of the streamside salamander via lasting impacts on traits critical to reproduction and survival.
ASIH Stoye - Physiology & Physiological Ecology / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2424: Fish coloration plays an important role in communication, sexual selection, and speciation. Although blue coloration in fishes is typically structural, one blue pigment protein, termed Sandercyanin, was discovered in Walleye (Sander vitreus). Sandercyanin is a homotetramer lipocalin chromoprotein binding biliverdin IX-α. We predict blue and green pigmentation in darters are homologous chromoproteins to Sandercyanin. We focus on comparing changes to the chromoproteins that influence the range of blue and green hues in Rainbow (Etheostoma caeruleum), Orangethroat (Etheostoma spectabile), Variegate (Etheostoma variatum), Banded (Etheostoma zonale), Greenside (Etheostoma blennioides), Bluebreast (Etheostoma camurum), and Tippecanoe (Etheostoma tippecanoe) Darters. Comparisons show differences in native protein size and absorption profiles. Mass Spectral analysis confirmed the chromophores in all 7 darter species are biliverdin IX-α. We hypothesize that the evolution of darter pigments involves variation in the protein structure. We developed PCR primers to amplify and sequence apolipoprotein D from darter genomic DNA for further comparison to Sandercyanin. Sequence analysis indicates a gene duplication event resulting in multiple copies of apolipoprotein D while ongoing peptide sequencing of pigments isolated from darter integument are used to determine which of these copies are used as darter pigments and if they are homologous to Sandercyanin. Some of the variation among darer pigments appear to involve differences in quaternary structure, which likely have underlying variation in primary protein sequence. Ultimately these data will contribute to understanding the evolution of pigments in one of the most colorful groups of freshwater fishes.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology II / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2425: Understanding adaptation is central to ecology and evolutionary biology with introduced species playing a prominent role in this pursuit. Mediterranean House Geckos (Hemidactylus turcicus) were introduced to Florida ~1910 and have spread to 26 US states and four climates. Our lab has quantified likely adaptive climate-associated variation in body size, integument morphology, thermal tolerances, evaporative water loss, and metabolism among US populations. Yet we do not know whether these responses represent plastic, genetic or epigenetic change. Answering this question requires reconstructing their invasion history to identify ancestral and descendent populations and assessing whether genetic change occurred between them as geckos spread from one climate to another. We are identifying the pathways of spread across the USA using population genomics (RADseq). We hypothesize that (1) geckos disperse unidirectionally from the earliest established populations toward cities inland from the Gulf of Mexico, (2) western populations are descended from those introduced to Brownsville, TX, and (3) southern and eastern populations are descended from those in New Orleans, LA. Using a dataset of ~10K single nucleotide polymorphisms from 480 geckoes collected in 30 counties across 13 US states, we are conducting assignment tests to group genetically similar individuals, independent of geographic location. Genetic variation will be quantified using allelic richness, expected heterozygosity, and F-stats. Informed by these statistics and estimated dates of introductions, we will test dispersal scenarios via approximate Bayesian computation. Our investigation is the first step in identifying the pathways underlying putative adaptive changes in introduced populations of H. turcicus.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology II / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2426: The West Texas shiner Notropis megalops is a small, spring-associated fish restricted to a highly fragmented geographic range in the lower Rio Grande basin. Despite being recognized as a conservation priority by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, no formal conservation programs exist due to a lack of basic biological data, including data pertaining to standing genetic variation. To address this gap, we used ddRAD sequencing to assess genetic variation, population structure, and effective population size across the species range. Genetic analyses revealed strong neutral population structure, with the Pecos River, Devils River, and San Felipe Creek forming distinct genetic groups. Within the Pecos River, hierarchical structure was observed, with its tributary Independence Creek emerging as a distinct genetic unit, and an isolation-by-distance pattern detected among the sites in the mainstem Pecos River. Estimates of genetic diversity and effective population size varied among populations, with some exhibiting reduced diversity, which may reflect genetic drift or recent bottlenecks. Landscape genomic analyses identified multiple environmental variables as significant drivers of genetic variation, suggesting potential local adaptation. These findings provide critical insight into the genetic health and connectivity of N. megalops, identifying distinct genetic units and informing conservation strategies aimed at maintaining genetic diversity and population viability.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology II / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2427: For some species, gonadal sex determination relies on environmental cues and thus ought to match local conditions, which can be accomplished through changes in maternal behavior and / or the sex-ratio reaction norm. Here, we investigate the evolution of the latter at broad spatial and phylogenetic scales for turtle species with temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD). We find evidence that pivotal temperatures (Tpiv, where a 1:1 offspring sex ratio is produced) increase with average temperatures during incubation, but only over macroevolutionary time, while on contemporary timescales, they increase with incubation temperature variability. Limited evidence also indicates that the breadth of the logistic-shaped reaction norm decreases with temperature variability, contradicting expectations and suggesting this reaction norm feature may relate to intrinsic biological factors rather than to environmental conditions alone. In sum, these findings indicate that adaptive sex-ratio reaction norm variation within turtle species with TSD is driven by climate variability, while adjustments to the maternal behavior of nest site choice may primarily compensate for differences in climate averages.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology II / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2428: Bioluminescence refers to the ability of living organisms to produce and emit light. This captivating phenomenon is found in more than 700 genera of animals throughout the tree of life, predominantly in ocean-dwelling species. In ray-finned fishes, bioluminescence has independently evolved over 27 times, predominantly in deep-sea lineages as well as in some nocturnal in-shore species. Ray-finned fishes that are bioluminescent possess various structures, including photophores and lures, that are involved in the emission of light. Overall, the genetic pathways linked to light production and emission in vertebrates that do not rely on bioluminescent bacteria remain largely unexplored. This study aims to use comparative genomics to analyze the genetic mechanisms behind bioluminescence in previously unstudied vertebrates. The main objectives of this project are (1) to assemble transcriptomes of intrinsically bioluminescent deep-sea fishes, and (2) to conduct a comparative genomics analysis to identify candidate genes involved in producing luciferin and/or luciferase in these bioluminescent species.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology II / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2429: Dam construction significantly alters aquatic ecosystems, influencing biodiversity through changes in flow regimes and habitat structure. In this study, we investigated the effects of the São Domingos Dam on fish biodiversity by analyzing species richness, species diversity, and species-specific abundance trends upstream, within the reservoir, and downstream. Using gill nets before and after dam closure, we assessed biodiversity metrics through catch per unit effort (CPUE) calculations and statistical analyses. Our results indicate a significant decrease in species richness following dam closure, while species diversity remained relatively stable. However, species-specific abundance trends revealed shifts in community composition, particularly within the reservoir, where five species increased in abundance while no species exhibited growth upstream or downstream. These findings suggest that dam construction leads to a reorganization of fish communities, with potential changes in trophic structure. Additionally, our results highlight the need to examine biodiversity responses above and below the reservoir. Future research should focus on functional group responses and spatial biodiversity shifts to better understand long-term ecological impacts of dam construction.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology II / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2430: The phototransduction cascade represents the initial stages of vision involving over 35 proteins, but little attention has been paid to evolutionary and functional variation in these proteins across taxa. Instead, most work in this area was focused on visual pigments, which are responsible for the initial detection of light. Functional differences in the downstream proteins can also have substantial effects on visual ability and thus a complete understanding of the initial steps of vision requires studies of these genes. Turtles provide an ideal system to test for potential functional differences in phototransduction across a deep evolutionary divide, with two suborders that are ~200 mya diverged, and among distinct light environments, with species that inhabit marine, freshwater, and terrestrial habitats. We hypothesized that that long divergence time combined with unique selective pressures imposed by the distinct light environments will have resulted in considerable functional differences in phototransduction between the suborders. To test this hypothesis, we extracted phototransduction genes from one pleurodiran eye transcriptome, four pleurodiran genomes, and 24 cryptodiran genomes. Our initial survey recovered 85% of phototransduction genes expected in vertebrates, with recovery similar between the two suborders. Using codon-based models to estimate selective pressure we found evidence for shifts in selection that appear to be driven by primarily by phylogeny rather than habitat. Overall, our results suggest that light environments may not play as important a role as expected in turtle visual evolution and that, remarkably, turtle vision may be largely conserved over ~200 million years of evolution.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology II / NIA Best Student Paper Award
2431: Inhabiting tropical to subtropical waters worldwide, pelagic eagle rays (Family: Aetobatidae) are represented by 5 species and a single genus, Aetobatus. As primarily coastal species with diets dominated by hard-shelled mollusks and crustaceans, interactions with the shellfish industry are episodic though widely reported across their range. For example, in Ariake Bay, Japan, A. flagellum (recently renamed A. narutobiei) damages to multiple bivalve fisheries were purportedly so severe that a predator control program was initiated for this species and has persisted for decades. In French Polynesia, A. ocellatus has been reported to interact with perliculture industry, and is a known depredator in the Kona crab (Ranina ranina) fishery off Hawaii. In the Greater Caribbean, A. narinari has been implicated in damaging queen conch (Aliger gigas) restoration projects off the U.S. Virgin Islands and Turks and Caicos, with anecdotal reports of interactions with hard clam (Mercenaria mercenaria) shellfish aquaculture in Florida. Additionally, A. narinari has been uniquely involved in a series of recreational boating incidents in the southeast U.S., one of which led to a loss of human life, while entanglements with recreational and commercial fishing gear are also emerging. Here, we discuss biological and ecological factors that facilitate these conflicts with humans and, in some cases, the body of evidence (or lack thereof) supporting them. Lastly, we review attempted mitigation measures to date and make suggestions on novel ways to better capture and potentially reduce these negative interactions as the conservation status of some aetobatids has recently declined.
2432: In Florida, reports of shark depredation in charter-for-hire fisheries have increased over the last decade. The rise in reported depredation has been attributed to recovering shark populations, increased recreational fishing effort, shark learned behavior, and declining reef fish stocks. Currently, no management strategies to mitigate depredation have been developed, which could cause long-term consequences for commonly targeted fish populations, fishing-dependent businesses, and shark conservation. This study evaluates how the potential of shark depredation changed between 2009 and 2023 in Florida charter-for-hire fisheries. Two geostatistical models were developed to estimate the probability of presence of eight common depredating shark species and fish hooked during charter-for-hire trips off the West coast of Florida, using data from the NOAA Bottom Longline Survey and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission For-Hire At-Sea Observer Survey respectively. Depredation potential was quantified as the spatial overlap between the two models and was calculated by multiplying the probability of shark and hooked fish presence. Findings indicate that both the prevalence of depredating sharks and hooked fish increased between 2009 and 2023. Additionally, depredation potential increased throughout the timeseries and highlighted the Panhandle, South Florida, and Florida Keys as areas of high shark-angler conflict. Further research is needed to identify the environmental and anthropogenic factors that drive high conflict in these areas. These findings can guide future management strategies aimed at balancing conservation and fisheries interests.
2433: Shark depredation, the full or partial removal of a hooked fish by a shark before it is landed, is an increasing conflict in recreational fisheries, particularly in U.S. Atlantic. With more anglers on the water than ever before and some coastal shark populations showing signs of recovery after decades of careful management, these interactions will likely continue to increase without conscientious work towards solutions. Depredation can only occur when humans insert themselves into the natural dynamic between sharks and their prey. This presents a multifaceted conservation and management issue that requires incorporating knowledge from anglers along with techniques from spatial ecologists, social scientists, and sensory biologists to address it successfully. Our research shows that angler concern over the effects of depredation on their fisheries often varies by region and target species. However, those who experience frequent depredation are more likely to respond through retaliation, e.g., by targeting and harvesting sharks recreationally. Given the generally long lifespan and protracted reproductive cycle of sharks, illegal or unreported harvest in response to depredation could erode previous conservation progress. Due to the breadth of fishing techniques along with varying behaviors of target species and potential predators, challenges and solutions to shark depredation will be fishery specific. Drawing from our multifaceted research on depredation in high value recreational species, including Atlantic tarpon (Megalops atlanticus) and striped bass (Morone saxatilis), we map a path forward to address these needs through collaborative work among scientists, anglers, fisheries managers, and policy makers.
2434: Monitoring human-wildlife conflicts with threatened species, particularly marine species such as the smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata), is challenging and costly, but innovative approaches can be used to study this such as social media, Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and statistical modeling. This presentation will highlight a few of the novel approaches that have been used to study and mitigate conflicts and negative interactions between people and smalltooth sawfish. Understanding and mitigating bycatch risk of this critically endangered species is essential to protecting and conserving the ‘lifeboat’ population we have here in the United States.
2435: Cownose rays (Rhinoptera bonasus) are relatively large, coastal pelagic batoids that migrate seasonally along the East Coast of the U.S. in very large schools. Those that spend the summer months in Chesapeake Bay, generally spend their winters in Florida. Cownose rays are also conspicuous predators on a wide array of invertebrates including relatively weak-shelled mollusks and crustaceans. However, predation on bivalves of commercial importance has drawn the ire of commercial fishers for more than two centuries, though in some cases this anger has been misplaced. Along the East Coast of the U.S. there have been calls to develop fisheries for cownose rays for many decades, but the absence of viable markets limited development along with concerns over the potential to quickly overfish the rays, which have among the most conservative life histories of any sharks or rays. Females mature at about 8 years of age and have among the lowest fecundities (birth rates) among all vertebrates, typically producing one per year. These life history characters suggest cownose rays may be highly susceptible to over exploitation and developing fisheries should be monitored closely. More recently, unregulated fisheries as well as kill tournaments have been implemented under the guise of reducing predators on oysters and other commercial bivalves. In this talk, I will discuss the history of cownose ray – human conflict in the Chesapeake Bay region and various lines of research to understand the biology and ecology of cownose rays and find potential solutions to minimize these conflicts.
2436: Bycatch and depredation by elasmobranchs have become an increasing concern in fisheries. Bycatch occurs when a non-target species is incidentally caught, and depredation occurs when a non-target species partially or completely takes a target species from a line before it has been landed. Due to the impacts of these events, including gear damage and target species population decline, there is an increasing need for mitigation. One potential solution is the use of magnetic shark deterrents, such as the SharkBanz® Zeppelin. This study quantified the magnetic field produced by the Zeppelin and examined its effectiveness with sharks in the wild. The magnetic field declined rapidly with distance and reached the ambient geomagnetic field at 36-39 cm from the device. Zeppelin devices and non-magnetic controls were deployed with BRUVs, and the responses were recorded for four shark species: Carcharhinus falciformis, Carcharhinus plumbeus, Carcharhinus leucas, and Negaprion brevirostris. The number of sharks deterred differed significantly between the Zeppelin and control. The Zeppelin deterred sharks on 21.7% of their approaches within the effective range, whereas the control deterred them on 2.6% of their approaches. There were significantly more bites at the bait with the control treatment (7.4%) compared to the Zeppelin (3.8%). The reduced interactions suggest that the Zeppelin may be effective for bycatch mitigation, but tests with live fish that provide more sensory stimuli are needed to determine if it will be successful at reducing depredation. Small sample sizes with some species necessitates additional testing to elucidate species specific differences in response.
2437: The post-release survival of discarded reef fishes is often inhibited by pressure-related injuries known as barotrauma. Descender devices are designed to return a fish to its capture depth to lessen the effects of barotrauma and improve survival. While regulations require Gulf of America (GoA) anglers targeting reef fishes to be equipped with descender devices, their use is not enforceable. Consequently, benefits to reef fish stocks are contingent upon widespread angler adoption of descender devices. Many anglers, however, are reluctant to use descender devices due to concerns that they merely increase opportunities for depredation, defined as the partial or complete removal of a captured fish by a non-target species. Therefore, we sought to assess the prevalence of depredation on reef fishes released using descender devices across the GoA and identify the species responsible for depredation. We partnered with seven charter-for-hire captains to record reef fish descents on SeaQualizer™ descender devices using downward-facing GoFish Cams®. In total, 987 releases were successfully recorded off Texas, Louisiana, Alabama, and Florida between 2022 and 2024. Descended fishes were primarily red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) and red grouper (Epinephelus morio) but also included other fishes, such as jacks and triggerfish. Depredation on descending fishes was documented in only three instances, all involving carcharhinid sharks preying on red snapper off Louisiana. These results indicate that depredation on reef fishes released using descender devices is exceedingly rare. Therefore, GoA anglers should embrace descender devices as effective tools to mitigate barotrauma and improve post-release survival among reef fishes.
2438: Depredation, the whole or partial loss of a hooked fish before it is landed, has risen in the United States over the last decade. To date, research on depredation in recreational fisheries in the U.S. has predominantly focused on the Southeastern Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico. To fill knowledge gaps surrounding the perceptions and impacts of depredation in the recreational fishery in the Northeast United States Large Marine Ecosystem, waters between North Carolina and Maine, we distributed an online survey to anglers and fishing guides from July-October 2024. Of the 954 respondents, 87% had reported depredation encounters, with shark depredation occurring most frequently (54%), followed by seal depredation (25.5%). Sea birds and other predatory fish were also reported, but less extensively (5% and 14%, respectively). Similar attitudes were observed towards sharks and seals; however, sharks were considered more of a threat to humans. Results revealed distinct thresholds in attitudes towards management options for depredating species that could be related to the timeline and extent of seals' recovery compared to sharks in this region. The impacts and frustrations conveyed by anglers towards seal depredation may be a glimpse of how recreational anglers respond to shark depredation as populations continue to recover and encounter rates increase. Collectively, results from this study can be used to understand the socio-ecological dynamics between humans and depredating species, offer insights for characterizing angler perceptions, and inform future fisheries management strategies.
2439: Since the 1980s, Florida’s bays and coastal lagoons have supported field-based grow-out areas for hard clams (Mercenaria mercenaria) in the shellfish aquaculture industry. In this process, seed clams are deployed on the natural bottom within porous mesh bags or beneath protective netting. The high density of clams in these areas may attract certain elasmobranchs, which can either cause mechanical damage to the bags and clams, resulting in a loss of revenue, or pose an envenomation risk to shellfish farmers while managing their product. To gather information on this emerging issue, we 1) polled stakeholders on the dynamics of elasmobranchs and other potential shellfish predators on their shellfish leases, and 2) performed captive experiments using whitespotted eagle rays (Aetobatus narinari) as a model species to test the effectiveness of a magnetic deterrent (Sharkbanz “Zeppelin”) for incorporation into grow-out operations. Overall, four groups of elasmobranchs were reported by clammers, with hypanid stingrays (43%) and cownose rays (30%) as the most concerning groups with respect to damage. Of 33 respondents, 69% considered sharks and rays a safety concern while tending their leases and multiple individuals were willing to pay up to $10,000 a year for deterrents if proven effective. In captive trials, the number of damaged clams and broken bags was higher for the control treatment (bag without deterrent) in comparison to the zeppelin treatment (bag with deterrent). Overall, the SharkBanz Zeppelin was effective in reducing the time that rays spent interacting with the clam bags and overall damage to the bags.
2440: The Indo-Australian Archipelago (IAA) is one of the most geologically complex tropical regions, comprised of continental and oceanic islands with adjacent landmasses that act as mainland faunal sources. Heterogeneous topography and geological origins have all contributed to high levels of biodiversity and endemism in the IAA. Despite the potential of the IAA to serve as a model for vertebrate dispersal and biogeographic paradigms, such research is scarce due to the paucity of data available for closely related taxa across the IAA. We took a phylogenomic approach to investigate Lycodon and Stegonotus, two widespread, closely related genera of snakes that are distributed widely across the IAA. Using ultraconserved elements from ~200 fresh and museum samples, we disentangle the taxonomy of these snakes and use their reconstructed evolutionary history to draw patterns of dispersal and diversification in the IAA. Using ancestral range and divergence date estimations on a backbone phylogeny, we find that the Lycodon+Stegonotus clade originated in Mainland Southeast Asia during the Oligocene. Lineages that have dispersed past biogeographic barriers into island regions that are dense and fragmented (Philippines) or contain large land areas and historical land bridges (Australasia) were followed by regional in-situ speciation. We identify several instances of founder event speciation and discuss multiple, island region-specific diversification scenarios. Although taxonomic revisions are needed in this group of snakes, they nonetheless highlight the multiple speciation paradigms in the IAA.
2441: Founder-event speciation can occur when one or more organisms colonize a distant, unoccupied area via long-distance dispersal, leading to the evolution of a new species lineage. We investigate the occurrence and timing of the greatest known long-distance oceanic dispersal event in the history of terrestrial vertebrates—the rafting of iguanas from North America to Fiji. Iguanas are large-bodied herbivores known for overwater dispersal, including colonization of the Caribbean and Galápagos islands; however, the origins of Fijian iguanas had not been comprehensively tested. Leveraging genome-wide loci including ultraconserved elements (UCEs), and Rapidly Evolving Long Exon Capture (RELEC) loci—markers that maximize per-locus genetic variation, increase phylogenetic informativeness, and effectively resolve difficult evolutionary relationships—we estimated phylogenetic relationships and evolutionary timescales of the iguanid lizard radiation using modeling possible only for reduced numbers of loci. Our analyses revealed that the closest living relative of extant Fijian iguanas is the North American desert iguana, with a divergence estimated in the late Paleogene, coinciding closely with the onset of volcanism producing the Fijian archipelago. Biogeographic models further identify North America as the most probable ancestral range. By integrating the advanced resolution provided by RELEC loci, we strongly support the hypothesis that iguanas reached Fiji via an extraordinary oceanic dispersal event, rafting more than 8,000 km from western North America. This remarkable event underscores the importance of founder-event speciation in iguanid diversification and highlights the scope and evolutionary significance of long-distance dispersal events across terrestrial vertebrates.
2442: Amphibians are excellent models for studying biogeography due to their limited dispersal ability, yet studies at the community level are rare. The amphibians of Northeast China pose an interesting biogeographic conundrum as the species are unevenly distributed across similar latitudes. Specifically, most species are found only to the east of the Songliao Plain, a wide area of low elevation (<200 m) habitat, however most of these species are not upland specialists. To investigate the extent the Songliao Plain has shaped the biogeography of the amphibians of the region, we generated habitat suitability models to estimate species’ environmental preferences and used genome-wide SNP data from RADseq to analyze gene flow across the landscape. The habitat models showed limited suitable habitat for almost all amphibians within the Songliao Plain, despite the presence of many of these species at low elevations in other parts of their ranges. However, the genetic results showed that gene flow in this area is high for the few widespread species that straddle the Songliao Plain, indicating that it does not function as a biogeographic barrier to gene flow. These findings demonstrate that the factors shaping the distribution of amphibians vary among species within amphibian communities, and that habitat preferences may be more influential than biogeographic barriers in Northeast China. Further investigation of the demographic histories of each species can shed light on whether amphibians of the community share similar temporal and spatial patterns of population expansion and contraction.
2443: Anoles of the carolinensis group are among the most successful of anole colonists, with representative forms found in Cuba, the Bahamas, North America, and several outlying islands in the northwestern Caribbean. In addition to these native forms, human-introduced populations now occur across the world, from Brazil to California to Japan. Anolis porcatus, a carolinensis group anole native to Cuba, has become established in southern Florida, especially around Miami, where it is interbreeding with the native A. carolinensis. E. Ross Allen and Ralph Slatten reported collecting porcatus on Key West in 1937, a not unreasonable port of entry for a Cuban species, based on an identification by K.P. Schmidt. Re-examination of the specimens, however, shows that they are not distinguishable from Monroe County carolinensis, which differ from more northern carolinensis in approaching porcatus in some scale characters.
2444: The accumulation of biodiversity within Baja California has likely been influenced by both allopatric speciation across biogeographic barriers and divergence associated with environmental heterogeneity across the ~1,250 km long peninsula. Many species span the entire length of this peninsula, yet population genetic structure is largely unknown for most of these taxa. Masticophis fuliginosus, the Baja California coachwhip, is distributed along the entire length of the Baja Peninsula and has been variably regarded as a full species or subspecies within the larger M. flagellum species complex. Here we generate low coverage whole genome sequence data for 73 specimens across the range of M. fuliginosus to assess population structure, determinates of genomic divergence, and demographic history. Our results demonstrate that M. fuliginosus is deeply divergent from M. piceus in mainland North America. Furthermore, past seaway inundations, that would have separated the Cape Region of southern Baja, resulted in lineage divergence and potentially cryptic species within M. fuliginosus. We assess gene flow between these lineages and the effect that past changes in climate had on effective population sizes. Ultimately this work demonstrates the potential for unrecognized biodiversity within Baja California and elucidates the historical and current factors driving genomic differentiation in this region.
2445: Historical processes have shaped contemporary ecological communities. Studies have found that past climatic conditions shape contemporary diversity, however, the impact of other dynamic processes acting over deep timescales have been less thoroughly investigated. We evaluated competing historical and contemporary explanations for beta diversity (turnover) across communities of Dusky Salamanders (genus Desmognathus) in the contemporary Tennessee River drainage. Paleodrainage had a clear impact on contemporary beta diversity, despite major alterations occurring long ago in the Miocene. Our results demonstrate that ancient stream capture events play a key role shaping contemporary patterns of beta diversity even in semi-terrestrial taxa.
2446: The family Poeciliidae constitutes an important component of Neotropical freshwater fish fauna, especially in Middle America (Central America and insular Caribbean). In the West Indies, the genus Limia is the largest freshwater clade of the region and is thought to have experienced explosive speciation, with Hispaniola (Haití and Dominican Republic) as the center of said radiation, where 19 out of the known 22 species occur. Limia has been proposed as a case of adaptive radiation, but this hypothesis has never been formally tested. We are integrating genome-wide, morphological, and ecological data to study the diversification patterns and evolutionary processes behind this radiation of Caribbean livebearing fishes. To further our understanding of the patterns and mechanims of diversification in this clade, we used a reduced-representation genomic approach (i.e., ddRAD) to sequence and compare thousands of loci from across the genome of Limia to build a large-scale species-level phylogeny for the genus. We are also exploring their population-level and phylogeographical relationships as well as testing species delimiation hypotheses.
2447: The desert region of SW North America has provided an enduring natural laboratory for testing hypotheses of primordial and contemporary population subdivision in arid adapted reptiles.  The San Joaquin Valley of central California has recently been proposed as its own desert biome, the San Joaquin Desert, and is isolated geographically from the adjacent Mojave Desert by an elevational feature that includes the Tehachapi Mountains and the Southern Sierra Nevada.
