We are seeking to assess population subdivisions in populations of arid-adapted reptiles across this potential barrier. The yellow-backed spiny lizard, Sceloporus magister uniformis, is well known from the Mojave Desert, where it is widespread and abundant. It is less well known from Central California. We report on an intensive survey effort conducted in 2024 where we sought out S. m. uniformis across its potential range, using visual surveys and scat detection dogs / genotyping from scat. We found S. m. uniformis to be patchily present in the western San Joaquin Valley from the Panoche Hills in the north to the Lokern region in the south. We found the species present in the Transverse Ranges and abundant in the western Mojave. We found a significant distributional gap between the southernmost San Joaquin Desert and the Mojave, with potential historical corridors represented by the watersheds of Piru Creek, the Santa Clarita River, and the Kern River. We present an updated map of its distribution. This large lizard deserves increased attention due to its potential endemism and restriction to the San Joaquin Desert biome.
2448: Freshwater turtles play essential ecological roles in wetlands as omnivores, scavengers, food sources, and nutrient recyclers. Studying freshwater turtle assemblages is crucial because they are sentinel species when monitoring biodiversity and ecosystem health. Northern Illinois has undergone significant habitat modifications due to urbanization, agricultural expansion, and wetland loss, negatively impacting turtle populations. However, most studies in northern Illinois have primarily examined specific species rather than entire turtle assemblages. Our study aims to address the existing gap by investigating freshwater turtle assemblages across five urbanized sites in Illinois. Monitoring the sites used capture-mark-recapture surveys over an extended period; thus, we can assess species diversity, evenness, relative abundance, and richness across sites and years. Our research will determine if there are spatial and temporal variations in assemblage structure, highlight vulnerable species, and provide valuable insights into wetland health in northern Illinois.
2449: Austin blind salamanders (ABS; Eurycea waterlooensis) are fully aquatic, neotenic salamanders that are only known from four spring outlets that comprise the Barton Springs complex in Austin, Texas, USA. ABS are presumed subterranean specialists rarely observed at the spring outlets, whereas their syntopic cousins, Barton Springs salamanders (BSS; Eurycea sosorum), are much more abundant. Their subterranean habitat is inaccessible, so all field observations are restricted to individuals found at the spring outlets. In this report, we present an analysis of ABS observations from 1998 through 2024. We performed an analysis using generalized additive models to evaluate whether ABS counts are correlated with BSS, the status of the aquifer, and spring discharge rates. We also compared observations from count surveys to recent opportunistic sampling utilizing drift-nets. We found that descending aquifer levels during high discharge were positively correlated with counts, and that BSS counts were also an important predictor. Although approximately 1% of salamander observations during our standard surveys were identified as ABS, they made up 26% of the total salamanders caught during drift- net sampling. Among all surveys, most ABS observed were juveniles. These results confirm prior conceptions of ABS as subterranean specialists that rarely come to the surface, indicating that juveniles only accidentally occur at the surface as they are flushed out of the aquifer. Our observations from cursory drift-net sampling suggest that this may be a more effective way to quantify ABS movement to the surface.
2450: As valuable bioindicators of environmental health, anurans play an important role in assessing human impacts on tropical populations. Bioacoustics analysis can be used to determine the relative abundance of an anuran population, and a clearer understanding of environmental factor effects on anuran advertisement call patterns lends evidence for future conservation efforts.This analysis of Agalychnis callidryas (Red Eyed Treefrog), Craugastor fitzingeri (Common Rain Frog), Diasporus diastema (Common Tink Frog), and Hypsiboas rosenbergi (Gladiator Treefrog) advertisement calling frequencies aims to contribute to a larger understanding of how Anura calling behaviors depend on lunar illumination and lunar cycles. Understanding what is now thought to be a species-specific relationship is essential to informing conservation strategies when approaching urban planning and other anthropogenic changes to the natural environment. Over a two-and-a-half-month investigation period, calls were identified by species and categorized using the Karns Call Index. Such frequencies were analyzed using regression and a novel application of circular statics. Calling behaviors were deemed significantly correlated to lunar cycles, but not theoretical lunar illumination in all four species, with the mean calling occurring at 15 days after the last full moon (DFM), most concentrated calling occurring during the latter half of the lunar cycle and a secondary peak appearing at 9 DFM. The uniformity in trends of advertisement calling frequencies among all four species suggests lunar cycle may be less influential than previously considered, and instead more variable environmental factors hold greater influence.
2451: Large woody debris (LWD) insertion is an increasingly important stream restoration technique used to enhance aquatic habitats and support native fish populations such as trout and salmon. Instream wood jams interact with streamflow to create localized reductions of water velocity, resulting in increased organic matter retention, overbank flows, and stream habitat heterogeneity. As such, LWD management is likely to improve habitats for semi-aquatic plethodontid salamanders, despite limited insight into the effects of LWD management on amphibians. In 2024, we initiated a 2-yr study to evaluate the effects of LWD restoration on streamside salamanders. We sampled stream segments that received LWD treatment, i.e., log jams (N = 5) and segments that served as controls (N = 5) in the Monongahela National Forest, WV. To evaluate upstream and downstream treatment effects, we conducted flip-and-search transect surveys and in-stream leaf litter bag sampling to capture and identify larval, juvenile, and adult salamanders immediately above and below log jams. We expected salamander diversity, richness and abundance would be higher at LWD treatment sites. Preliminary results from the first year of the study indicate abundance, but not richness and diversity, is positively associated with LWD restoration. Salamander populations serve as reliable indicators of the health and stability of forested stream habitats, reflecting the effectiveness of LWD management practices. Results from this study will help natural resource managers evaluate the utility of LWD treatments in Appalachian streams, which support high numbers of salamander species diversity and abundance.
2452: Imagine visiting two wetlands with raging choruses of frogs. Now imagine they have had different hydrological regimes. Perhaps (maybe likely) they appear remarkably similar. Nearly all studies on the effects of drying investigate what happens to organisms in wetlands as they dry. Sirens estivate, fish die, tadpoles metamorphose or join the fishes. Studies generally end with the immediately obvious changes (death or persistence). We investigate the aftermath of drying... when water and vertebrates return. These findings ask us to reconsider what we thought we knew about drying-rewetting cycles and their impacts. Here, I touch on the take-homes of our work related to fitness consequences for amphibians colonizing previously dried wetlands. I’ll also introduce the effects of drying cycles on the elemental composition of aquatic systems and their interactions with amphibians. It will be more interesting than your undergrad chemistry lab where you add two beakers of clear liquids to make a white precipitate.
2453: When considering the use of pesticides, forest managers need to make decisions about potential trade-off among management objectives such as conserving target species while limiting non-target effects. Imidacloprid is a neonicotinoid insecticide used to suppress Hemlock woolly adelgid (HWA) and conserve Eastern and Carolina hemlock populations and the habitats they create. We conducted repeated depletion samples among 15 replicate plots at each of 15 imidacloprid-treated and 9 untreated reference sites across north Georgia, western North Carolina, and eastern Tennessee. We used a hierarchical N-mixture model in a Bayesian framework to estimate any potential association between imidacloprid application and the terrestrial abundances of two direct-developing plethodontid salamander groups (Plethodon spp. and Desmognathus aeneus/D. wrighti) and a stream-breeding plethodontid salamander guild. We also estimated the relationship between hydroclimate and plethodontid salamander abundance because climate is a known driver of plethodontid salamander ecology and provides a comparative scale for any potential effect of imidacloprid use on salamander abundance. Mean daily vapor pressure deficit from 2011-2020, a measure of hydroclimate, was strongly, negatively associated with abundance of all three salamander groups. For Plethodon and D. aeneus/D. wrighti we found no evidence of an association between salamander abundance and imidacloprid dose within a 15 m radius of a plot; however, for the stream-breeding guild, we found a negative association between terrestrial abundance and imidacloprid dose within a 15 m radius. The estimated negative relationship between imidacloprid use and stream salamander abundance was comparable to the effect of climate on natural variation. Our results suggest any measurable effect of hemlock management with imidacloprid on the abundance of fully terrestrial plethodontid salamanders is negligible compared to natural variation related to climate. However, imidacloprid might be negatively affecting stream-breeding salamanders, perhaps through exposure larval exposure in aquatic habitats. The potential for negative effects on stream-breeding species may require caution. Hemlocks are an iconic and ecologically important tree that conservation independent of potential benefits to salamanders. None of the stream-breeding species we encountered are considered rare or threatened and all occur in areas with and without hemlocks. Therefore, the continued use of imidacloprid near streams may be warranted at those sites where the salamander species present are common and widely distributed. However, managers treating sites where there are rare or threatened stream-breeding salamander species present should weigh potential risks to those species until more is known.
2454: Climate change significantly threatens biodiversity, particularly by altering the geographic distribution of endemic species. The Bleeding Toad (Leptophryne cruentata), a critically endangered and legally protected amphibian in Indonesia, faces considerable conservation challenges. This study employs ecological niche modeling (ENM) to project the potential distribution of the Bleeding Toad under future climate scenarios and assess its vulnerability to environmental stressors. Using an ensemble approach that integrates five machine learning algorithms, we predict species distribution under sustainability and business-as-usual (BAU) scenarios for 2050. Our findings indicate that water availability and temperature are the primary determinants of the species' distribution, with climate change exerting only a marginal impact on its range. Under future scenarios, the Bleeding Toad's habitat is projected to decline by 9.12% and 5.69% under sustainability and BAU conditions, respectively. However, we identify a habitat shift consistent with our conclusion that the species' distribution is heavily influenced by the ecological integrity of the landscape. Mountain ecosystems with intact forest cover provide greater resilience against climate change, while the species’ ability to traverse terrestrial areas enhances its adaptability. To ensure the long-term conservation of the Bleeding Toad, strategic efforts should focus on habitat management, ecological refugia preservation, and improved habitat connectivity. Integrating these factors into conservation planning will be essential for safeguarding this species amid ongoing environmental change.
2455: Many animals exhibit daily patterns of behavior that differ between day and night.  For example, some animals may seek refuge during the day and become active at night. By lighting up the darkness, anthropogenic light pollution at night can disrupt natural patterns and induce daytime behaviors at night.  We took advantage of the March 2024 total solar eclipse to investigate if the opposite pattern would occur: does darkness during the day trigger nocturnal behaviors?  We studied two amphibian species with different types of behaviors:  foraging behavior in juvenile wood frogs (Rana sylvatica) and breeding vocalizations in adult spring peepers (Pseudacris crucifer).  Juvenile wood frog behavior was observed as part of a long-term behavior study in which the activity of frogs in outdoor pens was recorded using trail cameras that logged photos at frequent intervals.  During the eclipse totality, which occurred in the mid-afternoon, juvenile wood frogs were active at a much higher rate than at the same time on days before or after the eclipse. Juvenile wood frog activity during totality was similar to activity shortly after sunset. Spring peeper vocalizations were documented at two wetlands using audio loggers. Spring peeper calling activity dramatically increased during totality, and was much greater than at the same time on other days. Calling activity during totality was nearly as intense as calling activity after sunset.  Our work shows that the amount of light is a key trigger of two distinct types of nocturnal behavior in two distantly related frogs.
2456: Individual variation in behavioral patterns (i.e., temperament or animal personality) is increasingly recognized as an ecologically important characteristic of animal populations. Long-term studies are essential for understanding behavioral trait repeatability and fitness consequences, yet studies are generally conducted over short periods of time or in controlled environments. Turtles are one of the groups of animals most threatened with extinction and are especially difficult subjects of population studies due to their long lives but are increasingly the focus on research on behavioral diversity. In this study, we capitalize on long-term capture records for a well-studied population of the Florida Box Turtle (Terrapene carolina bauri) to determine the repeatability and ecological consequences of shell-closing behavior, an analogue of a boldness assay used in closely related turtles. We found that whether turtles withdrew and enclosed themselves in the shell while being handled was repeatable across years, and females and juveniles were more likely to keep the shell open. Bolder turtles tended to have reduced size-adjusted growth rates, though this pattern may have been reversed in subadults. No effects of boldness on survival or capture probability were found. This work suggests some potential fitness consequences of behavioral differences that are repeatable over long time periods in a way that contrasts with findings in other species.
2457: As urbanization intensifies, freshwater ecosystems are experiencing unprecedented change that present aquatic species with unique challenges. The cognitive buffer hypothesis suggests that complex environments should promote higher cognitive performance to process increased information loads. However, the interaction between cognition and environmental complexity in aquatic species remain poorly understood. We define environmental complexity as the degree of heterogeneity in physical habitat structure, including variation in sediment and vegetation. The Western Mosquitofish, Gambusia affinis, is a generalist species tolerant of urban environments in Texas and inhabits a range of habitats of varying environmental complexity. In contrast, the Largespring Gambusia, Gambusia geiseri, is a specialist species restricted to spring-fed habitats. Contrary to predictions of the cognitive buffer hypothesis, Gambusia affinis populations from low-complexity environments exhibit greater risk-taking behavior and higher inhibitory control than those from high-complexity habitats. To examine how environmental complexity interacts with cognition and niche specialization, we compared risk-taking and inhibitory control between generalist species Gambusia affinis and specialist species Gambusia geiseri across varying habitat complexities. Understanding cognitive and behavioral differences between these species may provide insight into the mechanisms facilitating Gambusia affinis' urban tolerance and the environmental factors shaping niche differentiation.
2458: Key aspects of lizard activity have long been attributed solely to thermoregulation, especially behaviors linked to habitat use. However, emerging evidence shows that ultraviolet (UV) exposure needs may also drive these interactions. Outside of this photoregulation context, however, the role of UV in influencing other traits relevant for habitat use—such as the social dominance behaviors that impact territory establishment and defense—remains largely unexplored. I relied on manipulations of a classic social dominance experimental design using adult tree lizards (Urosaurus ornatus) to test whether social dominance behavior varied between thermal (heat lamp) versus UV (UV lamp) resource contexts. I then recorded movement frequency, as well as several behaviors commonly used to assess social status in lizards, for each pair of lizards in each trial. Overall, lizards moved more frequently in the UV treatment; however, movement frequency did not affect use of other behaviors. In terms of social behavior, the likelihood of initiating any dominance behavior during a trial was unaffected by treatment; however, males engaged in dominance behaviors more often in the UV treatment compared to the temperature treatment. Post-hoc analyses reveal that the latter difference was driven primarily by a greater usage of fullshow displays when exposed to UV light. Collectively, these results support that social dominance behaviors are resource-dependent, with displays of increased aggression under UV suggesting a greater perceived value in that resource compared to temperature. Ultimately, these results enhance our appreciation of the range of factors influencing social behavior and territoriality in reptiles.
2459: Understanding the relationship between personality, behavior, and mating success provides valuable insights into the evolutionary dynamics of lizards. Studies have shown bolder individuals, regardless of size, achieve greater mating success than shyer conspecifics. Since 2013, a group of Spiny-tailed Iguanas (Ctenosaura similis) in Costa Rica has been studied, revealing stable personalities and behavioral syndromes. However, in this sexually-selected species, it remains unclear how behavioral traits influence male copulation success. Shy and bold males attempt to prevent peripheral males from mating with females in their territory, but increased monitoring by bold males may lead to missed copulation opportunities. We hypothesized that males who spend more time courting females vs. monitoring rivals have increased mating success as peripheral males may exploit male absence from a territory. In year one of this study, we tested personality through flight initiation distance and observed copulation success for males with varying personalities. Home use area was also determined. In a first for this species, we recorded multiple copulations by an individual male during a single day and females mating with multiple dominant males. Unlike most descriptions of dominant and peripheral male breeding attempts, we observed peripheral male forced copulation attempts and aggression only at the end of the peak breeding period, suggesting little temporal overlap among these hierarchical levels. As the most successful male was defending multiple territories, it remains to be seen if a territory size reduction may increase bold males' monitoring in the coming seasons.
2460: Amphibians display an extraordinary array of reproductive strategies, exceeding those of other tetrapod vertebrates. A detailed understanding of their reproductive ecology is fundamental to protecting the species and preserving their natural habitats. India's tropical and subtropical rainforests, spanning nearly 7-8% of its total area, serve as vital habitats for most of its 458 known amphibian species. The remarkable diversity of these Indian amphibians’ contrasts with the limited research on their natural history, which remains largely unexplored. Alarmingly, over 30% of these species are currently classified as threatened under IUCN criteria. Over the last decade (2014 – 2024), I conducted extensive field studies across India, primarily during the monsoon months (June–September), to investigate the reproductive behaviour of over 30 amphibian species in their natural habitats. This study also aimed at documenting and analysing amphibian vocalizations, which play a crucial role in their social interaction during the mating season. My findings unveiled several novel behavioural adaptations, including unique courtship displays, reciprocal calls, underwater vocalizations, other rare call types, territorial behaviours, distinctive oviposition strategies, and insights into their microhabitat preferences and activity patterns. Furthermore, nearly all these species are increasingly threatened by human-induced pressures such as habitat destruction, climate change, pollution, road mortality etc. and immediate conservation measures are needed to mitigate population declines. In this context, a thorough understanding of their breeding biology is vital for designing and executing effective conservation strategies.
2461: Over the last decade, there has been a marked increase of methods in science that make use of three dimensions of information. This multidimensionality comes through CT scanning, 3D geometric morphometrics, XROMM, and descriptive science. The time ripe for stepping back and assessing where these methods are taking research questions. In this talk, I will introduce the symposium topic and themes and I will present a brief overview of the background and current advancements in morphology as we add in another layer of understanding in ichthyology and herpetology.
2462: Characterizing the 3D anatomy of soft tissue structures has historically been more challenging than doing the same for hard tissues such as bone. Soft tissues are deformable and do not have clear homologous landmarks, which are often required for geometric morphometric analyses. Fortunately, new techniques such as automatic landmarking now allow us to quantitatively examine soft tissue structures in 3D detail, opening the door to new paths of research. One such path is the study of genitalia. Snake genitalia are exceedingly diverse, but we lack an evolutionary understanding of the mechanisms responsible for this diversity. Here, I will present recent work conducted on the genitalia of snakes to demonstrate what is possible to achieve with these new technologies, highlight the benefits of increasing diverse perspectives in science, and discuss future avenues of research which may soon become possible with the development of 3D technologies such as micro-CT scanning, X-Ray Reconstruction of Moving Morphology (XROMM), Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), 3D modelling, 3D printing, and Finite Element Analysis (FEA). Together, these tools will allow us to answer new, complex questions about the biomechanics and evolution of anatomical structures in vertebrates.
2463: The use of 3D geometric morphometric (GMM) approaches to quantify shape play an increasingly important role in studies of morphological adaptation, disparification, and development. Methodological advances allow for high fidelity transfer of landmarks between models and facilitate the rapid construction of large 3DGMM datasets. We leveraged this to study the morphological adaptations in the axial skeleton associated with the unusual defensive behavior of Armadillo lizards, Ouroborus cataphractus. When threatened, this species curls up ventrally and bites their tails, turning them into a spiky, difficult-to-swallow torus. We constructed a comprehensively sampled Computed Tomography dataset for cordylids and their close relatives, isolated all presacral vertebrae, and then used GMM to quantify and analyze sequential vertebral variation. To test the effects of landmark type, position and number on the output shape scores, we ran analyses using several different landmarking strategies and compared these with the output from a neural network approach that utilizes a signed-distance-function (SDF) to capture and quantify 3D shape Information. In all cases, the vertebrae of each species shows a stereotyped progression through morphospace from the cervicals to the sacrum. The vertebrae of Ouroborus appear similar to other cordylids but displayed some notable differences in the cervical region, suggesting that critical adaptations to the tail-biting behavior occur in the anterior axial skeleton.
2464: John Hutchison Garnier (1823–1898) was a pioneering herpetologist based in the town of Lucknow, Ontario. Some mystery surrounds his birthplace as well as his birthname. Garnier was a physician but spent much of his time hunting and observing wildlife. He built a huge private natural history collection by exchanging specimens with correspondents all over the world. Among his papers on amphibians and reptiles was the first list of the herpetofauna of Ontario published in 1881 and augmented in 1882 and 1894. Although his species list was inflated with misidentifications and synonyms, he appears to have recognized 39 of the 50 species of amphibians and reptiles currently recognized as present in the province or recently extirpated. Garnier’s publications included several novel nomina. He described two species of Necturus from Ontario. While one is generally acknowledged and included in the synonymy of N. maculosus, the other has only been cited once in 144 years. Additional new varieties named by Garnier have likewise escaped notice. He also published on the two rattlesnake species in Ontario, including the now extirpated Crotalus horridus, and on treatments for snakebite. Most of Garnier’s work is now forgotten and only 50 Ontario specimens are extant from his collection, now housed in the Royal Ontario Museum and the U.S. National Museum of Natural History. His activities as a frontier naturalist in the mid-19th century represent a starting point for herpetological studies in Ontario.
2465: As the primary repositories of source material, publicly held collections that include genetic resources enable foundational research in biology; each sample is a critical snapshot in time of a population, held safe for current and future investigation. A major consumer of these resources is phylogeography, where productive studies are only feasible in the presence of adequate sampling, with key sampling gaps or lack of representation in putative contact zones sometimes disrupting the ability to distinguish biogeographic pattern and process as well as confound downstream interpretation such as taxonomic revisions to a system. We examined records of snake tissues deposited in North American herpetology collections as well as tissue use in modern molecular phylogeographic studies for signs of phylogenetic, ecological and other biases. While demand for larger, more inclusive datasets increases, deposition of materials into collections peaked during the early stages of phylogeography and museums are receiving very little contemporary material. In the face of the Anthropocene biodiversity crisis, it is more important than ever to deposit tissues and vouchers in museums, particularly from incidental or salvage occurrences. We highlight some key cases where just a few pieces of reference material could make all the difference in an investigation and share tools we’ve developed to demystify the process of collection to allow non-specialists, citizen scientists and avocational herpetologists to contribute.
2466: Natural history collections are invaluable resources that scientists have used to describe the biodiversity, ecology and evolutionary biology of organisms. Museum specimens also serve as a set of permanent records that scientists can employ to infer historical distribution, occupancy/abundance and demography of declining or even relict populations of species. The University of Alabama Herpetological Collection (UAHC) was created in the late 1940s by Ralph L. Chermock. Previous efforts to ensure the security of specimens and digitize their associated collection data have fallen short meaning obscure or erroneous collection data, misidentifications and outdated taxonomy were still common issues. Moreover, UAHC specimen data are not publicly available meaning it is difficult for researchers and educators to access this information. The UAHC received a collections improvement grant in 2023 to completely re-curate the collection as well as digitize and upload all collection data to biodiversity data aggregators (i.e., GBIF, iDigBio, VertNet). To date, we have quality checked and labeled >17,000 physical specimens (~98% of all holdings), georeferenced all collection localities and updated taxonomy. The UAHC and other herpetological collections will be essential to future studies regarding the natural history of these organisms as well as efforts to effectively manage populations of vulnerable and rare taxa in an era of rapid environmental change. Although not always considered a priority, it is important to continue to support natural history collections (e.g., time, expertise, funding) as we continue to expand our knowledge of the natural world.
2467: Development of a non-lethal liver sampling method could reduce the need for animal sacrifice while furthering research in various fields of study. However, a tradeoff exists between the amount of tissue that can safely be sampled to maximize animal survivability and the minimum volume of tissue necessary to conduct the laboratory analysis to meet the goals of the study. With regards to toxicological studies, 1 gram of tissue is traditionally used, but since elasmobranch livers can accumulate high contaminant levels, a non-lethal liver biopsy method using less tissue could potentially be employed. The objectives of the study were to 1) determine the minimum amount of tissue we could extract before analytes of interest were lost and 2) determine if a non-lethal biopsy method could be used in a field setting while demonstrating animal survivability post-procedure. In the laboratory, liver samples of varying quantities were taken from the same source sample, solvent extracted, and a suite of POPs were quantified by GCMS. Results show that 0.2g-samples reflected >85% of the 1g-samples, and 0.5g-samples were all >91% of the 1g-samples. In the field, liver biopsies were taken from three species of elasmobranchs that were also outfitted with internal acoustic tags to track their movements post-procedure. Movements were species-specific, with bat rays traveling long distances compared to angel sharks and leopard sharks. We demonstrate here that liver biopsies can be sampled in field settings that reduce animal sacrifice while meeting the objectives of the study.
2468: In the Yucatan Peninsula (Gulf of Mexico and Mexican Caribbean), the Whitespotted Eagle Ray (WSER) is traditionally fished and consumed by local communities as a primary source of fish protein. This study aims to evaluate the concentrations of heavy metals in muscle samples of WSER collected from artisanal fisheries in Campeche and Quintana Roo. The predominant metal distribution observed was As > Ni > Cr > Pb > Cd. Statistical analysis revealed significant differences in Pb, Ni, Cr, and Cd concentrations between the two locations, with Campeche exhibiting the highest levels. Our findings indicate that WSER can accumulate substantial amounts of heavy metals, particularly arsenic. The elevated concentrations of heavy metals not only pose serious health risks to individuals consuming WSER—known to adversely affect hormonal functions and the nervous system in marine species—but also raise significant conservation concerns. These health risks to human consumers highlight the urgent need for public awareness regarding the potential contamination of local seafood. Furthermore, the impact of heavy metal accumulation on WSER populations threatens their sustainability, underscoring the dual significance of our findings for both public health and conservation efforts. Addressing these issues is crucial for protecting marine biodiversity and safeguarding the health of local communities.
2469: Stable isotope analysis of individual molecules, such as amino acids (AAs), is an emergent technique that continues to provide novel insights into the trophic behavior and energetic resource use of elasmobranchs. However, recent work has suggested that changes to physiological status associated with processes such as starvation or gestation, can elicit substantial variation in AA carbon (δ13C), nitrogen (δ15N), and hydrogen (δ2H) stable isotope values in wild populations. Here, we illustrate the potential of AA isotope analysis to discern changes in physiological status using a case study taxon, the bonnethead shark (Sphyrna tiburo). Amino acid δ13C, δ15N, and δ2H values were measured in liver and muscle tissues obtained from wild females spanning a full gestational cycle (~5 months). We hypothesized that shifting energetic demands at different gestational stages would elicit unique patterns of AA isotope fractionation. Significant differences in δ13C, δ15N, and δ2H values were observed between individuals associated with earlier and later term gestational stages. These differences were consistent across essential and non-essential AAs and most pronounced in δ15N and δ2H values of liver tissue, which were substantially lower in individuals at later gestational stages. Given the central role of the liver in AA biosynthesis, these findings imply potential changes to nitrogen and water balance as females proceed through gestation. More generally, these results underscore the role of physiology in promoting isotopic variation in wild elasmobranch populations.
2470: The individual effects of high temperature and low oxygen have been assessed in a model species of elasmobranch, the little skate (Leucoraja erinacea). These abiotic environmental variables often co-occur in nature, however, and the potentially synergistic impacts of these stressors are unknown. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by exposing little skate embryos to a factorial combination of temperatures (15°C, 18°C, 20°C) and dissolved oxygen levels (> 85%, 45%) for the entire embryonic stage. We will measure embryonic standard metabolic rate (SMR) using intermittent flow respirometry every month, and will determine yolk sac consumption rate and eye growth rate via imaging every week. We will also measure days until hatch and overall survival rates of the embryos. Following hatch, we will measure maximum metabolic rate (MMR), SMR, blood-oxygen binding (Hb-O2 % saturation), hematocrit (Hct), and hemoglobin concentration ([Hb]). We will use MMR and SMR to calculate aerobic scope (AS), use Hct and [Hb] to calculate mean corpuscular hemoglobin content (MCHC), and use Hb-O2 % saturation to identify the and partial pressure of O2 at which Hb is 50% saturated (P50). Blood samples from the parent population of skates will be compared to blood analysis metrics from the offspring to analyze phenotypic plasticity in oxygen transport mechanisms. This work has implications for understanding population health of species with a long reproductive cycle in a rapidly changing marine environment.
2471: Species that thrive across diverse environmental conditions typically consist of populations occupying only a subset of these conditions, frequently exhibiting population-specific traits that enhance fitness. The mechanisms underlying these traits fall along a spectrum. At one extreme, phenotypic plasticity allows individuals to modify their traits in response to new environments, facilitating survival and performance across different conditions. At the other extreme, strong local adaptation results in populations so specialized for their native environments that they struggle to persist elsewhere. Our study aims to disentangle the contributions of plasticity and genomic adaptation that enable populations of the Desert Horned Lizard (Phrynosoma platyrhinos) to inhabit an exceptionally wide climatic range—from some of the hottest, driest places on Earth (e.g., Death Valley) to cold deserts where freezing temperatures persist for six months of the year. We integrate population genomics, transcriptomics, acclimation experiments, and thermal biology to assess these mechanisms. Our findings reveal a combination of plastic and adaptive responses, varying across populations, detectable at the genomic level, and linked to fitness-related traits. This research provides key insights into how organisms persist across extreme environmental gradients.
2472: Many have found the vast literature on discovering species and species concepts frustrating and trying to stay current on methods. Species in nature are known as Individuals in a Natural Class.   Natural Classes include things that participate in natural processes. You cannot define an Individual.  Individuals have a beginning and an end and are temporospatially bounded. They are always “slippery,” and humans feel uncomfortable with them. On the other hand, there are things that humans feel more comfortable with, and these entities are part of an Artificial Class.  They do not have a beginning or an ending – they are timeless.  They have definitions and are not temporospatially bounded. They have operational definitions and instructions to follow to find things that fit the definition. This difference stands at the root of decades of controversy.  Why? Most of us, unfortunately, are not skilled in the philosophy of science, an essential grounding for scientists to observe and describe the world. Rarely are there opportunities to learn about the philosophy of science. However, species in nature are Individuals that cannot be defined. Still, the species category is an Artificial Class that can and requires a definition that does not intentionally exclude things we would agree are species as lineages. Any concept of species that is easy to use and operational is inappropriate as the definition of the Artificial Class Species and can have disastrous downstream impacts.  The pure lineage concepts best serve us for this Artificial Class. All other concepts are operational and simply exclude some biodiversity.
2473: Female mimicry in vertebrates is a rare and valuable phenomenon, particularly given that it informs our understanding of suites of traits and/or genes that explain the mechanisms of alternative reproductive strategies. Despite the age and diversity of snakes as a group of vertebrates, female mimicry has been robustly documented in only one species (Thamnophis sirtalis). Female garter snake mimics have testes, produce sperm, court and mate with females, and even have significantly elevated circulating androgens compared to normal males during the spring breeding season. However, mimics are also significantly attractive to other males and produce substantial amounts of female sex pheromone but are not as attractive as even the smallest females in the population. For the past 10 years, we have been studying female mimicry in wild red-sided garter snakes (T. s. parietalis) to determine how mimics differ from both male and female snakes at multiple biological levels: sex pheromones, steroid hormones, gene expression, and mating behavior. We recently discovered two key attributes of mimics that explain the activation and/or maintenance of mimicry. First, mimics are heavier per unit length than males, but are smaller than females, and this may be a result of differential investment in body fat. Second, in their skin, mimics exhibit female-typical gene expression of a network of enzymes central to skin lipid synthesis. Unlike males, mimics have a gene network that ultimately produces significant amounts of long-chain, modified lipids that comprise the female sex pheromone blend. Our results reveal that female mimicry is complex because the combination of body composition and specific expression of key genes permit or activate the mimic phenotype without disrupting normal male reproductive physiology. How the mimic phenotype is initially established, whether mimicry is obligate, and if sexual size dimorphism is a prerequisite for mimicry are all open questions. Our studies have demonstrated for the first time that female mimics exemplify biological intermediacy between female- and male-typical biology and at multiple scales.
2474: Chemical communication, facilitated by the secretion and recognition of pheromones, plays a vital role in the behavior of squamate reptiles. These chemical signals are linked to various intraspecific and interspecific interactions, such as kin recognition, mate choice, and aggression. Whiptail lizards of the genus Aspidoscelis possess femoral glands, which likely play a key role in their chemical communication. However, the composition of the pheromones and the genetic mechanisms regulating expression of the glandular content are not well understood. In this study, we compared the expression of pheromone-related genes between parthenogenetic and sexually reproducing whiptail lizards, anticipating minimal differences due to the presence of pseudocopulatory behavior in all-female parthenogens. We collected lizards in the field, extracted gland chemicals, and excised femoral gland and forelimb tissues for transcriptomic analysis. We used gene ontology and combined pathway analyses to investigate the diversity of proteins associated with glandular tissue and infer potential biochemical pathways. Finally, we performed differential gene expression analyses to compare glandular gene expression between male and female A. gularis. Our findings shed light of the genetic machinery that maintains the evolutionarily ubiquitous femoral glands and contribute to our understanding of chemical communication in reptiles, paving the way for future research in this field.
2475: Hybridization is a prominent evolutionary force throughout the animal kingdom, generating numerous evolutionary outcomes driven by the dynamic of genomic consequences introduced in hybrid populations.  The smooth greensnake (Opheodrys vernalis) is widely distributed across the United States that consist of two lineages that likely experienced allopatric divergence during the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) and recent secondary contact following post-LGM northward advancement. Although known to hybridize in Ohio, the specific selective forces driving hybridization and any potentially associated genomic consequences remain unknown. I used ddRADSeq to generate a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) dataset to assess the genomic composition between both O. vernalis clades and hybrids. I located an isolated hybrid population in Killdeer, Ohio composed of only late generation hybrids (F2 and later) with low inbreeding, abundance of private alleles, and a near uniform ancestral proportion biased towards western ancestry. Hierarchical Bayesian genomic cline analysis identified a collection of predominately freely introgressing outlier SNPs with shallower clines than genome average. Of the few SNPs that were resisting introgression, most indicated evidence of directional selection against eastern ancestry. Outlier SNPs identified from genotype-environment analyses using WorldClim bioclimatic variables indicated minor but significant environmental associations with O. vernalis genetic variation. Altogether, Killdeer hybrids show evidence of heterosis, and directional selection may be characterized by factors not limited to climate such as transitional habitat between the primarily agricultural western and deciduous eastern regions. However, genetic drift likely exaggerates and obscures true selection signals as most western populations are small, isolated, and highly inbred.
2476: Color polymorphism, the occurrence of multiple discrete color morphs with co-adapted sets of traits within the same population, may provide the raw materials for rapid species formation. It has been hypothesized that fixation of a single morph can result in character release, whereby the monomorphic form evolves without the constraint of accommodating multiple adaptive peaks. However, the rates of evolution between populations fixed for different morphs likely depend on the specific adaptive zones occupied by each morph. We studied the evolution of dorsal color polymorphism (striped and unstriped morphs) in woodland salamanders (Plethodon), a North American radiation in which the polymorphism can be found in even the most distantly related species (~44 Ma divergence). We estimated a phylogenomic tree of Plethodon, representing all extant taxa with multiple samples for most species. Morphometric data suggest that between-species variation exists predominantly along an axis of relative body elongation, likely corresponding to a terrestrial–fossorial continuum. Polymorphic species occupy an intermediate phenotypic space between the evolutionary optima of striped and unstriped species, although polymorphic species did not have elevated speciation rates. Faster rates of body shape evolution were observed in unstriped species, suggesting that body elongation, which is co-adapted with the unstriped morph, is constrained by the polymorphism. Striped species had slower rates of evolution than polymorphic species, despite lacking the genetic constraints often associated with polymorphism. Our results demonstrate that rates of phenotypic evolution and speciation following character release can be asymmetric and idiosyncratic depending on the alternative adaptations of each morph.
2477: Population monitoring is an essential tool for wildlife conservation. Protocols based on individual identification, such as mark–recapture, allow for the modelling of population sizes and dynamics. In this context, the viability of studies depends on the available technologies for reliable identification of individual animals. Studies focused on squamate populations have used methods such as scale and toe-clipping, heat-branding or internal emitters, which are invasive and can induce stress and pain for the individuals. Photo-identification is another potential method that uses long lasting natural patterns such as spots or scales to recognize individuals without applying a mark or an emitter. However, it can be time-consuming if pictures are analyzed manually. To overcome this, several photo-recognition programs have been developed. But which should you use for your focus species? And what part of the animal should be photographed? To answer these questions, this study tested efficiency of three commonly used programs (I3S Pattern, WildID and HotSpotter) for individual recognition of squamates using pictures of the head, jaws and chest. At the time of writing this abstract, species from 15 families spanning the squamate phylogenetic tree have been studied, with more being analyzed. The results will allow to provide recommendations on area of interest to photograph and software choice for the different groups, from geckos to colubrids and more.
2478: Camera traps are becoming increasingly popular in wildlife research because they can be deployed for long periods with little maintenance and are less invasive than traditional trapping methods. We tested the efficacy of the Adapted-Hunt Drift Fence Technique (AHDriFT) for surveying eastern diamondback rattlesnakes (Crotalus adamanteus; EDBs), which are imperiled and declining across their range. Because EDBs are cryptic and difficult to detect visually, passive sampling techniques have the potential to assist in surveys. We deployed 20 AHDriFT arrays across our study site in South Carolina where we are concurrently conducting a long-term mark-recapture and radio-telemetry study on EDBs. Between August 2022 and May 2024, we collected 79 independent EDB observations (images) from camera traps. We used mixed effects logistic regression to evaluate covariate effects (e.g., weather, changes in day length, and EDB behavioral season) on the probability of detecting EDBs in camera traps and evaluated candidate models using AICc model selection. The probability of detecting EDBs was low and associated with interactive effects of air temperature and photoperiod, with detection increasing in the fall as photoperiod shortened and temperatures decreased. In the spring, as photoperiod increased, detection increased when temperature was above average. Stationary camera traps are inefficient at surveying for EDBs, likely reflecting the species’ sit-and-wait ambush foraging strategy that limits movement activity.
2479: Describing the space use and activity patterns of small animals is important to evaluating reintroduction projects. The development of miniaturized tracking devices, such as UHF (ultra-high frequency) transmitters, has provided opportunities to better understand the ecology of many smaller-bodied species and assess conservation efforts using automated radio telemetry systems (ARTS). The blunt-nosed leopard lizard (BNLL; Gambelia sila) is an endangered species endemic to the San Joaquin Desert of Central California. We are releasing captive-produced BNLL to bolster an almost-extirpated population in Fresno County, CA where we installed an ARTS of >300 nodes. Stationary tag calibration tests indicated a median location error (true - estimated) of 29.5 meters. We also performed moving tag calibration tests: home ranges were similar between those generated with known and estimated locations. In June 2024, we released 10 captive-reared BNLL equipped with UHF backpacks and later equipped four wild lizards, and plan to release more in 2025. We monitored lizards with a combination of hand and automated tracking, using multilateration methods to estimate >200,000 lizard locations. The use of ARTS data resulted in better home range estimates than hand-tracking alone, provided insight into post-release movements, and confirmed that both released and wild lizards selected habitat near dirt roads. Additionally, we used data from the ARTS to predict when lizards are below ground, detect late season activity, and determine likely mortality events. Our results confirm ARTS can be a powerful and cost-effective tool for monitoring small-bodied terrestrial vertebrates at high resolution.
2480: We need accurate data about species occurrence for recovery plans to be effective. Turtles are a highly imperiled group. Baited, aquatic traps are often used to monitor freshwater turtles. Recent studies show that trail cameras can detect turtles, but we lack comparative studies contrasting these approaches. We ask which method is more effective at detecting turtles in Minnesota. In summer 2022 and 2023, we pointed trail cameras at basking platforms at 15 sites in two state parks. We also used aquatic traps at 12 sites. Aquatic traps captured four species, including the Painted (Chrysemys picta), Blanding’s (Emydoidea blandingii), Snapping (Chelydra serpentina), and Spiny Softshell Turtles (Apalone spinifera). Camera traps documented these same species as well as map turtles (Graptemys spp.). Daily detection probabilities for Painted (aquatic = 0.653 vs. camera = 0.691) and Blanding’s Turtles (aquatic = 0.104 vs. camera = 0.100)  are similar between methods. Snapping and Spiny Softshell Turtles are more likely encountered via aquatic traps. Map turtles were only detected at one site where we did not trap. We further explore these data using hierarchical occupancy models to investigate covariates that impact detection of and site use by these species. Trail cameras require less personnel time and have lower equipment costs compared to aquatic traps. Additionally, for some species, such as the rare Blanding’s Turtle, trail cameras are just as effective. For these reasons, we recommend incorporating trail cameras into survey efforts for freshwater turtles aimed at documenting species use.
2481: Frogs are one of the most threatened groups of animals on the planet, yet our current understanding of global frog species diversity, distributions and population trends remains poor. Professional biologists are working hard to gather the information needed to conserve frogs but cannot do it alone. In 2017, the Australian Museum launched FrogID, a national citizen science project based upon a smartphone app used to record calling frogs. The project has now engaged almost 100,000 people to collect over 1.2 million records of frogs across the continent, revolutionising revolutionised both our understanding of Australian frogs and public engagement in frog conservation. The dataset is growing rapidly, with a peak of over 6,200 frog records in a single day. These occurrence records and audio recordings have helped uncover the true diversity and distributions of Australia’s frogs, along with the impact of threats such as fires, drought, climate change and habitat modification. People across Australia have clearly demonstrated the power of community engagement in frog conservation.
2482: A combination of visualization techniques provides a multidimensional assessment of gross and microscopic anatomy. The olfactory organs and associated tissues in larval, aquatic adult, and terrestrial adult phase rough-skinned newts, Taricha granulosa, were examined by Diffusible Iodine-based Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography (diceCT), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and traditional histology. DiceCT enabled comparison of the overall morphology of larval and adult main olfactory cavity (MOC) and vomeronasal organ (VNO). Histology and SEM provide detailed information about the sensory and supporting cells of the MOC and VNO. In both aquatic and terrestrial individuals, the olfactory epithelium of the MOC has strips of sensory and supporting cells set between ridges of respiratory epithelium. In aquatic adults, the respiratory epithelium is covered with long, presumably motile cilia; the olfactory epithelium has much shorter cilia. In contrast, terrestrial animals largely lack cilia on the ridges of non-sensory epithelium of the MOC, and the respiratory ridges are much more pronounced. The respiratory epithelium of the lateral nasal groove is ciliated in both aquatic and terrestrial forms, with long, thick, presumably motile cilia, while the vomeronasal epithelium has short, slender cilia. Changes in epithelial characteristics between aquatic and terrestrial forms have also been reported in European newts (Lissotriton, Triturus) and in Asian newts (Cynops), though differing in detail from those in Taricha. This morphological transition between media likely indicates a change in both olfactory mechanism and in sensitivity to chemical cues from conspecifics, as T. granulosa move between water and land as part of their annual reproductive cycle.
2483: The Non-Clinical Tomography Users Research Network (NoCTURN) is an international community of students, educators, and engineers dedicated to advancing the use of CT scanning technology in research and education. We promote resources available in online repositories, like Morphosource, and 3D models published by the open Vertebrate project (oVert). Although tomography data are becoming increasinlgy accessible to researchers, educators, and natural history enthusiasts, with some freely available for download, adoption and integration of open-access 3D data into K–12 education remains poor. Addressing limited classroom integration is a major interest area for the NoCTURN. Through its Education and Outreach (E&O) initiative, NoCTURN aims to cultivate the use of outputs from cutting-edge scientific tools in K-12 classrooms by providing accessible, CT-based educational resources. One approach we have taken is the development of education kits (Ed-Kits) geared towards specific age groups alongside learning objectives to support teachers in accessing, using, and instructing with freely available tomographic data. Examples include exploring homology and an introduction to Morphosource. These kits are published to QUBESHub (BioQUEST Curriculum Consortium), which allows assignment of persistent identifiers to track usage metrics and versioning to adapt content for evolving education and technological needs. Here we discuss our recent Ed-Kits, their deployment, reception by the community, and use them to provide an overview of the process of developing and publishing broadly accessible Ed-Kits using non-clinical tomography resources. We plan to continue expanding our Ed-Kit topics and add content designed specifically for different age groups within the broader K-12 range.
2484: Newer methods of scientific research have led to the increased use of 3D data when examining morphologies of organisms. I’ll be the first to admit that I jumped on that train when starting my own independent research. What started as CT-scanning neotropical electric fishes to examine craniofacial morphologies transitioned to identifying possible structural similarities across taxa with elongated faces. This brought me to the idea of “convergent evolution.” What started as CT-scanning afro-tropical electric fishes to examine craniofacial morphologies transitioned into a closer examination of the secondary sets of jaws in these species (the tongue-bite-apparatus). This brought me to the idea of “ecomorphology.” And what started as examining the diverse body shapes of minnows and shiners native to Minnesota transitioned into an interest in the tuberculation patterns on their faces. This brought me to the idea of “secondary sexual characteristics.” In all these projects, old and new, incorporating 3D data into my investigations has allowed me to expand my visual examinations of fishes, but also allowed me to expand into new fields as I attempt to connect shape to the vast number of factors influencing organismal evolution and ecology.
2485: Over the past decade, diffusible iodine-based contrast-enhanced Computed Tomography (diceCT) has commonly been used to create 3D representations of the soft tissue anatomy of vertebrate specimens preserved in natural history collections. It has been successfully used to uncover a treasure trove of anatomical characters and natural history records hidden within these specimens. While the technique has been widely applied, there has not been systematic documentation of protocols that can be adapted to a diverse range of vertebrates. Here, we apply diceCT to the most taxonomically and morphologically broad sampling of vertebrates, 3D imaged for the open Vertebrate (oVert) Thematic Collections network. We document our methods, adaptations, outcomes, and observations throughout all stages of the process: preparation, staining, scanning, and data processing.  As expected, larger specimens take a longer time to stain, but the final staining time depends on the taxon, whether there is dermal and/or bony armor present, and whether any internal structures (e.g., eggs, embryos, large fat deposits) require large amounts of iodine to become fully saturated. We establish a scoring system for diceCT-imaged soft tissues that reflects the usefulness of the data for research. As well as high-quality CT scans, we also provide examples of specimens that exhibit severe soft tissue damages, incomplete preservation, permanent specimen alteration, and understaining. All datasets produced have been made freely available for download via the data repository MorphoSource, and we hope that our work can serve as a resource for scientists and the public to explore and study vertebrate anatomy.
2486: The adhesive toes of geckos and other lizards are an amazing example of naturally occurring nanotech, comprised of complex micro and nano-scale structures called setae. A basic step in understanding their structure, function, and variation is the ability to accurately measure their dimensions. This can be a difficult endeavor. Electron microscopy is a common high-resolution imaging approach, yet electron microscopy can suffer from optical distortions. To address this challenge, we used high resolution laser confocal microscopy to generate 3D scans. Geckos (and other pad bearing lizards) use a wide variety of surfaces in the wild. We focused on four sympatric species of Phelsuma geckos from the island of Mauritius suspected of using different surface textures. Our scans allowed us to measure setal length, diameter, and density across the rear toes of our focal species. These measurements will allow for comparisons to surface texture to infer how these species may be adapted to specific scansorial microhabitats. Gaining a better understanding of their adhesive morphology is an exciting first step to better understanding patterns of niche partitioning and character displacement.
2487: Many current methods for assessment of the brain are destructive, which can compromise the relative positions of various structures and can be impractical for the study of rare and/or valuable specimens. Bioimaging techniques, including computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), are unique in their ability to non-invasively acquire high-resolution, digital, 3D data in situ. These techniques facilitate highly accurate and efficient visualization and analysis of internal anatomy that have been applied to both extant and even extinct chondrichthyans. Although many of these cutting-edge technologies and methods are more extensively developed for applications in human brain research, their utility in comparative neurobiology in other taxa has been comparatively underexplored. This talk will focus on the application of MRI as an investigative tool for neuroanatomy in cartilaginous fishes, including optimization and advances in instrumentation, contrast and resolution, and applicability of MRI to understand peripheral (olfactory rosette, eye, inner ear) and central (brain) anatomy in sharks and batoids. These techniques have greatly broadened our understanding of brain evolution in this group by expanding our capacity to include rare and/or endangered specimens into comparative datasets (e.g. the Greenland shark, Somniosus microcephalous; whale shark, Rhincodon typus; sawfishes, Pristis spp.), where dissection is sub-optimal. Further, digitization of specimens serves a critical role in preserving biological material in perpetuity, enabling worldwide access to specimens, development of new teaching tools, and allowing for new questions of the same tissue by future generations of scientists.
2488: As natural habitats change rapidly, understanding how wildlife responds to environmental shifts is crucial for assessing population health and stability. Glucocorticoids (GCs), primarily corticosterone (cort) in amphibians, regulate the vertebrate stress response and play a key role in maintaining homeostasis, reproduction, energy allocation, and behavior. Changes in GCs, from baseline to stress response and negative feedback to recovery, can indicate an organism's coping capacity in a given environment. We measured waterborne cort in lesser sirens (Siren intermedia) over 2 years and across life stages. Our goal was to gain a better understanding of the environmental pressures sirens face and how they are coping with environmental change. We also wanted to understand if there are vulnerable periods across a sirens life when coping may be limited. We measured GCs across 3 time points (baseline, stressed, and recovery) to assess coping capacity in 3 populations of lesser sirens. We repeatedly captured and sampled individuals to assess endocrine responses through time. We found that larval sirens exhibited strong stress responses and efficient negative feedback, characteristic of a ‘healthy’ endocrine profile. Cort levels peaked in spring, coinciding with the onset of the breeding season, and was higher in smaller individuals. Temperature was positively correlated with cort levels, but only in stressed and recovery samples, suggesting heightened sensitivity to environmental factors under stress. These findings indicate that S. intermedia are currently coping well but are vulnerable to increasing temperatures. Given high larval mortality, understanding stress responses during early life stages is critical for conservation.
Stress and Welfare in Organisms throughout Lifetime (HL)
2489: Temperature affects organisms across all ontogenetic life stages, but the embryonic stage, in particular, is often sensitive to changes in temperature. For ectotherms that inhabit large latitudinal ranges, environmental factors, such as temperature, create gradients to which local populations must adapt. These gradients thus result in phenotypic variation across populations spanning the species range. For embryos, traits such as developmental time and metabolic rate can interact in response to the shifting environmental conditions, resulting in shifts in associated costs and benefits. This study investigates adaptations associated with embryonic development in Prairie Lizards (Sceloporus consobrinus) across a latitudinal thermal gradient. Gravid adult females were collected from two latitudinally distinct populations. Eggs from each clutch were randomly assigned to two temperature treatments (25°C and 31°C) in a split-clutch design and checked daily for hatchlings to determine developmental time. Embryonic metabolism was measured as both whole organism respiration and heart rate at respective incubation temperatures. Results show the expected response of warmer temperatures decreasing development time with general increases in respiration and heart rates. Populations differed, however, in how developmental time, heart rate, and respiration rate collectively responded to temperature treatments, suggesting evolution in plasticity has occurred in these traits. As temperatures become more variable, understanding how temperature influences embryonic physiology will be important for determining whether developmental pathways of ectotherms will respond to changing temperatures in adaptive or maladaptive ways.
Stress and Welfare in Organisms throughout Lifetime (HL)
2490: Environmental heterogeneity can present a challenge for many organisms. Overcoming this challenge can be difficult, especially for embryos of oviparous species who are subject to the stochasticity of the environment unable to behavioral change their circumstance. Adaptive developmental plasticity is one route by which embryos can cope with environmental heterogeneity. The environmental matching hypothesis (EMH) predicts that organisms will develop phenotypes suited to their environment when the developmental environment matches the post-developmental environment. We collected eggs (n = 2,296) from a wild-caught colony of brown anoles (Anolis sagrei) and subjected them to incubation profiles that mimicked the shaded and open environments in the field. Hatchlings (n = 1,535) were released on one of two islands that corresponded with the incubation conditions in the lab: an open island that has very little structure or a shaded island that was mostly covered with trees. Our reciprocal transplant design ensured that the developmental environment either matched or mismatched the post hatching environment on the island. We recaptured hatchlings over a 5-month period to access growth and survival. Preliminary results show that hatchlings from the open incubation treatment have increased survival on the open island compared to those from the shaded incubation environment regardless of post developmental environment. These results provide evidence that the fitness consequences of the developmental environment may depend on the post-hatching environment.
Stress and Welfare in Organisms throughout Lifetime (HL)
2491: Suites of coevolved traits related to reproduction and demography enable species to persist in the face of environmental change. In the case of biological invasions, the suite of life history traits, “life history strategies”, can be linked to successful establishment after an introduction. Conservation translocations share many similarities with biological invasions, yet studies examining the relationship between life history and translocation outcome are scarce. We collected data on key life history traits for all herpetofauna profiled in the IUCN Global Conservation Translocation Perspectives series to examine how life history can predict outcomes and difficulties of conservation translocations. For reptiles, our model showed that age at maturity showed a significant positive association with higher probabilities of more successful outcomes, while increased clutch/litter size and lifespan predicted less successful outcomes. We found no relationship between any life history trait and translocation outcome for amphibians. Our results showed that difficulties with conservation translocations are related more to phylogeny than life history. Amphibian translocations faced more difficulties due to the physical environment of release sites, but reptile translocations experienced more socio-political difficulties. These relationships provide important insights for conservation practitioners that can be used in the feasibility and planning stages of translocations to anticipate and avoid challenges facing this complex and increasingly common form of conservation intervention.
Stress and Welfare in Organisms throughout Lifetime (HL)
2492: Endocrine-disrupting chemicals like bisphenol A (BPA) are widespread in aquatic environments and can impact organisms’ health, especially when exposure happens during critical developmental stages. We examined the effects of pre and postnatal exposure to BPA on two live-bearing fish species: Heterandria formosa and Gambusia affinis which differ notoriously in the level of matrotrophy. Gravid H. formosa females (highly matrotrophic) were exposed to 200 µg/L BPA, and BPA’s effects were assessed in ~3-week-old offspring. Subsequently, gravid females G. affinis (lecithotrophic) and 1-week-old offspring were exposed to 1 µg/L BPA (environmentally relevant concentration) for 1 month, with consequences evaluated between pre and post-natal exposed fries, and between 1 month-old BPA-exposed offspring and their control. Differentially Expressed Genes (DEGs) were obtained for the three comparisons. Although we found no DEGs between 1-month-old BPA-exposed offspring of G. afinnis and their controls, most DEGs were downregulated in the other two comparisons. Interestingly, in 3-week-old fries of H. formosa, those downregulated genes in BPA-exposed fry were mainly involved in immunity and development. In 1-month-old fry of G. afinnis, despite many downregulated genes may reflect the silencing of embryonic pathways in postnatal fish, others are involved in immunity, detoxification, cancer, cognition, and metabolic disruption, potentially due to BPA toxicity. Our findings suggest that prenatal BPA exposure can cause long-term effects in fish and that even environmentally relevant BPA concentrations can potentially impair the immune function and cognition, highlighting risks of BPA exposure during key stages of development in aquatic viviparous organisms possibly independently of matrotrophy.

2493: Landfall of hurricanes that form in the Atlantic Ocean has shifted earlier into the year over recent decades, and these early-season hurricanes will coincide with the reproductive season of many organisms. Due to flooding associated with these storms, species that rely on ground habitats for reproduction are particularly vulnerable, such as ground-nesting reptiles whose developing embryos would experience periods of seawater inundation and/or highly saline soils. For example, the brown anole (Anolis sagrei) inhabits coastal and island habitats prone to these disturbances, and their nests are often in areas inundated by seawater. Unfortunately, relatively few studies have considered the consequences of inundation or substrate salinity despite their potential impacts on embryo survival. The primary aim of this study was to test the hypothesis that saltwater submersion and subsequent development in saline substrate would negatively affect embryonic development because of the desiccating effect of the hypoosmotic condition of the eggs. We conducted a full factorial experiment with three submersion treatments (no submersion, freshwater submersion, and saltwater submersion) and two egg incubation treatments (sand mixed with freshwater or saltwater). Our results provide evidence that eggs rapidly lose mass when exposed to saltwater, and embryos cannot survive either saltwater submersion or incubation in a substrate mixed with saltwater. These findings have important implications for understanding how major storms associated with global change can impact reptile populations that inhabit coastal or island ecosystems.
