2494: In 2010, the Deepwater Horizon oil spill had a devastating immediate impact on the DeSoto Canyon and adjacent areas. As the spill occurred at 1500 m, deep-sea communities were among the first to be affected, followed by those in shallower habitats. Extensive research on the effects of the spill has been conducted on surface-dwelling megafauna such as sea turtles and marine mammals, in addition to coastal fisheries.  Deep sea benthic communities were studied following the oil spill, however elasmobranchs and teleosts, or the benthopelagic organisms, living at depths greater than 200 m, have been understudied. To address this gap, we investigated ecosystem-wide changes to deep sea elasmobranch and large teleost communities post-oil spill residing across a depth gradient from 200-2000 m. Through bottom longline surveys coupled with sediment sampling, community structure and any relative changes over time are described from multiple lenses spanning across an eight-year period. The overall community structure of deep-sea elasmobranchs and teleost did not deviate over the sampling period: however, there were variances on a species-specific basis influenced by depth and region sampled, indicative of unique community gradients. Whole community diversity trends follow similar studies of the deep sea, with a variable distribution of diversity (H’), catch-per-unit-effort, and species richness at shallower depths that stabilizes as depth increases. Sediment data support previous findings related to organic carbon flux following the oil spill and indicate the system is nutrient-dense enough to support biodiversity regardless of year and depth. Further sampling effort is recommended to identify small-scale spatial trends, especially as deep-sea ecosystems experience increased exposure to anthropogenic efforts.
2495: Fisheries independent surveys can be used to identify long term abundance trends in sharks and rays. For many species globally abundance data is lacking. Long-term ecosystem sampling regimes, using unbaited gear, allow analysis of species populations, identifying species-specific interactions, and determining environmental impacts upon study species over extended periods of time. The north-western Cape York region is a unique environment, and its elasmobranch species composition is not well understood. From 2016 to 2024, gillnet surveys for sharks and rays were conducted in the waterways of Mapoon (Port Musgrave, Ducie River, Wenlock River) and Weipa (Albatross Bay, Hey River, Embley River), in the Gulf of Carpentaria, north-western Cape York, Queensland.  A total of 916 elasmobranchs belonging to 37 species were captured. Factors that affect capture rates and distributions of elasmobranchs were analysed for the five most abundant species in the data set; ocellate eagle ray Aetobatus ocellatus, bullshark Carcharhinus leucas, winghead shark Eusphyra blochii, sicklefin lemon shark Negaprion acudentis and graceful shark Carcharhinus amblyrhynchoides). Environmental (depth, visibility, salinity, temperature, tidal state, time of day) and geographic factors’ influence upon species capture rates are examined using generalized linear mixed models, along with yearly abundance estimates based on CPUE, sampling methods and juvenile-to-adult ratios examined for the five study species. The implications of using these methods to examine the influence of the Queensland gillnet ban in 2027 are presented.
2496: The giant manta ray (Mobula birostris) was listed on the U.S. Endangered Species Act as a “Threatened” species.  In 2020, the Florida Manta Project was the first to describe the highly-developed coastline of southeastern Florida as a potential manta ray nursery habitat. Here, we provide updated results on the demographics of the nursery habitat, and attempt to define its boundaries using acoustic and satellite telemetry data. Since 2016, we have identified 212 individuals (52% resighted) in south Florida using in-water photo identification. Aerial surveys revealed that most (89%) manta sightings occurred between July and January across years. Additionally, acoustic (n=27) and satellite (n=40) tag deployments on both juvenile and adult mantas along the eastern coast of Florida highlighted both long distance movements and site fidelity. Taxonomic and genetic evidence suggests that manta rays in the Western Atlantic are a separate species (M. cf. birostris) and little is understood about the ecology and life history of this putative species. Understanding the spatial extent of this manta ray nursery habitat will facilitate management decisions of this threatened species in an area where juvenile manta rays are frequently harmed by vessel strikes and fishing gear entanglement.
2497: Species distribution modeling is often used to predict species’ habitats and how these may shift under climate change. However, these models commonly assume that all members of a species have the same environmental niche, which is problematic when applied over a broad environmental range, since local adaptation can lead subpopulations to have different optimal conditions. Here, we use a simulated dataset to develop a hierarchical modeling framework that can predict optimal habitat for locally-adapted populations of a widely distributed species. We apply this framework to occurrences of juvenile tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier), large marine predators with evidence for genetic differentiation between subpopulations. Our approach relies on generalized additive mixed modeling built on a joint likelihood framework that allows information-sharing between adaptive groups, unlike previous methods that either split data from each population into separate distribution models or pool into one without accounting for local adaptation. Using the simulated dataset, we test different model parameterizations, identify the optimal use of predictors, explore implications of inconsistent sampling across space, and assess the model’s specificity when inferring differences between adaptive groups. We find that models that include a variable representing adaptive subpopulation have better predictive power than models that do not. Model results for tiger sharks include population-specific predictions under climate change that account for local adaptation to different optimal oceanographic conditions. This model framework serves as a valuable first step toward accounting for local adaptation in species distribution modeling, representing important advances to fishery research and management in a changing ocean.
2498: Genomic variation within species is key for adaptation and survival in changing environments. Determining what factors influence that variation is thus an important goal for managing wildlife populations and conserving biodiversity. Amphibians are lacking from many comparative studies of genomic variation because they have large, complex genomes, and few studies have characterized genomic diversity across geographic space in a comparative framework. In this study, we generated new genome-wide sequence data for 46 frog species sampled across eastern North America to investigate the influence of historical processes and contemporary landscape on within-species variation. For two years (2022–2023), we launched a large-scale fieldwork effort across 30 states in the USA, producing >1,900 holistic specimens from >40 species, which are searchable via the Arctos collection management system and available for loan from the Museum of Southwestern Biology, University of New Mexico. We supplemented these samples with >900 frozen tissues through loans from 23 other natural history collections to fill in geographic sampling gaps. We used a double-digest Restriction Associated DNA (ddRAD) sequencing approach to generate genome-scale data for >2,600 frogs, with an average of 48 individuals per species. We use these data to map genomic diversity within species, identify potential ‘hot spots’ of diversity across species, and test predictions about the role of historical climate stability on current patterns of genomic variation. This resource will help address pressing questions about the determinants of genomic diversity, a fundamental component of biodiversity needed to ensure population persistence.
2499: Temperature is a critical environmental factor that profoundly influences the life histories of organisms, particularly ectothermic animals that rely on external heat sources for thermal homeostasis. This study explores the molecular evolution of temperature-sensitive ion channels, specifically TRPA1, on Neotropical frogs, a group of organisms facing the imminent threat of accelerated climate change. We generated RNA-seq data for 50 Neotropical frog species. We then isolated TRPA1 sequences and used Bayesian and maximum likelihood models to detect positive selection at different amino acids. We spatially visualized those sites under selection by performing 3D modeling of the protein. Finally, we compared our results with results obtained in other vertebrate groups. Preliminary findings show a novel insertion of approximately 15 amino acids in TRPA1 upstream of the transmembrane domain in poison frogs, suggesting possible adaptations to deleterious temperature changes. Furthermore, distinctive modifications in pre-S1 and linker, ARD, and pore regions are identified in poison frogs, suggesting possible behavioral consequences linked to temperature-sensitive pore opening. Further examination of TRPA1 sequences from different families reveals considerable variation in the ARK regions, which is important in temperature activation. Comparative analyses between TRPA1 pore-forming regions reveal conserved amino acid changes (I905L, I906M, S910T, R919H, E920D) in hTRPA1. These changes likely underlie the observed differences in temperature activation, as humans show sensitivity to cold temperatures and frogs respond to higher temperatures. This research provides an understanding of molecular adaptations in temperature-sensitive ion channels in Neotropical frogs, shedding light on their resilience strategies amidst the challenges of climate change.
